22719-old-fort-snelling-1819-1858:
Marcus L. Hansen wrote Old Fort Snelling, 1819–1858, a history of the famous frontier post at the meeting of the Mississippi and Minnesota rivers. The catalog record gives no year. Fort Snelling guarded the upper Mississippi, hosted fur traders and soldiers, and stood at the center of early Minnesota history.

The preface tells the book's own story: the work began as research at the State University of Iowa and was accepted as a graduate thesis in June 1917. At the urging of Dr. Shambaugh of the State Historical Society of Iowa, Hansen enlarged its scope, consulted many new sources, and rewrote the whole manuscript. The result is a documented history of the fort's first four decades. Hansen later became a leading historian of immigration, and his care with sources shows here.
aelian-works-hercher-1858:
Claudius Aelianus, a Roman-era Greek with a storyteller's ear, left two great stores of lore. Aelian's works, in Rudolf Hercher's 1858 edition, gather all that survives of him in one set. Seventeen books On the Nature of Animals stand first in the file.

Beside them sit the Historical Miscellany, a heap of short tales and facts, plus his letters and fragments. Bees, elephants, kings, and fools pass through his pages in bright, brief scenes. Naturalists mined him for animal lore; tale tellers mined him for plots. Hercher's edition is the full Aelian in one scholarly home.
allibone-critical-dictionary-english-lit:
Samuel Allibone, a Philadelphia bookseller and bibliographer, published Volume One of his Critical Dictionary of English Literature in 1858. It covers authors from A to J. The full work notices some 30,000 British and American writers.

Each entry gives the author's life, a list of works, and judgments gathered from reviews and histories. Forty subject indexes help readers find writers by theme, from poetry to voyages. Allibone labored for years among his own vast book collection. The dictionary became the great Victorian bio-bibliography, the first place to learn what an author wrote and what critics said of it.
arxiv-2511-20258:
Wang, Cheng, Zhong, Chen, and Zhou balance fast and slow senses in multi-modal learning. Their 2025 paper proposes MBCD for domain generalization. Models must work on unseen domains, not just training ones. Weight averaging usually helps by finding flat minima. In multi-modal setups it backfires early though.

Fast modalities dominate averaging before slow ones mature. The fused model then leans on one sense too much. MBCD starts with adaptive modality dropout in the student. Randomly muting strong senses curbs the early bias. A gradient consistency rule aligns branch learning signals. Uni-modal and fused gradients are pushed to agree. A weight-averaged teacher then distills fused knowledge back. Each single-sense branch receives cross-modal teaching. Convergence steers toward flatter, sturdier solutions. EPIC-Kitchens and HAC benchmarks tested the framework. Accuracy and robustness beat prior methods across settings. Balanced fusion survives domain shift better.
arxiv-2511-20658:
Ashlae Blum'e argues in 2025 that the pictures scientists use for sound quietly shape what they can learn from it. Waveforms, spectrograms, and editing screens modelled on recording-studio software dominate audio research, yet each carries design assumptions from the era and industry that produced it. Because a display steers how people group and connect patterns, Blum'e warns that tools built for older jobs may no longer fit today's research questions.

The argument walks through a long history of sound tools. It starts with the phonautograph of 1857, which etched sound onto glass, and the phonograph of 1877. It reaches the Fast Fourier Transform of 1965, the maths still underpinning digital sound processing. Studio software followed, from the Soundstream editing system of 1977 and the Fairlight CMI synthesiser of 1979 to Steinberg's Pro-16 in 1986, whose layout resembles modern editors. Blum'e urges designers to add dimensions back into sound displays, so analysis and creative work both gain.
arxiv-2511-21458:
Guilherme Inacio and four coauthors switch on a forbidden solar effect with an electric field, in a 2025 condensed matter paper. The bulk photovoltaic effect lets some crystals generate current from light with no junction, but only when their structure lacks a center of symmetry. Many layered semiconductors are centrosymmetric, so the effect is ruled out, unless something breaks the symmetry from outside.

Inacio and his coauthors bake a static out-of-plane electric field, a gate bias, directly into the material's quantum ground state using a Wannier-based Hamiltonian dressed by the field. Applied to molybdenum disulfide, the method produces a genuine shift current in centrosymmetric bilayers where none should exist. The response grows linearly at small fields, then saturates as the field weakens the coupling between bands. Polar stackings, which already respond, become tunable instead, and a Taylor expansion ties the whole picture to the third-order optical response.
arxiv-2512-00258:
Mixed polynomials involve both a complex variable and its conjugate, which complicates their geometry. Davi Lopes Medeiros, José Edson Sampaio, and Eder Leandro Sanchez Quiceno study the Lipschitz geometry of such polynomials in 2025. They work with two-variable polynomials satisfying a Newton inner non-degeneracy condition.

The authors investigate bi-Lipschitz equivalence, which asks when two singularities have the same shape up to controlled stretching. They show conditions under which families of perturbations stay trivial in a precise sense. Singularity theory uses such results to classify the possible local shapes of algebraic objects. Bi-Lipschitz maps distort distances by at most a fixed factor in both directions. Newton non-degeneracy ties the polynomial's geometry to its Newton diagram. The work is pure math, and its worth lies in clean lines. It tells us which forms can match, and which can not, when we stretch space in tame ways.
arxiv-2512-00458:
The method of image charges solves electrostatic problems by replacing a conductor with imaginary mirror charges. Farhang Loran and Saman Moghimi-Araghi, at Isfahan University of Technology, ask whether a curved mirror honestly reflects identity in 2025. Their setting is a multipole placed before a grounded conducting sphere.

Standard problems treat single charges near conductors, while multipoles have received less attention beyond the flat plane case. Multipole images reveal how the sphere distorts a structured charge distribution, not just a point. The study is a careful piece of classical electrostatics, useful for teaching and for boundary-value problems in physics. Grounded spheres are a textbook geometry, so the multipole extension is a clean next step.
arxiv-2512-00858:
Saiful Mondal and Ahmad Al Abdulaali study special classes of analytic functions in a 2025 math paper. An analytic function can be written as a power series, and its shape can be sorted into families. One family, lemniscate starlike functions, is defined by how the function's values relate to a figure-eight curve called a lemniscate.

The authors derive conditions on the power series coefficients that place a function in this family. Their tools include the Cauchy product of series and inequalities involving the Pochhammer symbol and the Gamma function. They also apply the results to special functions. Coefficient tests make membership in such families easy to check.
arxiv-2512-00958:
Vladimir Dzhunushaliev and Vladimir Folomeev build a charged object out of a wormhole in a 2025 physics paper. A wormhole is a tunnel-like shortcut through spacetime, usually an exotic idea. Within Einstein-Dirac-Maxwell theory, they study an asymmetric wormhole held open by a complex spinor field.

The spinor field has a bare mass near the Planck mass and gives the system its topology and an intrinsic spin. An electric field supplies the charge, and a magnetic field completes the setup. Their goal is a realistic classical model of charge, where charge and spin arise from spacetime structure rather than a point particle.
arxiv-2512-01058:
Youssof Abdullah, Violet Hart, and Moumita Das model how neurons fire in a 2025 biophysics paper. An action potential is the spike a neuron uses to signal, and voltage-gated sodium channels drive its rise. These channels come in several isoforms, versions with slightly different behavior.

Their conductance-based model pairs a six-state Markov description of sodium channels with a first-order potassium channel model. They vary the maximal sodium and potassium conductances and compare nine sodium channel isoforms. The stability analysis shows which settings let a neuron generate spikes reliably. Such models link channel mutations to excitability problems in disease.
arxiv-2512-01858:
Jakub Czartowski, Adam Sawicki, and Karol Zyczkowski extend quantum pushforward designs to approximate forms. Pushforward designs average quantum states or channels in a structured way. Exact averaging is often out of reach. Approximate forms settle for finite precision.

Using Schatten norms and Lipschitz arguments, they bound the approximation traits. Builds come from complex projective spaces, simplices, mixed states, and channels. Bounds tell users how close an easy build sits to the ideal. That helps in tomography and benchmarking of quantum devices. Projective builds are explicit, so a user can construct the design rather than merely know that one exists somewhere in theory.
arxiv-2512-02058:
Language models can be dressed up as personas, a man, a woman, a Muslim, a political supporter, and asked to answer as that person would. Tabia Tanzin Prama, Christopher Danforth, and Peter Sheridan Dodds test in 2025 how well such personas match real people in a low-resource setting, Bangladesh.

They compared human answers with those of eight model-generated personas on culturally specific questions. The models' shallow grasp of local context, culture, and emotion is the suspected weak point, and the study measures the gap quantitatively. Findings like these warn against using synthetic personas as cheap stand-ins for surveying real communities.
arxiv-2512-02558:
Yufei Xiao and Shangfei Wang work on predicting empathy, the felt sense of sharing another person's state. Most past methods read text alone, which misses tone of voice and facial cues. They also ignore extra documents that describe a scene and could enrich the reading.

Their 2025 method joins video, audio, and text in one multi modal system. Supervisory documents, holding privileged extra information, assist training as well. Richer inputs should help machines judge empathy in settings like counseling, education, and care, where missing a cue can change the right response. A judge who can hear, see, and read at once is far less prone to miss a key cue.
arxiv-2512-02658:
Teresia Stranden and five co-authors build a bridge between light flying free and light guided in chips. Free space beams are easy to shape into many spatial modes, while waveguides on chips are compact and stable. Joining the two worlds is key for larger multi mode communication networks.

Their multimode interface passes several spatial modes between the two domains at once. A good interface loses little light and keeps modes separate and clean. Such links could let chip based processors handle the rich beams used in high capacity optical communication and sensing. A clean bridge lets chip gear tap beams that roam free, which is how most light based links start out.
arxiv-2512-02758:
Klaus Jansen, Lis Pirotton, and Malte Tutas show that optimal bin packing can need a surprising variety of bin layouts. In the classical problem, items of a few different sizes must fill as few bins as possible. The support of a solution counts how many differently filled bin types it uses.

The authors prove the needed support can grow exponentially in the number of item sizes. Even an optimal plan may mix a huge range of layouts. That lower bound limits how compactly optimal packings can be described, guiding algorithm designers who compress solutions for huge inputs. Wide bins are not a flaw of one code; they are a trait of the task that plans must own up to.
arxiv-2512-02858:
Mahrokh Ghoddousi Boroujeni and three co-authors control noisy nonlinear systems with guarantees attached. Stochastic nonlinear optimal control seeks plans that minimize cost under random disturbances. The true expected cost is usually intractable, so practice averages over a finite sample of disturbance scenarios.

That empirical shortcut needs proof it will generalize to unseen noise. Their PAC-Bayesian approach comes with stability and generalization guarantees in the title's promise. Guaranteed control matters for robots, vehicles, and medical devices, where a plan that works only on sampled noise is not safe enough. A plan with a proof is a plan a board can sign. That mark of trust is what moves such plans from labs to streets and wards.
arxiv-2512-02958:
Rajat Adak and L. Sunil Chandran count cliques, the tightly linked groups inside a graph. For a simple graph, the key count records how many copies of a complete graph on t vertices appear inside it. Complete graphs, where every vertex joins every other, are the densest possible patterns.

Their generalized Zykov theorem extends a classic result about such counts. Zykov's theorem long tied clique counts to edge counts in extremal graph theory. A broader version gives sharper bounds for networks where dense clusters drive behavior, from chemistry to social graphs. Dense groups drive much of graph life, from pals to parts, so sharp counts for them pay rent in more than one trade.
arxiv-2512-03058:
How word pieces move inside a Transformer model is the focus here. Duy-Tung Pham and six co-authors study trained Transformers in this 2025 work. They look at self-attention, the step that lets each piece weigh the others, and at codes that mark word order.

The team treats the model as a system that flows over time. They describe how its paths settle in the long run. Knowing that behavior could help builders make models more stable and clear. It may also guide small changes that lift how well these models work. Model builders can use these long-run patterns to judge training choices with more confidence.
arxiv-2512-03158:
Sewage can reveal which virus variants move through a town. Adele Chinda, Richmond Azumah, and Hemanth Demakethepalli Venkateswara work on that task in this 2025 work. Wastewater checks give a broad view of health across a whole community.

The data are messy, with high noise, low virus coverage, and broken reads. Worse, there are no labels to train on. The authors use contrastive deep learning, which learns by comparing samples, to spot variants. Better tools could warn health teams earlier when a new variant spreads. Communities could gain earlier warnings than clinic reports alone can give, since sewage reflects whole neighborhoods at once.
arxiv-2512-03258:
New satellite data show the ocean surface in fine detail, plus noise. J. W. Skinner, J. Callies, A. Lawrence, and X. Zhang work on cleaning that data in this 2025 work. The SWOT satellite measures sea surface height over wide swaths.

The team isolates the balanced part of the signal, which reflects steady ocean flow. They use a Bayesian method based on Gaussian processes to fill the gap under the satellite. The method pulls out flow structures at medium and small scales. Cleaner maps help track currents, eddies, and ocean heat. Balanced flow is the part tied to currents, while waves and noise must be set aside first.
arxiv-2512-03858:
Shining light through a single cell and watching how it scatters can reveal the cell's dry mass, volume, and inner structure. Cael Warner compares the tools for interpreting such scattering in a 2025 computational physics preprint. The Born-Rytov approximation estimates a cell's effective refractive index from scattered intensity, polarisation, and phase, but its accuracy against fuller methods needed checking.

Warner benchmarks the approximation against an exact analytical solution, a finite-difference time-domain method on a Yee lattice, and a discrete-dipole method, all solving Maxwell's equations. Test cases cover a simple sphere and a tomographic reconstruction of a yeast cell, scored on accuracy, memory, and compute time. Against a commercial time-domain package, Born-Rytov and discrete-dipole approaches matched the yeast cell's far-field pattern better. The comparison gives experimentalists a practical guide to choosing a method.
arxiv-2512-04158:
The Higgs boson's mass is oddly light. Dark matter's favourite candidate happens to sit near the same scale. Maximilian Detering, Thomas Steingasser, and Tevong You argue the two facts explain each other. Their 2025 particle physics preprint links the hierarchy problem to weakly interacting massive particles, or WIMPs, the classic thermal dark matter candidate.

In their scenario, the Higgs mass is dynamically driven toward the WIMP scale, because the true vacuum lies near a phase transition boundary. That arrangement destabilises the Higgs potential just above the weak scale. Rescuing it requires the new physics naturalness expects: light fermions, heavy bosons, and a WIMP whose Higgs couplings set the boundary. A higgsino-like model shows the mechanism working. If the WIMP proves heavier than a threshold value, the scenario tightly bounds the Higgs mass and the stabilising physics scale.
arxiv-2512-04358:
Ao Xu and a team of co-authors built MAFNet, a network that judges depth from two camera views fast enough for phones. Stereo matching pairs points across left and right images to build a depth map. Older designs lean on heavy three-dimensional filters or slow step-by-step refinement. Both strain small devices and block real-time use. Their 2025 arXiv paper takes a leaner route built on two-dimensional filters alone.

MAFNet splits its cost data into high and low frequency parts and treats each with its own attention filter. Fine edges live in the high part, broad surfaces in the low part. A low-rank attention block then blends the parts with care for context. The result is a crisp depth map at real-time speed on modest hardware. That opens stereo vision to mobile robots, drones, and phones that cannot carry server-grade chips.
arxiv-2512-04558:
Yue Yu, Qiwei Di, and Quanquan Gu probe the limits of spending extra compute at answer time to make language models smarter. Test-time tricks include sampling many answers and keeping the best, or revising drafts in sequence. Their gains are real, yet their ceilings were unclear. Their 2025 arXiv paper studies a model where answers are drawn from a mix of reference policies, and proves the popular best-of-many rule is inherently short of optimal.

The authors then study a simple upgrade: reward-filtered sequential inference. Only generations with high reward join the working context, so compute piles onto strong candidates and weak ones fade. Theory shows this rule earns strictly stronger guarantees than standard test-time methods. Experiments across varied tasks back the math. The lesson guides labs that must choose where each extra unit of inference compute goes, a choice that now shapes both cost and quality.
arxiv-2512-05158:
Byung Gyu Chae reformulates a neural network design built on reentry — signals looping back into the network — as a continuous-time system of differential equations. In the Fast-Weights Homeostatic Reentry Network, a fast associative memory works alongside a global control that keeps activity near a set level, like a thermostat for the population. Casting the update rule in continuous time reveals the coupled system underneath.

The analysis shows the dynamics settle onto attractors organized by an energy-like quantity, forming ring-shaped structures. A study of the system's stability identifies a reflective regime in which the reentry produces stable oscillations rather than runaway growth or collapse. Unlike continuous-time recurrent networks, which stabilize through fixed wiring, this design holds steady through population-level gain control. Liquid networks adapt neuron by neuron instead. The result is a distinct class of self-referential dynamics that computes recursively without blowing up.
arxiv-2512-05658:
Pietro Ferrazzi, Aitor Soroa, and Rodrigo Agerri aim to make medical question answering by language models work across languages, not just English. Most systems borrow their knowledge from general models by distillation, which raises doubts about reliability. Their 2025 method instead grounds the reasoning in medical text drawn from Wikipedia. From it, they generate reasoning traces for questions from two known medical exam sets.

The traces number about five hundred thousand and appear in English, Italian, and Spanish. The question sets were also extended into Italian and Spanish. Used as examples in the prompt, or as training data, the traces lifted scores on medical tests inside and outside their home domain. Among models of their size, results reached the best reported level. The team releases the traces, the translated sets, the medical Wikipedia corpus, and tuned models. The hope is more open, checkable support tools for doctors in many languages.
arxiv-2512-05958:
Sara Patel, Mingxun Zhou, and Giulia Fanti tackle the money question inside generative search: who gets credit when the answer is assembled from other people's pages? Language model search engines read sources, then write. The fair yardstick, the Shapley value, costs exponentially to compute exactly. MaxShapley is their way out: a special case built on a utility that splits into a sum of maxima.

That structure makes fair attribution computable in polynomial time. On three multi-hop question answering datasets, MaxShapley matched the exact Shapley attribution's quality while consuming a fraction of the compute. It cuts resource use up to ninefold against prior methods at the same accuracy. The stakes are the economics of the open web. Search once paid in clicks. A credit system that is both fair and cheap enough to run is the missing plumbing for paying the sources the answers stand on.
arxiv-2512-06258:
Chaoyang Wang and eight co authors uncover a flaw in models that answer questions about images: they often land on the right answer by a wrong path. The model may know the facts it needs, yet it picks shaky or tangled chains of steps, so results jump around from run to run. Tests that allow many tries show the right answer is in reach far more often than single tries suggest.

The team answers with a two stage fix. First, the model is trained with rewards for neat step by step work and for right final answers. Next, it samples its own paths, grades them, and learns to favor the sound ones, while bad paths are kept in a store of hard cases to learn from. The work shifts the goal for these models: not just knowing more, but picking the sound route to what they already know.
arxiv-2512-06358:
Mingjia Li and six co authors tackle a stubborn photo problem: wiping window reflections out of a picture taken through glass. A single photo mixes the scene behind the glass with the scene bouncing off it, and past tools often guess the layers wrong, so they fail on real shots. The team reframes a large image editing model, built on diffusion, to reason about such stacked images.

They argue the core snag lies in the model's inner code, which was never built to read one picture as the sum of two layers. Their fix has three parts. An encoder is reshaped so the code honors how reflections add up. A learned text cue guides the model without vague words. A depth guided sampling plan branches early toward good results. On standard tests it set new best scores and held up on hard real photos.
arxiv-2512-06458:
Rishiraj Bhattacharyya and four co authors build a better way to check whether a sampling program really draws from the distribution it claims. Samplers sit at the heart of probabilistic AI, and a wrong sampler quietly poisons every result built on it. Known checkers were designed for worst case speed, and none could handle samplers over endless domains, such as the natural numbers, which arise in astronomy, finance, and network security.

Their checker adapts its effort to the instance at hand, so easy cases finish fast. The core is a new way to estimate the distance between an unknown distribution and a known one, using a trick called interval conditioning. That trick links the job to estimating probability mass for continuous cases. In experiments the new checker ran up to a thousand times faster than the best known rivals, opening routine checks for samplers once thought out of reach.
arxiv-2512-06558:
Md Mofijul Islam and seven co authors teach robots to understand pointing, not just words. When a person says that one there while gesturing, a robot in a shared workspace must fuse the speech, the gesture, and the scene to find the target. Data sets for this skill were small, one view, thin on gestures, and mostly indoors, leaving models brittle.

The team built Refer360, a large data set of spoken and gestured references filmed from many viewpoints, indoors and out. They also built MuRes, a module that sifts each input stream for its strongest signals and feeds them back into a pretrained model's features, sharpening the mix. Across four data sets, current models missed much of the embodied content, but adding MuRes lifted their scores throughout. The pair of data set and module gives the field a firmer base for human robot teamwork.
arxiv-2512-06758:
Zilong Wang and Shuai Li close a gap in the theory of learning in matching markets. In online matching platforms, one side, the players, does not know its own preferences and must learn them by trying matches with the other side, the arms, over many rounds. Under serial dictatorship, the arms share one ranking of the players. Earlier work set a lower bound on the regret any learner must suffer. The best known algorithm sat above it by a factor tied to the market's size.

The authors propose a multi level successive selection algorithm that peels the problem into layers, matching the structure of the lower bound. Their analysis aims to show the remaining gap, which ranged between the number of players and the number of arms, can be shut. Tight regret bounds tell platform designers the true cost of learning preferences while the market is already running.
arxiv-2512-06858:
Chayan Patra and co-authors try to make quantum computers more useful for chemistry by cleaning up the noisy data they produce. Their setting pairs a quantum machine with a classical supercomputer. The quantum side samples likely arrangements of electrons, and the classical side then solves for the energy of the chosen set. Noise corrupts many samples, so finding and fixing the good arrangements is the bottleneck.

Their workflow, called PIGen-SQD, adds a generative learning model that proposes further promising arrangements, guided by physics-based screening. Cheap estimates rooted in perturbation ideas steer the search toward the part of the space that matters most. Tests run on current IBM quantum hardware produced compact, high-quality sets of arrangements. Those sets cut the cost of the classical step while keeping chemical accuracy, even where electron interactions are strong. The authors pitch the method as a step toward dependable quantum chemistry.
arxiv-2512-07358:
Neethu Mohan Mangalassery and Abhishek Kumar Singh predict how atoms settle in high-entropy carbides, materials that mix many metals into one stubborn crystal. Finding the relaxed atomic structure normally takes first-principles calculations whose cost explodes with chemical complexity. Their edge-aware graph attention model is a neural network built for the job: atoms are nodes. Bonds are edges, and attention weighs each neighbor using both the atoms' traits and the bond's geometry.

The descriptors fed to the network are informed by chemistry and local structure, and the whole design ignores global orientation and position, as physics demands. Trained on carbides from simple binaries to full high-entropy mixes, the model proved accurate, quick to converge, and transferable across compositions. It is deliberately lightweight, with a small computing footprint suited to screening huge candidate lists.
arxiv-2512-07558:
Shimin Zhang, Xianwei Chen, and Yufan Shen wrote this 2025 machine learning paper with Ziyuan Ye and Jibin Wu. Training reasoning models with checkable rewards sharpens their thinking. The same training can also make a model too rigid too early.

When rewards push only toward proven answers, exploration dies down. The policy settles early and stops finding better routes to solutions. Many fixes stir up diversity at the level of single tokens. The authors argue the real action sits deeper, in the hidden states. Those latent dynamics carry a richer structure for steering the balance. Koopman operator theory gives them a linear view of that hidden motion. A new metric, Dynamic Spectral Dispersion, measures how varied the dynamics are. Their framework, ReLaX, uses that signal to govern exploration during training. Benchmarks span text-only and multimodal reasoning tasks. ReLaX beats token-level methods across that range in their tests.
arxiv-2512-07858:
Da Zhang, Bingyu Li, Zhiyuan Zhao, Yanhan Zhang, Junyu Gao, Feiping Nie, and Xuelong Li wrote this 2025 machine learning paper. Classifying time series matters in medicine, environmental monitoring, and motion tracking. Deep models read temporal patterns well but cost much, fear noise, and overfit small data.

Their model, FAIM, is a lightweight design built around the Mamba architecture. A frequency-aware block opens the pipeline with a Fourier transform. Learnable thresholds inside it suppress noise in the frequency domain. Global and local filtering are coupled element by element for depth. An interactive Mamba block then mixes information across scales. Fine detail and broad context trade places inside that block. Self-supervised pretraining rounds out the design before classification begins.  Robustness improves as a result. On many benchmarks, FAIM beats the state of the art outright. It keeps a favorable balance of accuracy and cost.
arxiv-2512-08358:
Jiahao Lu, Weitao Xiong, Jiacheng Deng, and colleagues, computer vision researchers, posted a study on arXiv in December 2025. Their system, TrackingWorld, follows nearly every pixel of a video in three dimensions from a single camera. Earlier trackers blur camera motion together with object motion, and they miss new moving subjects that enter the frame partway through.

The pipeline starts by lifting sparse two dimensional tracks into dense ones with a tracking upsampler. Applying it to every frame, and pruning tracks in overlapping regions, lets the system catch newly emerging objects too. An optimization stage then back projects the dense tracks into a world centered coordinate frame, estimating camera poses and three dimensional positions together. On synthetic and real world datasets, the system achieved accurate, dense three dimensional tracking. The authors present it as a step toward full scene motion capture from ordinary monocular video.
arxiv-2512-08558:
Kristof Verslype, Florian Kerschbaum, Cyprien Delpech de Saint Guilhem, Bart De Decker, and Jorn Lapon, computer security researchers in Europe, posted a study on arXiv in December 2025. Governments hold citizen data split across many agencies, and linking it could improve healthcare, catch fraud, and ground policy in evidence. Doing that linking without exposing sensitive records is the challenge their protocol solves.

Their tool is delegated private set intersection, which finds shared records across providers through a separate collector, revealing nothing else. Working with a real governmental data organization, they extend the method with composable outputs: encrypted payloads delivered only for matching records, and pseudonymized identifiers for safe handling. They prove the protocol secure in the standard model, against colluding providers and a possibly malicious collector. Earlier work had cut protocol costs but skipped these practical functions. With them in place, data linking is ready for public sector use.
arxiv-2512-08758:
Martin Burger and coauthors review learning based penalty method for inverse problems, with an emphasis on methods that can be explained and analyzed. Machine learning has become a popular tool for solving inverse problems in the last decade. Its basic theory, covering stability, approach, and the structure of learned penalties, are still young.

The chapter studies simple designs that remain tractable even in the infinite limit. For spectral designs, new results give error rates and highlight how smoothness in the training data shapes results. The authors also study robustness to hostile attacks and show that hostile training can itself act as a convergent penalty method method. Extensions to frame systems and filter based designs for energy based penalties are discussed. Carefully designed numerical tests reveal structural traits of those penalties, guiding more trusted use in practice.
arxiv-2512-08858:
Reima Ishii, Takaaki Fukai, and Takahiro Shinagawa present NecoFuzz, a fuzzing method aimed at nested virtualization in cloud hypervisors. Nested virtualization is widely offered by major cloud vendors, but it greatly expands hypervisor complexity and attack surface. Prior hypervisor fuzzing has not targeted the nested case, because generating useful virtual machine inputs with a huge state space is hard.

NecoFuzz builds executable fuzz harness virtual machines whose internal states sit near the boundary between valid and invalid. A rough model of the hardware virtualization specification guides that generation, since bugs often arise from unexpected machine states. Coverage of nested specific code is high on both major hardware platforms tested. The tool also found several earlier unknown flaws across three hypervisors, including two that received formal vulnerability identifiers. The work shows that specification guided, boundary focused generation is effective for this security critical code.
arxiv-2512-09158:
Tomas Buzek compares Riemannian and Euclidean ways to represent human gait. Accurate measurement of complex movement is essential for diagnosis and recovery, yet standard linear models rooted in flat geometry often miss curved dynamics and posture dependent links in the body.

Skeletal pose sequences are mapped onto a manifold of a special matrix family, using a log Euclidean metric to form shape feature vectors. Gait spread and smoothness are measured at slow, medium, and fast walking speeds. Flat metrics show spread rising in a straight line with speed, which reads as growing weakness. Manifold metrics instead show a curved upside down U pattern, with variance stabilizing at high speed. That suggests the motor system gains efficiency by following minimum effort paths at sprint pace. Manifold features offer stronger sensitivity to body motion efficiency for future diagnostic tools.
arxiv-2512-09358:
Gaku Omiya and Fumiyasu Komaki propose optimization methods that follow the geometry of the space where a problem lives. Many statistical models, especially exponential families, form dually flat spaces, a setting from information geometry where two natural notions of straight line coexist. The shape of the objective function and the shape of the space are closely tied there.

Their geodesic descent methods move along those natural curves instead of straight lines in raw coordinates. One update, following m-geodesics, directly optimizes the log-likelihood and can in theory reach the best-fitting parameters in a single step. The other, following e-geodesics, is easier to use when the parameter space has no boundary problems, since it avoids handling constraints explicitly. The main application is maximum likelihood estimation, finding the parameters that make observed data most probable. The authors prove the methods' key properties and confirm them in numerical experiments.
arxiv-2512-09458:
Sławomir Nowaczyk argues, in a book chapter on agentic AI, that whether autonomous AI systems are reliable is mainly a matter of design. Agentic systems are goal-directed, tool-using decision makers that operate in closed loops, perceiving, planning, acting, and checking. Whether such a system behaves reliably depends less on the underlying model than on how it is built.

Nowaczyk breaks the system into disciplined components: a goal manager, planner, tool router, executor, memory, verifiers, a safety monitor, and telemetry, joined by strict interfaces that validate and limit every tool call. He proposes a practical grouping covering tool-using, memory-augmented, planning and self-improving, multi-agent, and embodied or web agents, and studies how each pattern changes the failure modes. The guidance distilled covers typed schemas, idempotency, permissions, memory hygiene, runtime budgets and stopping rules, and simulating before acting in the real world.
arxiv-2512-09758:
Yuhao Zhou and Stavros Tripakis work on automating proofs in TLA+, a language used to check that system designs are correct. Writing these proofs takes deep expertise and much effort. Large language models have helped with other proof systems, but TLA+ proofs have a layered structure that makes direct transfer hard. The authors use prompts to have the model break a hard proof obligation into simpler sub claims, while symbolic provers do the actual checking.

The key move is to limit the model to producing normalized claim decompositions rather than full proofs, which cuts syntax errors sharply. The team also builds a benchmark suite of well over a hundred theorems, drawn from established mathematics collections and from inductive proofs of distributed protocols. Across that suite, their approach consistently beats the baseline methods they compare against.
arxiv-2512-09958:
Dinh C. Nguyen and colleagues propose QFLchain, a framework marrying quantum federated learning with blockchain for sixth generation networks. Federated learning trains models across many devices without gathering their data. Adding quantum devices promises faster learning and resistance to quantum era attacks. But future networks will be dynamic, decentralized, and data heavy, which strains the usual central coordinator. A blockchain offers a tamper resistant shared record for trustless collaboration.

The paper examines four pressure points for such a system. They are communication and consensus overhead, scalability and storage costs, energy inefficiency, and security vulnerabilities. A simulation based case study illustrates the design. In that study, QFLchain showed potential advantages over leading approaches in training performance. The article is a framework and agenda paper, mapping what must be solved before quantum federated learning on blockchains can serve real 6G intelligence.
arxiv-2512-10058:
Dani Roytburg and Beck Miller document a split inside the field that studies how to make artificial intelligence safe and good. Safety research centers on scaled intelligence, deceptive behavior, and existential risk. Ethics research centers on present harms, social bias, and production pipelines. The authors test whether the divide is structural, not just rhetorical, using bibliometric and coauthorship analysis.

Their dataset covers several thousand papers from twelve major machine learning and language conferences over six years. More than eighty percent of collaborations stayed inside one community. A tiny share of papers, about five percent, supplied most of the bridging links between the camps. Removing a few broker papers sharply deepened the segregation, showing exchange hangs on a handful of actors. The authors argue for shared benchmarks, joint venues, and mixed methods.
arxiv-2512-10658:
Wei Wang studies the smallest parts function, which counts, across all partitions of a number, how many times the smallest part appears. Partition functions like this one are famous for hidden patterns, congruences that hold modulo a prime and recurrences that tie large values to small ones. Wang's paper adds Euler-style recursive formulas of a new, generalised kind.

His recurrences express the function through Hecke traces of values of twisted quadratic Dirichlet series, tying a counting problem to objects from the theory of modular forms. As a corollary, he gives a closed form, modulo a prime, for the generating series along an arithmetic progression. The form is again stated in terms of Hecke traces. Those traces are taken for cusp forms on the full modular group. He also proves an incongruence result, a case where an expected pattern provably fails, which is often as telling as a congruence.
arxiv-2512-10858:
Dimitri von Rütte and co-authors chart how discrete diffusion language models scale. These models generate text by gradually uncorrupting tokens rather than writing left to right, and they may rival autoregressive models, but earlier work suggested they need more data and compute to match. Nobody had mapped their scaling behaviour carefully, and it turns out to hinge on the kind of noise used to corrupt the text.

Interpolating smoothly between masked diffusion, where tokens vanish. And uniform diffusion, where tokens are randomised, the authors ran compute-bound scaling studies with close attention to batch size and learning rate. All noise types reached similar losses for a given compute budget, but uniform diffusion wanted more parameters and less data, making it attractive when data is the bottleneck. They confirmed the prediction at scale, training a ten-billion-parameter uniform diffusion model, the largest of its kind made public.
arxiv-2512-10958:
Ao Liang and a large team introduce WorldLens, a benchmark for judging video world models that generate driving scenes. Such models can make streets that look convincing yet break physical rules or fail to support driving decisions. No shared standard existed for checking geometry, physics, and behaviour together.

WorldLens scores models on generation, reconstruction, action following, downstream tasks, and human preference. No current model excelled everywhere: systems with strong textures often violated physics, while geometrically stable ones behaved less faithfully. To match human judgement at scale, the team built a large set of human scored videos with written reasons. They also trained an evaluation agent on those labels to give scalable, explainable scores for future models.
arxiv-2512-11158:
Andrzej Czarnecki and Ting Gao review a subtle debate about spin effects in a uniform gravity field. Some calculations suggested gravity might separate particles by spin, in a pattern resembling the anomalous Hall effect seen in magnetic materials. The two problems are written with similar math, which made them look alike.

The authors explain why the resemblance misleads. Hidden momentum, a stored mechanical momentum in certain systems, changes the accounting in the gravity case. Drawing out the differences from the ferromagnetic effect, they argue that no spin Hall effect arises in a perfectly uniform gravitational field. The short review clarifies the recent papers and separates genuine gravity spin physics from mere echoes of similar looking math.
arxiv-2512-11358:
Fabian Wiesner and colleagues prove that the most common strategy for verifying quantum states from an untrusted source cannot be both fast and secure. In cut and choose verification, many copies of a state are prepared, most are measured to check quality, and a few survivors are trusted for use. Such checks underpin many quantum cryptographic protocols.

Their no go result covers all cut and choose approaches for arbitrary quantum states. The trade off holds for both stand alone security and the stronger composable security used when protocols are combined. The lower bound on security parameters scales so badly that the technique becomes effectively unusable in this general setting. The theorem supersedes the authors' earlier weaker bound and redirects the field toward verification strategies outside the cut and choose family.
arxiv-2512-11458:
Jingmin Zhu and fellow authors boost skeleton based action spotting for actions a system has never seen, without any retraining. Recognising actions from body joint movements rather than video helps with privacy and lighting, but zero shot systems must generalise to new action classes at test time. Their setup, Skeleton-Cache, turns inference into a quick lookup process.

A non parametric cache stores structured skeleton pictures, combining whole body descriptors with fine grained local ones. For each candidate action, a large language model supplies meaning based importance weights saying which descriptors should count most for that class. Fusing descriptor predictions under those weights lets the cache adapt dynamically to unseen actions. Tests on three standard skeleton benchmarks showed steady gains for several underlying models, in both plain zero shot and harder generalised settings. Code is publicly at hand.
arxiv-2601-07358: Raphaël Ruimy and colleagues wrote a 2026 arXiv preprint. The work covers pro-étale motives and solid rigidity. ArXiv posted the preprint in 2026 under its PAPERS collection. The authors introduce coefficient systems of pro-étale motives and pro-étale motivic spectra with coefficients. In any condensed ring spectrum and show that they afford the six operations. Over locally étale bounded schemes, étale motivic spectra embed into pro-étale motivic spectra. The work gives specialists a compact account of the problem and one proposed way to handle it.
arxiv-2601-07758:
R. Benbrik and colleagues ask whether a future muon-proton collider could reveal a heavy partner of the top quark. They study single production of a vector-like top partner. The setting is the type-II two-Higgs-doublet model, which adds a second Higgs doublet. Within that model, a produced top partner can signal charged Higgs bosons. Their 2026 preprint assesses discovery prospects at high-energy muon-proton colliders.

Muon-proton machines are proposed as a possible next step after current colliders. Knowing which signals they could see guides their design. A vector-like top is a favored target because many theories predict one. Tying its production to a charged Higgs gives two discoveries for one signal. The paper serves collider phenomenologists who map the reach of future machines. It links a concrete channel to a concrete model.
arxiv-2601-07858:
Nina Peire, Yupei Li, and Björn Schuller test whether continual learning methods suit EEG-based emotion classification. Generalizing to unseen subjects is hard because brain signals vary greatly between and within people. Continual learning promises progress by learning tasks in sequence without catastrophic forgetting. Regularization-based methods are the common baselines here. They include Elastic Weight Consolidation, Synaptic Intelligence, and Memory Aware Synapses.

Despite their popularity, these methods' suitability for EEG emotion data remains underexplored. The authors examine that gap directly. EEG signals are noisy and personal, which stresses any method that protects old knowledge by freezing important weights. Knowing the limits of standard baselines guides better method choice. The paper speaks to affective computing and brain-computer interface scholars. It checks a default assumption before the field builds further on it.
arxiv-2601-07958:
Surya Subramani, Hashim Ali, and Hafiz Malik build a varied corpus for catching fake speech and tracing its source. Speaker-specific anti-spoofing needs data that systematically vary how fakes are made. Progress was hampered by datasets lacking such variety. Their 2026 preprint introduces LJ-Spoof, a speaker-specific, generatively diverse corpus. It varies prosody, vocoders, generative hyperparameters, prompt sources, training regimes, and post-processing.

Tracing a fake to its synthesis pipeline helps investigators and platform moderators. Detectors trained on one generator often fail on the next. A corpus that varies the generation recipe stresses detectors properly. LJ-Spoof builds on the well-known single-speaker LJ Speech base. The paper serves audio forensics and speech security scholars. It supplies training and test material the subfield has lacked.
arxiv-2601-08158: Yuqing Zhou and co-authors present WISE-Flow, a way for service agents to learn from their own workflow history. Their 2026 arXiv paper notes that language model agents in user-facing services stay error-prone on new tasks. They repeat the same failure patterns and vary a lot between runs. Fixing failures with task-specific training or manual patches costs much and scales poorly. WISE-Flow instead induces structured experience from workflows themselves. The aim is a self-evolving agent that improves from past service runs without constant human repair.
arxiv-2601-08358: Hilde Hummel and co-authors test underwater acoustic target recognition with pre-trained audio embeddings. Their 2026 arXiv paper starts from ship noise, which adds to underwater sound pollution and risks marine ecosystems. Passive acoustic monitoring systems record years of sound across diverse soundscapes to track that impact. The authors probe what linear methods can extract from general audio embeddings. Their title gives the verdict shape: the features are decodable but not structured. The study guides marine monitoring teams choosing models for ship detection.
arxiv-2601-08658: Rachael Boyd introduces the geometric and combinatorial group theory of Artin groups. The 2026 arXiv paper gives a brief entry point to these groups, which generalize braid groups. A central topic is the K(pi,1) conjecture for Artin groups, a major open problem in the field. Boyd surveys known results on the conjecture as of January 2024. New readers get the main definitions and the state of the art in one short account. The survey serves graduate students entering geometric group theory.
arxiv-2601-08758:
Juntao Jiang and nine co-authors build a test for AI that reads health scans. Good care needs step by step thought, not just a fast call. New large models can think in steps and can also look at images. The team asks if that step thought helps on hard health image tasks, and where it fails.

Their test is called M3CoTBench. It holds health image tasks that need both sight and step thought. Each task lets staff grade the steps, not just the last call. That makes it clear if a model saw the right clue. A reader in health AI gets a strict test set. It can show which models think in a way a doctor can trust.
arxiv-2601-08858:
Tejaswini Bollikonda sets out trust scores for teams of chat models in strict fields. Such fields are health, banks, and law. In them, a wrong reply can cause real harm, and rules demand proof of care. One trust score for one model is not enough when models pass work to each other in a chain.

She gives a frame where trust scores shift as facts shift. A model that was sound last month may drift on new data. Scores must track that drift and flag it fast. The frame also ties scores to the rules of each field. A reader who runs AI in a strict field gets a plan to watch trust live, not just at launch.
arxiv-2601-09358:
Paul Pružina, Nathanaël Schaeffer, and David Cébron study fluid motion deep inside giant gas planets. Their 2026 arXiv paper deals with semi-convection in rotating spherical shells. In these regions, heat pushes the fluid toward motion, while a gradient of heavy elements holds it back. The clash of the two gradients drives slow, layered flows.

The team asks how such flows organize into layers and whether they can drive a dynamo. A dynamo is the process that builds a planet's magnetic field. Semi-convection may help sustain those fields, so its behavior matters for models of Jupiter-like worlds. The paper links fluid physics to the magnetic life of gas giants.
arxiv-2601-09758:
Austin Talbot and Yue Ke hunt for hidden batch effects in genomic tests. Their 2026 arXiv paper presents likelihood clustering to detect batch heterogeneity. Batch effects are a major confounder in genomic diagnostics, especially in copy number variant detection from sequencing.

Many detectors compare a sample's read depth against a reference built from its processing batch. That works only if the batch truly matches. Reagent changes, sample quality, or multi-site processing can break the match quietly. A wrong reference creates false variant calls or hides real ones. Detecting mixed batches early protects patients from bad calls.
arxiv-2601-09958:
Zhongyang Li studies spread on flat graphs that go on with no end. Each site is open with chance p. At low p, open clumps stay small. Past a key point, one vast clump can form. Two key points mark the start of spread and the start of one vast clump.

A known guess links these points to the end shape of the graph. The guess is the Benjamini Schramm claim. Li brings the end shape of the graph into the test. Flat graphs have ends that can be one, two, or vast in count. His work probes when the two key points must match.
arxiv-2601-10058:
Renpu Liu and Jing Yang show that free text can boost how models learn in context. A model can learn a task from a few shown cases in its prompt. But marked cases cost time and funds. Few can fit in one prompt. That caps how well the model does.

Raw text with no marks is vast and grows each day. Some of it links to the task at hand. The pair show that such text can help for sure, not just by luck. They give a proof based claim. It says raw text can lift in context grades past the cap set by marked cases.
arxiv-2601-10358:
Jay Nandy, Arnab Kumar Mondal, Anuj Rathore, and Mahesh Chandran shrink large graphs for fast training. Graph nets learn from vast nets of nodes and links. Training on the full graph costs much time and power. A shrunk graph can stand in for it. That shrink is named condensation.

Past shrinks lean on clean hand marks. Real graphs have few marks, or marks with noise. The team add fake marks to guide the shrink. Their plan is named PLGC. It makes a small graph that trains a net well. It holds up when true marks are thin or flawed.
arxiv-2601-10858:
Sébastien Kuchly and co-authors measure the mechanical traits of sea ice with fiber-optic sensing. Ice mechanics drive processes from meter scales to hundreds of kilometers. Polar ice is changing fast, so models need accurate values for thickness, density, Young's modulus, and Poisson's ratio. Distributed Acoustic Sensing turns a fiber cable into a dense line of vibration sensors.

With it, the team takes high-resolution readings of how sea ice bends and rings. Dense data can separate traits that sparse gauges blur together. Better trait values feed forecasts of ice drift, breakup, and shipping risk. The work shows how a telecom-born tool can serve polar science in a time of rapid change.
arxiv-2601-10958:
Christo Kurisummoottil Thomas and Mingzhe Chen set fundamental limits for quantum semantic communication. Semantic communication sends meaning instead of raw bits, saving bandwidth in multi-agent systems. Agents may hold very different inner representations, shaped by their sensors and AI designs. Perfect bit transmission then no longer guarantees mutual understanding.

The authors use sheaf cohomology, a tool from geometry that tracks how local data glue into global data. It fits the question: when do local meanings compose into shared meaning? Their limits mark what no quantum semantic system can beat. The work guides engineers who want agents that swap understanding, not just signals.
arxiv-2601-11258:
Pingzhi Tang, Yiding Wang, and Muhan Zhang argue that facts alone do not teach. Their 2026 preprint deals with large language models and new facts. A model's built-in memory is frozen at a cutoff date. New facts must be added by extra training runs.

The usual add-on is supervised fine-tuning on the new facts. That step can store the facts in the model's weights. Yet the model may fail to use them when asked. The team says the gap is one of skill, not storage. They inject skills trained with reinforcement learning instead. The skills teach the model to apply new facts in answers. That blend aims at models that keep learning over time.
arxiv-2601-11358:
Bernd Finkbeiner, Martin Franzle, Florian Kohn, and Paul Kroger guard runtime monitors. Their 2026 preprint deals with stream-based health checks. Such monitors read sensor streams and give a verdict stream. Safety-critical systems lean on those verdicts to stay safe.

Sensors are flawed, though monitors treat their data as exact. Calibration and measurement errors ride along with each value. Errors grow as the monitor's math runs on the stream. The final verdict can warp far from the truth. The team uses zonotope abstractions to track the doubt. A zonotope is a shape that bounds where values may lie. Tracking bounds keeps verdicts honest about sensor error.
arxiv-2601-11458:
Five years of Mini-EUSO results are summed up in this 2026 report. Mini-EUSO is a detector that flies on the space station. It is the first space-borne unit of the JEM-EUSO program. That program hunts extreme-energy events from orbit above Earth.

The detector has run on the ISS since October 2019. It seeks ultra-high-energy cosmic rays past 10 to the 21 eV. Such rays are the most energetic particles ever seen. The team logged more than 150 observation sessions. Total data come to near 750 hours over five years. The runs set a strict upper limit on the rare flux. That limit paves the way for bigger space observatories.
arxiv-2601-11558:
Nilesh Rijhwani bridges two fields of medicine with a DICOM frame. The 2026 preprint maps both data kinds in one view. Sound diagnosis depends on specialties working well together. One side reads scans; the other reads tissue under the scope.

Departments often use distinct systems and proprietary formats. That split hinders joint study of data that fit together. Separate viewers for each modality restrict collaboration further. DICOM is the standard frame for medical imaging data. Extending it to tissue maps could unify the two worlds. The frame supports joint mapping and merged views. Clinicians could then read scans and slides side by side.
arxiv-2601-11758: Arnab Das Utsa studies early signs of anxiety in posts on social media. Anxiety touches a vast share of people round the world. Yet large scale checks for it stay rare. Word use in posts may give a cheap way to spot risk at scale. His method rests on word traits that a human can read and check. He tests it with care for word bias and for clean splits of users. Tests cross more than one data set and domain.
arxiv-2601-11958:
Zefeng Chen and Darcy Pu ask if a fully agentic AI can nowcast stock returns. They run a state-of-the-art large model each day to rate each stock in the Russell 1000 index. The run starts in April 2025, when AI web tools gained live search.

Each stock gets a daily score for how attractive it looks. The team then check if those scores track later returns. Their data set is new in three ways, which they set out in the work. The study tests AI stock calls in real time, not on past data alone.
arxiv-2601-12058:
David Dos Santos Ferreira and Benjamin Florentin solve two inverse problems for a magnetic field case. They work on closed Anosov manifolds with a simple length spectrum. The data are the eigenvalues of a magnetic Schrödinger operator.

From those data, they recover an electric potential. They also recover a magnetic potential, up to a natural gauge choice. They use trace invariants of the wave flow as the key tool. Such results show how much of a system its spectrum can reveal.  Gauge choice is part of the result, not a flaw in it.
arxiv-2601-12158:
Isaak Mengesha and Debraj Roy measure growth and convergence at the mesoscale, between city and nation. Global gaps have shifted inward, with more spread now inside countries than between them. They use 8,790 harmonised Functional Urban Areas, which are labour-market regions.

Those areas hold 3.9 billion people and about 80% of global GDP. At that scale, national means hide the true dynamics of growth and structural change. The pair show how that hiding has grown. Policy based on national means may thus miss where growth truly lags.  City scale data show trends that nations hide in means.
arxiv-2601-12458:
Nils Dencker, at Lund University, works on preparation theorems in analysis. The classic results of Weierstrass and Malgrange let one rewrite a function in a clean local form near a point. Dencker extends those results to systems whose values are symmetric matrices. The systems in view are analytic or smooth, and they vanish to first order.

A symmetric version of preparation is more than a cosmetic change. Matrix valued systems show up in partial differential equations and spectral problems. A clean local form can turn a hard system into one that is easier to solve or classify. The work sits in several complex variables and related fields. It gives analysts a sharper tool for symmetric systems.
arxiv-2601-12558:
Alan Muniz bounds a key invariant of a foliation, a way of slicing a space into sheets. The invariant is the second Chern class of the tangent sheaf of the foliation. He works with foliations of codimension one. Chern classes are numbers that capture global twists in a geometric object.

The bound has a concrete form for projective space. For a foliation of degree d there, one part of the singular scheme must have degree at least d plus one. Singular points are where the sheets fail to be smooth, so their size matters. Bounds of this kind limit which foliations can exist at each degree. They are core tools in the classification of foliations.
arxiv-2601-12758:
Shenyan Zheng and five co authors work on pluralistic alignment of language models. As models enter high stakes domains, outputs should reflect a range of human perspectives. Reflecting only average preference flattens real disagreement. Achieving pluralism remains challenging, though. Existing approaches consider limited values or rely on prompt level tricks.

Prompt tricks lack real value control and representation, the team argue. Their system, VISPA, works by automatic value selection and activation. It aims to select fitting values for a context and activate them in the model. Pluralistic systems could serve diverse users without erasing minority views. The work speaks to alignment research beyond one size fits all preference.
arxiv-2601-13558:
Mehrab Beikzadeh and co-authors mine social and dating app text for risk and guard acts in men who have sex with men. That group faces high rates of sex passed ills and harm from drink next to peers. Text from apps they use may hold early marks of risk or of guard acts, such as test or safe sex talk.

The team uses ChatGPT and other text tools to tag such acts at scale. Auto tags could let health teams aim help to a person, not a crowd. Care is need, though, since app text is private and tags can err. The work weighs that gain and risk in one frame.
arxiv-2601-13658:
Arthur Amalvy and Hen-Hsen Huang work on pulling time-stamped facts from text for the web in 2026. Big knowledge bases like Wikidata need facts that say when things held true. Temporal knowledge graph extraction pulls such facts as quadruples: subject, relation, object, and time. The hard part is facts not seen in training data.

Their work, framed by its title as going beyond known facts, makes new unseen temporal knowledge. Fresh facts help test large language models without data contamination. Contamination occurs when test items leaked into training data. Clean tests give a truer read on what models know.
arxiv-2601-13858:
Guixiang Zhang, Yiyuan Wang, and Marius Hoggenmüller design drone interfaces to help people cross risky roads in 2026. The roads in focus have no crosswalks or traffic lights. Drones can watch traffic in real time from above. Past work shows drones can aid navigation and street-level tasks.

The team explores how a drone's interface should guide a person on foot. It could signal safe gaps, warn of fast cars, or show its intent. Good design must be clear at a glance in a tense moment. Such help could cut risk at crossings that cities have left unmarked.
arxiv-2601-14058:
Joe Barton and co-authors prove a splitting theorem for curved spaces that mimic relativity in 2026. The spaces are Lorentzian pre-length spaces with global non-positive timelike curvature. A splitting theorem says such a space must break into a product of simpler parts. The team also extends a key tool, the first variation formula.

That formula now works for spaces with any timelike curvature bound. The bound can be from above or below, and different from zero. Splitting results reveal rigid structure hidden in weak assumptions. They help math models of spacetime stay close to physics.
arxiv-2601-14358:
Christian Ecker, Florian Ecker, and Daniel Grumiller solve a gravity problem in closed form in this 2026 paper. Their topic is critical gravitational collapse, the borderline case where matter is just strong enough to form a black hole. Discretely self-similar solutions govern that borderline. Since Choptuik's pioneering work, those solutions were known only from numerical runs.

The team constructs an infinite family of such solutions in analytic form. The system is the Einstein-massless-Klein-Gordon system, gravity plus a light scalar field. Their tool is the large-D expansion, which treats the number of space dimensions as large. Readers get exact formulas where the field long had only computer output.
arxiv-2601-14758:
Injin Kong, Hyoungjoon Lee, and Yohan Jo look inside a model conversion in this 2026 paper. Post-training pretrained autoregressive models into masked diffusion models has emerged as a cost-effective strategy. It aims to overcome the limitations of sequential generation. Autoregressive models write one token at a time. Masked diffusion models can fill many blanks in parallel.

However, the internal algorithmic transformations induced by this paradigm shift remain unexplored. It is unclear whether post-trained masked diffusion models acquire genuine bidirectional reasoning capabilities. They might merely repackage autoregressive heuristics. The title calls the question a mechanism shift. The test is strict. It asks what the net does, not what score it gets, so a fake gain can be caught. Looks can fool. A smooth text may hide a plain trick, and this work digs for that gap. Readers get a probe of what truly changes inside a converted model.
arxiv-2601-15158:
Yuval Ran-Milo, Yotam Alexander, Shahar Mendel, and Nadav Cohen ask when reward alone can teach a transformer to reason. Their 2026 arXiv paper deals with reinforcement learning that pays only for final outcomes. Trained this way, transformers can start to produce chain-of-thought steps on their own.

Yet how sparse rewards steer the training to find such reasoning stays unclear. The authors study a single-layer transformer on a synthetic graph traversal task. The task cannot be solved without chain-of-thought but has a simple iterative fix. Their results hinge on the training data being right.
arxiv-2601-15458:
Emily G. Light, Morgan E. Prior, Noah M. Daniels, and Najib Ishaq speed up a core task in biology. Their 2026 arXiv paper deals with multiple sequence alignment, lining up many DNA or protein sequences so matching parts sit in columns. The problem has been studied for years.

Sequence data now grows faster than the classic tools. Fast and accurate aligners that scale to large datasets are in demand. The authors present MuSAlS, an alignment approach based on hierarchical clustering. It groups similar sequences first, then aligns the groups, cutting the work sharply.
arxiv-2601-15558:
Man Luo and a large team test language models as editors for empathy in a 2026 arXiv paper. Clinical empathy is essential for patient care. Doctors must balance emotional warmth with factual precision. They do so under heavy cognitive and emotional strain. The study asks whether a model can refine a doctor's written replies. The edit should raise empathetic tone while keeping the medical content intact.

The framing shifts the model's role. It is not the author of the reply, but a collaborator who polishes it. That keeps the physician's judgment in charge of the facts. The risk is plain too: a warmer tone must not soften needed candor. For health systems, such editing could ease the burden of patient messaging. Clinicians write many replies a day, and tone is hard to sustain.
arxiv-2601-15658:
Aiswarya T and Srijanani Anurag Prasad build a fractal function in a 2026 arXiv paper. Fractal interpolation functions pass through given data points. Unlike smooth curves, they keep detail at every scale. The team's version is a hidden variable function. It uses Edelstein contractions inside an iterated function system. The system starts from a finite set of data points.

Variable functions act as vertical scaling factors in their construction. That yields a generalized vector-valued fractal interpolation function. The authors also compute its box-counting dimension. Dimension measures how rough the graph truly is. Such functions model jagged data, from signals to rough surfaces. A construction with a known dimension gives users control over the roughness they create.
arxiv-2601-15958:
Zihao Wu and a large team clean a blemish from space telescope images in a 2026 arXiv paper. The work belongs to Data Release 5 of the JWST Advanced Deep Extragalactic Survey, JADES. Wisps are scattered-light artifacts in JWST's NIRCam imaging. They haunt certain detector regions. They contaminate observations at brightness levels that matter for faint sources. Photometry of dim galaxies suffers when wisps add false light.

The team removes wisps with nonnegative matrix factorization. The algorithm models the artifact pattern, then subtracts it. JADES images the early universe in deep fields. Faint-source science is its core mission, so artifact control is not cosmetic. Cleaner images mean truer brightness for the most distant galaxies the survey can see.
arxiv-2601-16258:
Sriram Akella, Abhijit Gadde and Jay Pandey build tools to sum join traits of firm states. Their 2026 preprint deals with states shared by more than two parts. Two part join is well known, but multi part join is far less clear. A class of sums, called multi invariants, gives join marks for such states. Past sums of them were slow and hard to run.

The team gives a fast code sum for firm states. Firm states, called stabilizer states, have a clean maths form. That form lets the code sum marks for big states. Fast sums open multi part join to wide study. The work aids teams who build and test quantum states.
arxiv-2601-16358:
Aref Farhadipour and three coauthors build a clean speech set for voice checks in many tongues. Their 2026 preprint, named TidyVoice, deals with voice ID tools. Strong voice tools need big, open sets in many tongues. Such sets are scarce, most of all for read speech. Read speech counts for guards against fake voice use.

TidyVoice draws its clips from the Common Voice pool. The team cleans and sorts clips for voice check use. A clean open set lets teams train and test on shared terms. Shared terms make scores fair to weigh side by side. The set serves voice guard work world wide.
arxiv-2601-16458:
Wenbo Guo and coauthors guard code packs with expert facts in a search frame. Their 2026 preprint deals with bad packs in NPM and PyPI stores. Such stores face more supply chain hits each year. Past guards rest on hand rules or thin data traits. Both miss new hit tricks as they shift in form.

The frame, named IntelGuard, joins expert facts to model search. Facts guide the hunt for hit signs in each pack. Search pulls proof spans that back each flag call. Clear proof helps teams act fast on true bad packs. The work aims to cut both miss and false flag rates.
arxiv-2601-16558:
Wang and a large team study a super flare on the RS CVn star HD 22468. Their 2026 preprint uses more than one wave band for the flare. The flare was first caught in hard X rays by the SVOM craft. RS CVn stars are close pairs known for strong flare acts. A super flare sheds huge power in a short burst.

Joint views trace the flare from birth to fade in each band. Band by band acts test how loops of gas drive the burst. Hard X ray catch at the start is a rare, prized fact. Such facts pin the first steps of the flare maths. The work adds a full case to flare studies.
arxiv-2601-16658:
Sima Amirkhani, Mahla Alizadeh, Farzaneh Gerami, Dave Randall, and Gunnar Stevens study couples and phone privacy. Their 2026 paper asks how partners set limits with each other. Phones are both private and shared tools in daily life. That mix makes shared rules hard to fix.

Past work looked at how partners share or block phone access. It also looked at hard talks about rules, and at spying. Far less is known about quiet ways couples cope. The authors focus on hints, habits, and acts done with no words at all. Their study shows how trust can rest on small signs. It speaks to design of phones and apps for pairs.
arxiv-2601-16758:
Mirko Legnini and Julian Berberich test if a key quantum tool can shrug off noise. That tool hunts the low energy state of a system. It blends a quantum chip with a plain PC in a loop. Noise in the chip can throw the hunt off course. Their 2026 preprint seeks proofs that the hunt still lands true.

The team gives bounds on how noise bends the path. They also show when the loop pulls back to truth. Such proofs matter for drug and stuff design by chip. Firms need trust that noisy chips give sound states. This work helps mark where that trust is earned.
arxiv-2601-16958:
Paolo Bassani tests if bent space forms can ape dark matter's pull. Dark halos are vast clouds that hold galaxies in spin. Their pull shows in how stars move and light bends. His 2026 preprint builds halo forms in a bent space-time. The base form joins space chunks in the LTB style.

He tracks how shape rules of the core math form dark-like wells. Those wells rise in plain gravity and in a tweaked kind. The tweaked kind is Hořava-Lifshitz gravity. If bent forms can ape halos, dark stuff may be less key. Or the ape may fail, which firms the dark case.
arxiv-2601-17058:
Wei Zhou and a team of seven co-authors survey how chatbots prep raw data for use. Raw data oft comes dirty, split, and hard to join. Prep cleans it, links it, and mines it for worth. Need for app-ready data keeps on the rise. Chatbot tools and agent kits now make prep more flex. Their 2026 preprint maps that fast field in full.

The survey sorts prep tasks and the tools for each. It weighs where chatbots shine and where they slip. Dirty data wastes much pro time in all fields. Sound maps help teams pick prep tools with proof. They also mark gaps for the next wave of work.
arxiv-2601-17358:
Zbigniew Fiedorowicz and Muthu Veerappan Ramalingam link two classic curve families in a broader way. One family is sinusoidal spirals, curves set by a cosine power law. The other is Lamé curves, closed shapes that range from ellipse to near-square. A known tie joins the squircle to the lemniscate. The authors extend that tie to full families.

They relate arc length of the spirals to area of the Lamé curves. The link also reaches Keplerian dynamics, the math of orbits. Such ties let one hard problem borrow answers from another. Geometers gain a cleaner map of special curves. The orbit link hints at uses past pure geometry.
arxiv-2601-17458:
Shuhao Zhang and four co-authors design real-time VR training for novice doctors. Surgical crises can overload a new doctor's mind. Stress inoculation training uses practice stress to build calm skill. VR can stage such crises safely. Current systems, though, give weak help at peak stress. Help must come in real time, at the moment of overload.

The team designs interventions for those peak moments. The goal is support that steadies choice, not noise that adds load. Better timing could turn VR drills into true readiness. Hospitals could train rare crises without patient risk. The work links stress science to interface design. It asks what help looks like when seconds count.
arxiv-2601-17658:
Bich Ngoc Doan and three co-authors map the relational harms of QAnon radicalization. Conspiracy theories erode trust and fuel polarization in public life. The authors look past that public toll. They study harm to friends and family of believers. That personal toll is often missed in large-scale research. Their title frames the work as going beyond the rabbit hole.

Mapping relational harm shows what belief costs at home. Strained ties, lost trust, and family splits are part of that cost. Support groups and counselors need such maps. Policy that ignores home harm misses half the picture. The work gives a name and shape to quiet damage. It can guide help for affected families.
arxiv-2601-18658:
Max Behrens and seven colleagues build a tool to help teams choose how to fit a health model: one fit for all, or one fit per person. A fit for all is firm and cheap but may miss what makes one case stand out. A fit per person can catch those traits but may chase noise. The choice is made in most wards by gut feel, with no clear test.

Their tool turns both fits into one smart net so they can be set side by side. The net shows where the per-person fit parts from the joint fit in a strong way. Those spots mark where a ward may need its own fit. A clear tool could help teams spend their fit work where it counts. It could also stop waste on fits that add no gain.
arxiv-2601-18958:
Ramón Herrera and Carlos Ríos rebuild the early universe's fast growth phase inside a modified gravity theory. The theory, Einstein-Gauss-Bonnet gravity, adds extra terms to Einstein's rules. The pair work backward: given measures of how smooth the early cosmos was, they rebuild the background values that must have held.

Two key numbers guide the rebuild, both tracked against how much the cosmos grew. Fresh data from the Atacama Cosmology Telescope set the test the rebuild must pass. The work shows which forms of this gravity can still match what the sky shows about the first burst of growth.
arxiv-2601-19058:
Arantha Ranu shows a classic bound can break when the rules soften just a bit. The Gibbs inequality says a certain ratio stays trapped between two positive bounds. It holds for steady states of potentials that meet a smoothness test called Hölder continuity, on shift spaces.

For merely continuous potentials, Ranu shows the bound can fail. The gap between the two smoothness levels turns out to matter a great deal. Results of this kind map the true edge of theorems in dynamics, telling users exactly which assumptions carry the weight.
arxiv-2601-19158:
Qijiong Liu and ten co-authors squeeze user histories so generative recommenders can run in real time. Such recommenders get better as they read longer histories of what a user did. But reading long histories live is costly, which blocks their use in fast feeds.
