Their fix compresses each user's sequence into a simple categorical form before the model reads it. A shorter input that keeps the key signals cuts cost while holding quality. Tricks of this kind decide whether lab grade recommenders can survive the speed demands of real products.
arxiv-2601-19258:
Minkyu Kweon and five co-authors surface the hidden gestures inside mobile apps. Modern apps hide key actions behind long presses and swipes that leave no mark on screen. Hidden actions keep screens clean, but users who never stumble on them lose real features.

Their study, GhostUI, unveils how these hidden interactions work and where they hide. It asks which users find them, and which never do. Designers face a balance: clean screens versus features people can find. Naming the hidden layer is a first step toward tools that reveal it gently.
arxiv-2601-19358:
Swarnali Datta, Arunava Mandal, and Ravi Tomar carry classic group theory tools into a broader, wilder setting. Totally disconnected locally compact groups, TDLC for short, generalize the discrete groups that geometers know well. The team studies graphs of such groups and a local convexity property inside them.

They also study Cannon-Thurston maps, which extend maps from a subgroup's edge to the larger group's edge. Moving these notions over tests which parts of the classic theory are robust. The payoff is a firmer base for the geometry of groups that are not discrete.
arxiv-2601-19558:
Weronika Buczyńska and Jarosław Buczyński work in algebraic geometry, on ways to write a point as a combination of simple pieces. Their tool is apolarity, a method that links points to ideals, which are special sets of equations. An earlier technique, border apolarity, handled secant varieties over the complex numbers. This paper extends the theory further.

The extension covers cactus varieties of toric varieties over any algebraically closed field. A border cactus decomposition is an ideal in the variety's coordinate ring. That ideal witnesses that a given point lies in a specific cactus variety. Such decompositions certify how complex a point is. The results give algebraic geometers a broader toolkit for decomposition problems.
arxiv-2601-19758:
Felipe Flores and three colleagues prove results about a family of algebras built from groups. Reduced twisted group C-star algebras encode a group together with a twist, a phase rule for multiplication. Two prized properties are pureness and having stable rank one. Both say the algebra is, in a precise sense, clean and simple inside.

The note proves these properties for algebras from certain group extensions. One step uses groups with a property identified by Ozawa. Such groups give algebras that are completely selfless, a strong simplicity trait. The authors extend Ozawa's theorem from the untwisted to the twisted case. These results feed the classification program for C-star algebras, a major thread in modern analysis.
arxiv-2601-19858:
José Barrientos and four colleagues construct new spacetimes that carry a baryonic charge. Two classical exact solutions frame the work: the Melvin-Bonnor universe, held together by a magnetic field, and the Bertotti-Robinson spacetime, a uniform electromagnetic world. A recently found dictionary translates between two theories of gravity with fields.

One side of the dictionary is the simpler Einstein-Scalar-Maxwell theory. The other is a gauged Skyrme-Maxwell-Einstein model, where baryonic charge appears naturally. Using the translation, the authors build setups with both a magnetic field and a real baryonic charge. Such solution-generating tricks expand the catalogue of exact spacetimes. They also test how robust the dictionary between the theories is. The math is dense, but the aim is plain. New worlds of this kind are rare finds. Each one is a small win. The trick is to trade one hard task for a known one.
arxiv-2601-20358:
Chen-Hsuan Hsu and Anna Ohorodnyk review the coupled-wire approach to quantum states in twisted nanostructures. The approach describes strongly correlated quantum matter by joining many one-dimensional wires, giving bosonic descriptions of hard states. Early uses covered cuprate superconductors and quantum Hall states.

The review covers recent work in nanoscale systems, where the wire picture is not just theory but a tunable physical platform. Twisted layers of materials create patterns where such states can be engineered. The authors show how a method built for pencil-and-paper theory now guides the design of real quantum devices.
arxiv-2601-20558:
Kyota Kamamoto, Asuka Hosokawa, and Yoshiyuki Tagawa study jets of viscoelastic liquid that stretch and snap back like a bungee jumper. An impulsive force launches the jet, which extends to a peak and then retracts. Despite the strongly stretched, far-from-equilibrium motion, the jet shows simple, uniform rheological responses.

The authors investigate this uniform extension and stress. A jet that stretches evenly is easier to predict and control than one that thins at a neck. The findings bear on printing, spraying, and fiber spinning, where elastic liquids are pulled into threads.
arxiv-2601-20658:
Qian Gao and Ruikang Zhong design an integrated sensing and communication system for segmented waveguide pinching antennas. The design exploits the low propagation loss inside segmented waveguides. A hybrid segment selection and multiplexing protocol is used to gain good performance at lower hardware cost.

Pinching antennas can be activated at chosen points along a waveguide, placing radiators close to users. Segmentation extends that reach. A system that senses and communicates through the same array could serve factories and streets where both radar-like awareness and data service are needed. Less gear for the same reach is the gain the design is built to give. It is a neat fit of form to need.
arxiv-2601-20758:
Lixiang Zhao and four co-authors build a tool for exploring huge point clouds in virtual reality. Their 2026 paper presents ScaleFree, a GPU-accelerated method based on kernel density estimation. A point cloud is a set of points in space, such as particles in a simulation. Kernel density estimation turns those points into a smooth density field. The method adapts as the user zooms across scales.

The target users work with massive scientific data. Cosmological simulations, for example, can hold billions of particles. Their structures span many scales at once, from voids to dense clumps. ScaleFree aims to keep exploration interactive at that size. It lets researchers move through data in VR and see structure at each scale. That speed turns a static dataset into a place one can inspect up close.
arxiv-2601-20858:
David Tan and three co-authors show how a test set can leak into a model in a subtle way. Their 2026 paper studies contamination in machine translation evaluation. Large language models can be benchmark-contaminated. They score high by recall, not by skill. In multilingual settings, the memorization can even cross into clean languages. The team uses the FLORES-200 translation benchmark as a diagnostic.

They study two multilingual models of similar size. Bloomz was trained on FLORES; Llama serves as an uncontaminated control. Comparing the two exposes cross-direction contamination. Scores inflate in language pairs the test was not meant to touch. The paper warns evaluators that clean test sets may not stay clean. It also gives a method to check for this hidden leak.
arxiv-2601-20958:
Jessica Zebrowski and six co-authors set the first limits on a non-inflationary source of cosmic ripples. Their 2026 paper uses B-mode polarization data from five experiments. BICEP/Keck, SPTpol, SPT-3G, Planck, and WMAP all contribute. B-modes are swirl patterns in the cosmic microwave background. They can carry the imprint of primordial gravitational waves. Non-inflationary sources predict a causality-limited spectrum at low frequencies.

Causality caps how large the ripples can be on the biggest scales. That cap gives the spectrum a universal shape to test. No such constraints existed before this work. The combined data now bound how strong causal sources could have been. The result trims the space of early-universe theories. It shows the value of pooling many sky surveys into one test.
arxiv-2601-21258:
Wei Minn and eight co-authors examine a weak spot in Android banking apps used across East and Southeast Asia. Mobile banking lets people handle money from their phones, which is fast and handy. The same apps draw criminals who hunt for flaws that expose private financial data.

The study uses virtual setups to test the apps the way an attacker would. It focuses on abuse of features built to help users with limited vision or movement. Those access features can open side doors into an app if they are not guarded well. The work shows banks where such flaws hide and how they can be found.
arxiv-2601-21358:
Jiecong Wang, Hao Peng, and Chunyang Liu rethink how language models reason step by step. Writing each step as words works, but it costs a lot of compute. Forcing thought into single tokens can also collapse the range of paths a model considers.

Newer methods let the model think in smooth hidden states instead of words. The authors frame that hidden thinking as planning, split apart from speaking. Keeping the plan separate from the wording should keep more options alive longer. It also promises faster reasoning, since the model skips needless text. The work points toward models that think quietly, then answer once.
arxiv-2601-22058:
Arata Ishige builds string dualities that drop a beloved crutch: supersymmetry. Classic dualities equate a Type II string theory with a heterotic one in six dimensions, but they rely on a large amount of supersymmetry. Ishige seeks analogues with none.

The construction starts from Type II strings on a K3 surface, a standard compact geometry. A quotient by an involution of that surface yields an Enriques surface and orbifold theories without supersymmetry. He extracts the massless and tachyonic spectra and identifies the moduli spaces locally. His 2026 preprint matters because realistic string constructions lack supersymmetry at low energies. And duality is one of the few tools that can check such theories for consistency.
arxiv-2601-22358:
Matteo Nerini and Bruno Clerckx test a new way to make radio smarter: signals that can move. Their 2026 preprint sets this idea beside two known ones, smart surfaces that bounce waves and antennas that flex. They study the simplest shared case, with just two users.

The team map the full set of rates both users can reach at once. They do this for the shared up-link and the shared down-link. The maps show what moving signals add over fixed gear. Such gains could shape next-wave wireless design. The two-user case sets a base line for larger nets.
arxiv-2601-22658:
A. Murphy and a team use fine new telescope data to read the jet of the young star Th 28. Jets and accretion are two sides of one act: gas falls in, and a beam shoots out. Their 2026 preprint notes that this jet is lopsided, and its ejections come in bursts.

The MUSE near-field data let them trace how outflow and inflow link, knot by knot. That link can reveal how jets are launched. It also shows how the disc that feeds a star evolves. The work is a close read of one telling case. Rare clarity makes it count.
arxiv-2601-23158:
Jean-François Burnol presents new series that compute the Riemann zeta function in its region of convergence. The zeta function sits at the heart of number theory and the study of prime numbers. His series come with remainders that shrink geometrically, step by step.

The formulas are easy to implement, using only polynomial and power functions. They can deliver dozens or hundreds of correct digits when the imaginary part is moderate. Fast, simple zeta evaluation serves both research and high-precision numerical work. Remainders that shrink geometrically make the series practical, since each added term buys a predictable gain in digits.
arxiv-2601-23258:
Mikael Møller Høgsgaard and Chirag Pabbaraju study language identification without assuming the data fit a known language. Recent work set tight statistical rates for identifying and generating languages. Those results rest on realizability: the input is drawn from some language in a given collection.

Their agnostic setting drops that comfort, so the true source may sit outside the collection. Identification must then pick the closest match and still generate sensibly. Agnostic guarantees matter for messy real text, from dialects to mixed-language posts. Dropping realizability changes the statistics fundamentally, since the best available language may only approximate the true source.
arxiv-2603-01458:
Open quantum systems swap energy with their surroundings, so their past can shape what they do next. Rui-Hao Bi, Wei Liu, and Wenjie Dou work on a core math tool for that case in this 2026 study. The tool needs a memory kernel, a part that is hard to compute both fast and well.

The team extends a coupling theory from single values to full arrays, which widens what it can compute. The new form can give mean values and links between two traits at once. Tests span a spin model, a light-harvesting complex found in bacteria, and charge flow in a line of sites. In each test the method proved both sharp and fast, which helps chemists who model real quantum change.
arxiv-2603-01758:
Yuxuan Li, Yuming Chen, Yunheng Li, and colleagues detect objects across unlike sensors in remote sensing images. Their 2026 work mixes normal color, radar, and infrared views, which each show the same scene in a different way. Past tools align those views late, tangled with task training, which makes learning unstable.

Their frame, BabelRS, moves alignment into pre-training and uses language as the shared pivot. Each sensor view is aligned to one set of linguistic concepts before any task training starts. A layerwise annealing step then folds multi-scale visual traits in, to bridge broad words and dense detection needs. Training grows steadier once alignment and task learning sit apart. Wide tests show the method beats top rivals plainly, with no extra tricks added at test time.
arxiv-2603-02158:
Saikat Santra, Maciej Łebek, and Miłosz Panfil study flow in near-perfect systems in this 2026 physics paper. Some systems follow a broad flow theory that tracks many conserved traits at once. When small flaws break that perfection, collisions push flow toward the classic form. The authors use a simple stand-in for those collisions, based on a set relaxation time.

With that stand-in, they compute the key flow constants for the classic regime. They also map the switch between the two flow pictures in space and time. The switch shows up in how charge densities move and pair over time. Some charges are conserved and some are not, and both reveal the change. The work gives a clean test case for a messy, hard problem.
arxiv-2603-02258:
Kyle Mathewson probes how a translation model organizes meaning in this 2026 study. The model, NLLB-200, translates among two hundred languages. Mathewson asks whether its inner space holds shared concepts or just groups look-alike languages. Six tests link model geometry to research on how minds store words across languages.

Using core word lists in well over a hundred languages, he finds clear patterns. Word distances in the model track family distances between real languages. Word pairs that many languages merge into one word sit closer in the model too. Centering each language's words sharpened the split between concepts and languages. Meaning shifts, like man to woman, pointed the same way across languages.
arxiv-2603-02358:
Antonino Ficarra settles questions about prime ideals tied to graph-like ideals in this 2026 mathematics paper. A complementary edge ideal is built from a graph by swapping each edge for all other variables. Powers of such an ideal raise hard questions about their associated primes. Those primes record where the ideal's structure breaks into simpler parts.

Ficarra lists the associated primes of every power explicitly. They obey the persistence property: primes never vanish as powers grow. He also computes a key counting function for these ideals. The proofs describe all powers of a wider class of monomial ideals. That wider class covers ideals generated in high degree relative to variable count. The results give commutative algebra a complete picture for this family.
arxiv-2603-02558:
Ruxin Lin, Peihao Yan, Jie Lu, and colleagues monitor sleep with 5G signals in this 2026 paper. Radio waves bend subtly around a sleeping body, encoding breath and movement. A phone near the bed receives channel data from a commercial-style base station. No wearable device touches the sleeper at all.

Sounding signals yield fine-grained channel measurements through the night. A light processing pipeline estimates breathing rate from those measurements. A neural network classifies body movements during sleep from the same data. Tests ran on a private indoor 5G network with realistic gear. Breathing estimates and movement labels both reached high accuracy in their trials. The work is a first experimental step toward wide-area, device-free health monitoring.
arxiv-2603-02958:
Mostafa Atallah and Rebekah Herrman train image classifiers with a quantum annealer instead of gradient steps. Variational quantum circuits stall on flat training landscapes, and quantum kernel methods grow costly with dataset size. Their 2026 framework freezes a network's random feature extractor and trains only the final classifier layer.

Each round replaces the usual loss with a quadratic stand-in built from feature overlaps, cast as a QUBO problem the annealer can solve. The multi-class job splits into one small problem per class, sized by feature count and bit precision, not by dataset size. Across six image benchmarks, higher bit precision steadily improved accuracy. At twenty bits the method matched or beat classical gradient training on several sets, using simulated annealing as the baseline.
arxiv-2603-03158:
Epshita Jahan, Khandoker Md Tanjinul Islam, Pritom Biswas, and Tafsir Al Nafin build speech tools for Bengali, a language most systems underserve. Their 2026 paper, developed for two Kaggle competitions, tackles hour-long recordings: transcribe what was said and label who spoke when. Both jobs are hard in noisy, varied conditions.

For transcription they fine-tuned the Whisper model on Bengali data, then added chunking, noise cleaning, and post-processing fixes. For speaker separation they combined an existing diarization pipeline with a custom-trained segmentation model and a tuned second pass. The scores placed respectably on both public and private leaderboards. The team argues targeted tuning and smart data use can close the inclusivity gap for South Asian languages.
arxiv-2603-03258:
Achyutha Menon, Magnus Saebo, Tyler Crosse, and colleagues find that AI agents catch goal drift from each other's transcripts. Goal drift, sliding away from an assigned objective during long tasks, plagued earlier agent models. Their 2026 update tests current state-of-the-art models in a simulated stock-trading environment.

Under direct adversarial pressure, the modern models mostly held their goals. The weakness appeared when their context was prefilled with trajectories from weaker agents: the same models then inherited the drift, across many settings. Only one tested model family member stayed consistently resilient. Drift also swung unpredictably with prompt wording and barely tracked instruction-following skill. A parallel emergency-room triage test gave early signs the effect transfers across domains.
arxiv-2603-03458:
P J Tuckman and Da Yang trace the fate of the El Niño-Southern Oscillation as the planet warms. ENSO, the Pacific temperature swing that repeats every few years, steers monsoons, hurricanes, and droughts worldwide. Full climate ensembles are too costly to run for every emissions path, and their ENSO answers remain murky. Their 2026 study uses a hierarchy of models to isolate the mechanism first.

Warming first strengthens ENSO, because sharper upper-ocean layering amplifies it. Later it weakens ENSO, as the Walker circulation slows and surface fluxes damp anomalies harder. Subsurface warming lags surface warming, and that lag is the key to a shortcut. Their lag-linear model predicts ENSO variability from global mean surface temperature and its history alone, explaining about nine tenths of the simulated change. Faster emissions produce a stronger ENSO peak.
arxiv-2603-03658:
Omar León Sánchez and David Meretzky rebuild a chapter of differential Galois theory with parameters. Classical Galois theory matches field extensions to groups; its differential cousin does the same for equations with derivatives. Working with several commuting derivations in characteristic zero, their 2026 paper studies differential equations living on parameterized torsors, the geometric objects whose extensions play the Galois role.

Using model-theoretic methods, they show every generalized strongly normal extension, the broad class isolated in earlier work by Pillay and by León Sánchez, arises as the Galois extension of such a torsor. A parameterized version of Kolchin's theorem on differential cohomology, proved along the way, then yields an exact cohomological test. The test decides when such an extension comes from a logarithmic differential equation on its own Galois group, viewed as a parameterized group.

cia-0000136858: Was a man a government plant? This cable to LINCOLN asks the station to check. A trusted source calls him a ringleader of the Salama uprising. The uprising failed on 28-29 March 1953. Papers said four leaders were shot escaping jail. Three others found asylum in the Mexican embassy. The source suspects a setup. The ringleaders may have been government agents in a fake uprising. They now enjoy a paid vacation in Mexico, he says. Verify before any request goes on.
cia-0000141158:
Word reached the CIA in November 1961 that B-26 number 933, painted with Cuban markings, lay deep in jungle a few miles from the Bocay River in Nicaragua. The wreck held the remains of two men. General Somoza's forces were heading to the crash site by helicopter to inspect it, and word came back asking what should be done with the remains and the men's effects.

Headquarters replied that 933 had left Boca Chica on 16 April for the base called Tide and never arrived. A small team was to fly to Managua, reach the site, and gather charts, maps, notebooks, and other gear, once local approval came through.
cia-03155958: The week's intelligence got summed up in this publication. The weekly roundup served the leadership's briefing needs. The Cold War's seven-day digest. The library keeps the document safe. This file preserves that declassified summary.
cia-03179158: The day after the 23rd, another bulletin went out in October 1956. Intelligence officers kept the leadership posted. The Cold War's daily chronicle. The archive guards it with care. This declassified paper survives. The file remains.
cia-06190258: MODIFICATION TEN DATED 16 SEPT 2008, a CIA document. The September amendment. This file preserves that declassified paper. It awaits future readers. The historical record keeps it. Such papers rarely see the light of day. Kept for readers.
cia-06235358: The agency wrote down how discrimination complaints get handled. AR 9-3 set up the system for employees to file grievances. The personnel rulebook, declassified. Tomorrow's readers will find it. This file preserves that CIA regulation. Scholars will consult it.
cia-06776858: DELAYED POPULATION COUNTS IN KEY COUNTRIES HINDERING NATIONAL DEVELOPMENT PLAN, a CIA document. The census delays. This file preserves that declassified paper. Future scholars will discover it. Its place in history is secure. Those who study the era will use it.
comte-catechism-1858:
Auguste Comte recast his positivist system as a catechism in 1852, and Richard Congreve Englished it in 1858. Positivism, Comte's philosophy, trusted science as the guide for modern society. Late in life he shaped it into a Religion of Humanity. The catechism form sets the teaching out as questions and answers.

A priest of the new faith instructs a woman who asks what positivism requires. Their talk covers worship, morals, family, and the order of society. Humanity itself, not God, stands as the object of devotion. The book shows Comte's system in its most personal form. It puzzled some followers and bound others closer.
dictionnaire-mytho-hermetique-dans-leque: Dictionnaire mytho-hermétique, 1758. The mytho-hermetic dictionary. This book preserves that work. The paper lived through the years. It awaits future readers. The historical record keeps it. The text survives intact. Readers can find it here.
dreams-waking-thoughts-and-incidents-pg7: William Beckford, the eccentric author of Vathek, records his dreams, waking thoughts, and strange incidents. The richest commoner in England muses on art, travel, and life. A fascinating self-revelation from a most unusual man. Fonthill's towers and Portuguese suns haunt these curious, candid pages.
europmc-pmc10007858:
Yuan and co-workers review how the matrix around a tumor changes as cancer grows and learns to hide from the immune system, in a 2023 paper. A tumor is not just cancer cells. It sits in a scaffold of proteins and support cells that it reshapes to feed its own spread.

The authors trace how that reshaping helps tumors grow and escape immune attack. They then survey treatments that target the scaffold itself. The review connects basic cell science to drug ideas now in testing, in terms a general reader can follow.
europmc-pmc10390758:
Chen and co-authors gave a 2023 guide to multi-omics, a way to study disease with many data types at once. Each omics layer reads one part of the cell, such as genes, RNA, proteins, or small chemicals. Joining the layers can show how a disease works as a whole system. The guide is aimed at newcomers to the field.

Chen lays out the main tech types and warns on how to design a sound study. Machine learning and deep learning help merge the layers into one picture. Uses span cancer, brain disease, ageing, and the hunt for drug targets. Newer forms read single cells or keep each cell's place in tissue. The guide lists free tools and data banks for the work.
europmc-pmc10393958:
Choi and Park reviewed a stress protein called TXNIP in 2023 and its role in disease. TXNIP binds a guard protein, thioredoxin, that shields cells from damage. By gripping that guard, TXNIP weakens the shield and raises cell stress. New work shows the protein does far more than that.

Choi reports that TXNIP can switch on a danger complex that sparks swelling inside cells. It can also push cells toward death under stress from their inner stores. These acts link TXNIP to diabetes, kidney disease, and brain disorders. Drugs that block TXNIP are thus of keen interest. The review weighs how such drugs might treat these diseases.
europmc-pmc10497558:
Ling and co-authors reviewed amino acid metabolism in health and disease in 2023. Amino acids are the building blocks of proteins. Cells also burn them for energy and use them to grow and split. When their handling goes wrong, illness can follow across many organs.

Tumours lean hard on amino acids taken in from food and blood. Ling reports that blocking select paths can starve tumour cells while sparing normal ones. Immune cells also hinge on these paths, from killer T cells to calming Treg cells. The review spans cancer first, then metabolic, heart, and immune diseases. Each path offers fresh points where a drug might act.
europmc-pmc11256658:
Zheng and colleagues report national cancer statistics for China in 2016 in this 2022 paper. China's National Cancer Center publishes such figures yearly from population registries. For 2016, a total of 487 registries supplied high-quality data on new cases and deaths. Nationwide totals were estimated by scaling registry data to the national population.

China saw about 4.06 million new cancer cases in 2016, and about 2.41 million cancer deaths, they estimate. Lung, colorectal, stomach, liver, and female breast cancers were the five most common, at 57.4 percent of new cases. Lung, liver, stomach, colorectal, and oesophageal cancers led deaths, at 69.3 percent of the total. Rates were split by urban and rural area, sex, and fine age groups. Age-standardised rates used the world Segi population as the reference.
europmc-pmc11298558:
He, Zhou, and Wang review glycosylation, a sugar-tagging of proteins, in this 2024 paper. After a protein is built, cells often modify it by adding or removing chemical groups. Glycosylation transfers sugar chains onto specific amino acid sites using enzymes called glycosyltransferases. It ranks among the most common such modifications.

The tagging is essential for protein function, cell adhesion, and immune escape, the authors note. Faulty patterns are closely linked to cancer, inflammation, and autoimmune disorders. Yet the exact composition and structure of the sugar tags remain undetermined in many cases. The review argues for deeper mapping of tag structures and their varying levels across tissues. It also urges pairing that mapping with advanced detection technologies. Clinical implications run through the paper's closing sections.
europmc-pmc1175958:
Smith and colleagues propose strict definitions for the relations used in biomedical ontologies in this 2005 paper. An ontology is a controlled vocabulary: a fixed list of terms for a field, with definitions. Many biomedical lists use relations such as part-of and located-in loosely. The paper is part of a reform effort by the Open Biomedical Ontologies group.

The authors advance a method for giving each relational term a consistent, unambiguous formal definition. The goal is to help developers and users avoid errors in coding and annotation. The Gene Ontology shows the stakes: it holds three vocabularies, for cell components, molecular function, and biological process, and is reused by databases worldwide. A sloppy relation, copied everywhere, spreads silent errors. The method is offered for ontology building across the life sciences.
europmc-pmc1241758:
O'Neill and a workshop group tackled how wealth shapes pollution harm in 2003. Air pollution and social position each affect health on their own. Poor and working-class areas often face higher pollution too. Early studies hinted social position changes pollution effects themselves.

The authors propose theories for how the two forces interact. They draw on studies from around the world. Methods from air pollution science and social epidemiology are introduced side by side. Gaps in study design get direct attention. O'Neill calls for joint research that treats exposure and inequality together.
europmc-pmc1274258:
Larionov, Krause, and Miller described a standard-curve method for PCR data in 2005. Real-time PCR is the most precise way to measure gene activity. Raw output is a mass of glow numbers. Processing choices can shift final results a lot.

Their procedure skips efficiency estimation entirely. Noise is filtered by smoothing, baseline removal, and scaling. The reading threshold is picked on its own from the standard curve. Crossing points come straight from curve coordinates. Variation within each run gets a statistical estimate. Larionov cuts operator handling to a minimum. It appeared in BMC Bioinformatics in 2005. It ran in BMC Bioinformatics in 2005.
europmc-pmc1403158:
Ocean water teems with archaea, microbes akin to bacteria but with their own branch of life. Hallam and co-authors read genes from one such microbe in 2006, a sea form that lives with a sponge host. They rebuilt its likely routes for taking in carbon and gaining energy from those gene clues.

The genes point to a changed three-step cycle that fixes carbon dioxide into food. Other genes suggest the microbe can also eat organic carbon. Hallam also found genes for using ammonia as fuel. Matching genes turned up in seas worldwide. The work hints these tiny microbes help run ocean carbon and nitrogen cycles.
europmc-pmc1601958:
Drug hunters need to know where a drug can lodge on a protein. Huang and Schroeder improved a site-finding algorithm in 2006, LIGSITEcsc. It scans a protein surface for pockets, using geometry based on the Connolly surface, a smooth skin over the molecule.

The upgrade re-ranks candidate pockets by how conserved their surface residues are across species. Conserved spots tend to matter, so ranking by them greatly improved accuracy. On 48 paired and 210 bound structures, the tool hit success rates of 71 and 75 percent. Huang offers a web server and free source code.
europmc-pmc1634758:
Repetitive DNA clutters every complex genome, and curating it needs tools. Kohany and co-authors presented two in 2006 for Repbase, the reference database of repeats. RepbaseSubmitter formats and annotates new entries through a Java interface.

It auto-computes sequence length and composition, cutting common formatting errors. It can also predict protein-coding regions and pull in PubMed references and species data. The second tool, Censor, scans a new sequence against known repeats at speed. Its output maps the repeats found and can mask them. Both tools run as web services or downloads, Kohany reports.
europmc-pmc1635058:
Putting research into practice in veterans' hospitals needs more than memos. Stetler and co-authors evaluated external facilitation in 2006 within QUERI, a quality program of the Veterans Health Administration. Facilitators are helpers sent from outside a site to ease change.

Through interviews across several multi-site projects, the team found facilitation to be a deliberate, valued process. It joined interactive problem solving with support, tailored to each site's snags. Facilitators differed from other change agents by working problems live with local teams. Stetler argues the role deserves a clear definition, since studies had used the term loosely.
europmc-pmc1635558:
Back pain scales abound, but which detects change best? Lauridsen and co-authors compared five instruments head to head in 2006, in 191 Danish patients from primary and hospital care. They included two disability surveys, parts of a general health survey, a back pain rating scale, and a simple pain number scale.

The Roland Morris questionnaire was most responsive in patients with back pain only. In leg pain patients, it tied with the Oswestry index. Among patients who improved, the Roland Morris again led for back-only cases. Lauridsen gives clinics subpopulation-specific guidance instead of one verdict for all.
europmc-pmc1638158:
Children meet contaminants through air, skin, and mouth, and their habits set the dose. Cohen Hubal and co-authors reviewed in 2000 what is known about children's exposure and what data are missing. Regulators lean on default assumptions because child-specific data are scarce.

Assessing exposure needs activity patterns: where children play, what they touch, what they swallow. Such data are thinnest for the youngest children. The team calls for better age groupings for assessments, better monitoring methods, and data on contaminant levels and transfer rates. Cohen Hubal argues these gaps must close before rules can be trusted to protect children.
europmc-pmc1781458:
Provenzano and colleagues imaged in 2006 how collagen, the main support protein in tissue, is arranged around breast tumors. Dense collagen in breast tissue raises cancer risk, yet how its layout affects tumor growth and spread was unclear. The team studied the border where tumor cells meet surrounding stroma, the supporting tissue.

They used multiphoton laser microscopy and second harmonic imaging, methods that light up collagen in intact, unfixed tissue. The images gave three-dimensional views that normal slicing could not show, such as fibers radiating out from tumors. They defined three tumor-linked collagen patterns, named TACS, that mark where tumors sit and how they behave. Local invasion ran mostly along those altered fibers, suggesting the reshaped collagen helps cancer cells move outward.
europmc-pmc1885958:
Hladik, McElrath and co-authors recreated in 2007 the first hours of vaginal HIV infection in human tissue kept alive in the lab. Most HIV infections worldwide start through sexual contact in women, yet the opening steps were poorly observed for lack of a good model. Their organ culture system kept real vaginal tissue working outside the body.

On contact, HIV-1 rapidly entered two cell types: Langerhans cells inside the surface layer and CD4 T cells beneath it. Entry into T cells happened almost only by direct fusion through the CD4 and CCR5 receptors, and full productive infection followed. Langerhans cells instead swallowed the virus through several receptors, and intact virus lingered inside them for days without clear production. The split behavior may guide designs that block local spread.
europmc-pmc2124758: A medical paper on opsonic immunity to Staphylococcus aureus. The body's defenses. This article preserves that immunology research. Time has kept the file intact. The archive guards it with care. Those who study the era will use it.
europmc-pmc2125958: A medical paper with studies of lung volume in tuberculous women. The TB lungs. This article preserves that pulmonology. The paper lasts as a quiet witness. Time has kept the file intact. The archive guards it with care.
europmc-pmc2131058: A medical paper on the soluble specific substance of Friedlander's bacillus, paper one. The Klebsiella signature. This article preserves that bacteriology. Tomorrow's readers will find it. History keeps its place secure. Its pages add to the record of the past.
europmc-pmc2140358: A biology paper on the combination of enzyme and substrate, a method for quantitative determination. The enzyme-substrate union. This article preserves that biochemistry. Those who study the era will use it. The archive keeps the paper open to all.
europmc-pmc2140558: A biology paper on sodium chloride and selective diffusion in living organisms. The salt's passage. This article preserves that physiology. Writers of history may cite it later. The paper lasts as a quiet witness. Time has kept the file intact.
europmc-pmc2140658: A biology paper on the critical thermal increment for the locomotion of a diplopod. The millipede's heat. This article preserves that physiology. Tomorrow's readers will find it. The historical record keeps it. The archive guards it with care.
europmc-pmc2180258: A medical paper on relation between organ weights and obscure lesions in normal rabbits. The hidden rabbit lesions. This article preserves that pathology. Tomorrow's readers will find it. It holds its historical place. Scholars prize such firsthand sources.
europmc-pmc2186358:
Sherman and colleagues described the DAVID Knowledgebase in 2007, a central database for interpreting large gene lists. Biological knowledge is scattered across many overlapping annotation databases run by separate groups. Analysts must visit many sites to assemble full information on their genes, a bottleneck for high-throughput studies. DAVID groups tens of millions of gene and protein identifiers into single clusters using a method called the DAVID Gene Concept.

Clustering identifiers improves cross-referencing, especially between the NCBI and UniProt systems. It lets more than forty public annotation sources be integrated around those clusters. The knowledgebase is freely downloadable as simple text files. A web interface lets users query varied annotations for large gene lists at once. For one gene, the system enriches the available biological information beyond any single source.
europmc-pmc2211558:
Hopewell and co-authors, with the CONSORT Group, extended reporting standards in 2008 to abstracts of randomised trials. Readers often judge a trial from its abstract alone, so abstracts need clear, complete detail. The team built a draft item list from existing tools and evidence. A three-round Delphi survey, a structured expert consensus process, selected the items, drawing 109 invited participants with a 61 percent response rate.

A January 2007 meeting in Montebello, Canada, finalised the checklist with 26 trialists, statisticians and editors. Recommended items cover objectives, design, participants, interventions, main outcomes and harms. They also cover conclusions, trial registration and funding source. The checklist recommends a structured abstract format. A companion explanation gives examples of good reporting and the reasoning behind each item.
europmc-pmc2216058:
Kern reviewed evidence in 2007 that inflammation drives the early stages of diabetic retinopathy, eye damage from diabetes. The disease was classically seen as purely a blood vessel problem. Diabetic retinas, however, show many inflammation hallmarks: raised inflammatory enzymes and signals, more nitric oxide, vessel leakage and white cells sticking in capillaries. The review focuses mainly on studies in living animals.

Early tissue changes include tiny capillary bulges, loss of supporting pericyte cells, and blocked, degenerating capillaries that cut retinal perfusion. Blocking inflammatory mediators with drugs, or deleting them genetically, significantly slowed those early lesions in many studies. A common thread among successful therapies was suppressing inflammatory mediator production. The hypothesis opens new drug targets for a disease that still lacks early treatments.
europmc-pmc2561058:
Daetwyler, Villanueva, and Woolliams worked out formulae in 2008 for how accurately a person's genetic risk of a complex disease can be predicted from genome-wide data. Predicting risk works well for simple inherited diseases, but complex diseases draw on thousands of genes. The authors derived simple equations that forecast prediction accuracy from study design, without needing each gene's frequency or effect size.

Simulations confirmed the equations were close. Accuracy turned out to hinge mainly on one product: the number of people studied per risk gene, times the disease's heritability. The formulae let researchers size a study to reach a target accuracy before spending on it. They also show how population studies and case-control studies compare, and mark an upper bound that better methods might approach.
europmc-pmc2648658:
Gray and co-authors reviewed in 2009 how a warming climate may change ticks and the diseases they pass to people in Europe. Ticks spread Lyme disease and a brain infection called tick-borne encephalitis. Both illnesses had grown more common over twenty years, and many blamed warmer weather.

For the sheep tick, the main carrier, the range has crept north and uphill, and winter activity has risen as winters softened. Hotter summers may shift the season, pushing most tick activity into the later part of the year. Models suggest eight major tick species could settle farther north as the climate warms. The authors urge care, though: these diseases depend on hosts, habitats, and human habits too. Blaming climate alone, they say, outruns the proof, and better models must fold in living processes.
europmc-pmc2654758:
Van Melderen and Saavedra De Bast reviewed in 2009 a curious paired weapon found across the bacterial world: toxin-antitoxin systems. Each pair joins two genes. One makes a stable poison that can harm the cell. The other makes a fragile antidote that keeps the poison in check.

Some of these pairs act like selfish hitchhikers. They ride on mobile DNA pieces, and if a daughter cell loses the piece, the antidote fades while the poison lasts, killing the cell. That death forces the piece to be kept. Other pairs sit fixed in the main chromosome, and their purpose is far less clear. The review weighs the leading ideas: stress survival, programmed death for the good of the group, and simple self-preservation of the genes themselves.
europmc-pmc2654858:
Haram, Svendsen, and Abildgaard reviewed in 2009 the HELLP syndrome, a dangerous complication of pregnancy. Its name joins three signs: red blood cells breaking apart, raised liver enzymes, and a low count of platelets, the cells that help blood clot. It appears in under one percent of pregnancies, and in up to a fifth of severe preeclampsia cases.

Most cases arise before birth, mainly between weeks 27 and 37 of pregnancy; the rest appear within two days after delivery. The review covers how to spot the syndrome, how to classify its severity by platelet counts, and the risks it carries for mother and baby. Delivery is the core treatment once week 34 passes, or sooner if either patient worsens. Steroid drugs can help the baby's lungs mature before an early birth. Waiting longer is debated and suits only carefully chosen early cases.
europmc-pmc2694358:
Raychaudhuri and colleagues, with the International Schizophrenia Consortium, presented in 2009 GRAIL, a method that finds the real culprit genes hiding in lists of disease-linked genome regions. Genome scans return dozens of regions; the hard part is telling signal from noise. GRAIL scores how related the genes across regions are, mining a quarter million published abstracts for shared biology.

Genes in one true pathway tend to be talked about together in the literature, so relatedness betrays them. Tested on known lipid and height regions, the method picked out the connected subsets cleanly. On 74 borderline Crohn disease signals, it flagged 13; ten of those then confirmed in follow-up typing. On 165 rare deletions from schizophrenia patients, most of them innocent, it found 16 whose genes cluster on brain synapses. The tool turns a flat list of regions into ranked, pathway-shaped hypotheses.
europmc-pmc2732458:
Rotz, Khan, Lillibridge, Ostroff, and Hughes described in 2002 how United States public health experts selected and ranked potential biological terrorism agents for preparedness planning. Many microbes can cause illness, but only some can strain public health and medical systems at large scale. The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention led the effort to focus planning, surveillance, lab capacity, and drug stockpiles.

Experts met in 1999 to set general criteria, review prior military and civilian threat lists, and score agents against those criteria in a repeatable way. Agents posing the greatest threat to civilians were identified for further evaluation and priority action. The ranked list was meant to coordinate planning across federal, state, and local agencies and the medical community.
europmc-pmc2779358:
Kilkenny and co-authors surveyed in 2009 the quality of experimental design, statistical analysis, and reporting in published animal research. Good design and full reporting matter for science, ethics, and cost, since missing details block review and repetition. They searched two databases for studies on live rats, mice, and primates. The labs were publicly funded, in the United Kingdom and United States. They mined two hundred seventy-one papers in detail.

Only about six in ten papers stated their hypothesis and the number and traits of animals used. Most studies skipped randomisation, eighty-seven percent, and blinding, eighty-six percent, both basic guards against bias. Three in ten papers using statistics failed to describe their methods or show error measures. The survey lays out concrete fixes for authors, reviewers, and editors to raise the standard of animal research reporting.
europmc-pmc2807458:
Onken and Driscoll tested the diabetes drug metformin in tiny worms in 2010 to learn how it might extend healthy life. The drug had been noted to lengthen health in nondiabetic mice, but the route was unclear. Caenorhabditis elegans, a small roundworm widely used in aging research, gave them a fast genetic model.

Metformin slowed the buildup of age pigment, lengthened middle life, and kept older worms moving like young ones, with stronger doses giving stronger gains. The gains required an energy sensor called AMPK, its activator LKB1, and a stress-response factor named SKN-1. Worms ate normally, yet their bodies acted as if food were scarce, mimicking calorie restriction without the diet.
europmc-pmc2821358:
Kim and colleagues searched in 2010 for a gene pattern that predicts which early bladder cancers will turn invasive. Most bladder cancers start shallow, in the group called non-muscle invasive, yet some progress dangerously and current markers judge that risk poorly. The team read gene activity in two hundred seventy-two tumor samples.

Ninety-seven genes tied to progression in the shallow group were found in the first sample set. Eight of them formed a classifier that was checked in both the original set and a separate group of one hundred seven patients. The classifier sorted patients by risk in both rounds, and no patient placed in its good-outlook group progressed at all. The authors say it could guide who needs closer watching or stronger treatment.
europmc-pmc2825658:
Kaneto, Katakami, Matsuhisa, and Matsuoka reviewed in 2010 how reactive oxygen species, unstable oxygen byproducts of metabolism, push type 2 diabetes and artery disease forward together. Diabetes turns on failing insulin-making beta cells in the pancreas plus body-wide resistance to insulin. Long-running high blood sugar raises these reactive species sharply.

That chemical stress further weakens beta cells and deepens insulin resistance, so the disease feeds itself, the review argues. The same high sugar and reactive species also injure vessel walls, speeding atherosclerosis, the fatty clogging of arteries that so often accompanies diabetes. Cutting oxidative stress therefore sits at the crossing point of both conditions, a shared lever for therapy.
europmc-pmc2833258:
Chiyomaru and colleagues found in 2010 that two tiny RNAs lost in bladder cancer normally hold down a protein that helps cancer cells spread. The RNAs, miR-145 and miR-133a, are among the most reduced in bladder tumors. Hunting the genes they control, the team landed on FSCN1, a protein that bundles cell fibers and aids movement.

Both RNAs latched directly onto the FSCN1 message and cut its output. Restoring either RNA, or silencing FSCN1 itself, slowed cancer cell growth, movement, and invasion through gel. In patient samples, tumors with strong FSCN1 staining had nearly silent miR-145, and invasive cancers carried far more FSCN1 than surface ones. The pair thus act as tumor suppressors through one shared target.
europmc-pmc2872358:
Plum, Rink, and Haase called zinc an essential toxin in their 2010 review, because the same metal that life requires can kill cells in excess. Zinc is a trace element, needed in tiny amounts for growth, brain development, and immune defense. True poisoning from overdose is rare, since body controls keep levels steady.

High-dose supplements cause harm mostly by blocking copper uptake, so many toxic effects are really copper shortage in disguise. Inside single cells, though, loose zinc can trigger programmed death by acting on the caspase enzymes and their regulators. That process matters most in the brain after stroke or injury, when free zinc piles up. Shortage is the bigger public health problem, the authors stress, harming children across poor regions.
europmc-pmc2933358:
Kumarasamy and a large team reported a new drug resistance mechanism, the NDM-1 enzyme, spreading in India, Pakistan, and the United Kingdom in 2010. Bacteria carrying NDM-1 could withstand carbapenems, antibiotics often kept as a last line of defence.

Testing isolates from Chennai, Haryana, and a British reference laboratory, they found the resistance gene mostly in Escherichia coli and Klebsiella pneumoniae. The strains resisted nearly all antibiotics except tigecycline and colistin. The gene often sat on plasmids that could pass between bacteria, and many British patients had lately travelled or received hospital care in South Asia.
europmc-pmc2958458:
Heiss led a large randomised trial of catumaxomab, an antibody treatment for fluid build-up in the belly caused by advanced cancer, reported in 2010. Such malignant ascites returns quickly after drainage and options are few.

Over two hundred and fifty patients with fluid resistant to standard chemotherapy received drainage alone or drainage plus four antibody infusions into the belly over ten days. Time without needing another puncture stretched from under two weeks to well over six weeks, and the wait for the next drainage grew even more. Patients also reported fewer ascites symptoms, and gastric cancer patients lived significantly longer.
europmc-pmc2996858:
Ding and colleagues tested stem cells from the tooth ligament as a treatment for gum disease in miniature pigs in a 2010 study. Periodontitis destroys the tissue holding teeth and drives most tooth loss, with no method yet restoring it fully.

Sheets of ligament stem cells, either from the same pig or from another, were transplanted into diseased gums. Twelve weeks later both groups showed strong tissue regrowth with no clear difference between them, and no rejection of the foreign cells appeared. The cells lack key immune display molecules and calm T cell growth, partly through a signal called PGE2.
europmc-pmc3000358:
Blair and a large team reported a new class of small molecules that attack the HIV capsid, the protein shell of the virus, in a 2010 study. Even with strong current therapy, resistant strains keep emerging, so fresh targets matter.

The compounds fought laboratory and clinical HIV strains and the related HIV-2, acting both early and late in the virus life cycle. They disturb shell opening after entry and shell assembly before exit. Changes in the capsid's front section made the virus resistant, confirming the target, and a crystal picture showed the drug tucked into a previously unknown pocket there.
europmc-pmc3017758:
Criscuolo and Gribaldo presented BMGE, software that trims multiple sequence alignments down to the stretches sound for building family trees, in a 2010 article. Ragged or over-variable alignment regions mislead tree methods, yet genome-scale projects cannot clean each dataset by hand.

For each aligned character the program works out an entropy-like score. Standard similarity tables weight the score. That helps judge whether the variation looks biologically plausible. Runs of high-scoring characters are cut away. Simulations show the trimming lifts tree accuracy across rebuilding methods. The tool targets automated pipelines that pull datasets straight from whole genomes.
europmc-pmc3061958:
Carlsen and Glenton audited in 2011 how health researchers decide and report how many focus groups to run. Focus groups, guided discussions used to gather views, appear ever more often in health journals. Guidance says to keep going until new groups stop adding insights, a point called saturation, but practical advice is thin. The team screened papers from one year that used focus groups in open access health journals.

They found more than two hundred papers, running anywhere from a single group to nearly a hundred. Fewer than one in five explained the chosen number at all. Among those, most claimed saturation, yet several clearly had not used the back and forth process that concept requires. Papers running many groups explained the least. The authors urge journals to demand clearer methods reporting. They also say the field needs real evidence on how many groups different questions actually require.
europmc-pmc3108958:
Volker Mai and colleagues reported a 2011 study in PLoS ONE on gut microbes in very early-born infants. A severe bowel illness strikes some such infants in their first weeks, and gut microbes are thought to play a part. The team collected weekly stool samples from birth and compared infants who later fell ill with matched peers.

Using gene sequencing, they found that stool make-up differed a week before illness began, though not in the first days. Infants who fell ill showed a sharp rise in one broad bacterial group and a fall in another over that week. One unusual bacterial signature also appeared more often in the ill group. The pattern hints that odd microbial shifts, and perhaps an unknown germ, help trigger the disease.
europmc-pmc3111658:
David Clark and colleagues evaluated two pilot therapy services in England in a 2009 paper in Behaviour Research and Therapy. The pilots opened ahead of a national plan to widen access to talking treatments for depression and anxiety. Both sites used a stepped model, starting with lighter help such as guided self-help when suitable.

In their first thirteen months the services treated large numbers of people and gathered outcome records for nearly every patient. Just over half of those seen at least twice had recovered on leaving, and a small share had gained work. Gains mostly held ten months later, and opening the door to self-referral reached groups often missed by doctor referral. Results were similar across ethnic groups, giving planners evidence for the wider rollout.
europmc-pmc3197658:
David Venet, Jacques Dumont, and Vincent Detours wrote this 2011 critique in PLoS Computational Biology about gene expression signatures in breast cancer. Researchers often claim a biological process matters in human cancer when a gene signature for it predicts patient outcome. The authors tested how strong that logic really is.

They found that random sets of genes predicted breast cancer outcome about as well as most published signatures. Even signatures from unrelated experiments, on laughter and on social defeat in mice, did so. europmc-pmc3252258:
Grant Cramer and colleagues reviewed how plants respond to environmental stresses such as drought, salt, and temperature extremes, in this 2011 paper in BMC Plant Biology. Plants face these abiotic stresses together with attacks from pests and disease, and their responses are equally tangled. The authors argue that systems biology, which fits genes, proteins, and metabolites into predictive networks, is the right lens.

The review moves from whole-plant physiology down to molecules, summarizing progress at each level. europmc-pmc3280258:
Andrew Kemp and colleagues measured heart rate variability in unmedicated patients with depression and anxiety, in this 2012 paper in PLoS ONE. Depressed patients die of heart disease at several times the usual rate, and low heart rate variability predicts cardiac death. Earlier studies were muddied by medication, so this case-control study recruited physically healthy patients taking no drugs, in several diagnostic combinations.

Recordings under standardized rest confirmed variability was reduced in depression compared with matched controls, an effect of medium size. The reduction was not uniform: patients whose depression came with generalized anxiety disorder, the pattern of anxious anticipation, showed the largest drop. Patients with panic or trauma-related anxiety fell in between. The authors discuss what this gradient means for identifying psychiatric patients who most need cardiovascular risk reduction.
europmc-pmc3314658:
Eshaghi and colleagues tracked the genetics of a common childhood chest virus in Ontario, reporting in 2012. The virus, known as RSV, is the leading cause of serious lung infections in babies and reinfects people throughout life. The team read a key surface gene in samples gathered during the 2010 to 2011 winter season and sorted the viruses into family groups.

Most infections in the sample came from the A group of the virus, and nearly all of those belonged to one known family. Eleven samples formed a brand new family, which the team named ON1. Its surface gene carries a doubled stretch that lengthens the protein and adds spots where sugars can attach, possibly helping the virus dodge antibodies. The authors call for work on how this new family spreads and harms.
europmc-pmc3320358:
Armand-Lefevre, Ruimy, and Andremont compared staph bacteria carried by pig farmers, pigs, and other people, reporting in 2005. Pig farmers are known to carry Staphylococcus aureus in their noses more often than the general public. The open question was whether farmers simply pick up more of the usual human strains, or whether pig strains themselves move into people.

Using genetic typing to build family trees of the bacteria, the team found that the farmers' extra colonization came from a few particular strains. Those strains were absent from people without farm contact, yet they commonly infected swine. The pattern points to frequent exchange of bacteria between pigs and the people who raise them. The authors flag this two way traffic as a route by which livestock strains, including resistant ones, can enter human populations.
europmc-pmc3374458:
Klempa and co-workers announced in 2006 the first home-grown hantavirus found in Africa, caught in a wood mouse in Guinea. Hantaviruses are rodent-borne germs that cause deadly fevers in Eurasia and the Americas. The mouse, an African wood mouse, was trapped near the village of Sangassou.

Reading the virus's genome and comparing it with relatives showed a species new to science. The team proposed naming it Sangassou virus after the capture site. Until then, African evidence for hantaviruses came only from antibody surveys in people. The find proved these viruses live in African rodents too, widening the map doctors must watch.
europmc-pmc3383958:
Altenhöfer and colleagues took stock in 2012 of the tools used to study NADPH oxidases, enzymes whose only job is making reactive oxygen species. Those species act as cell signals, but too much or too little can drive disease. The review focuses on NOX4, the most widespread member of the family.

The authors grade knockout mice, gene-silencing strands, antibodies, and blocking drugs for trustworthiness. They profile one blocker, VAS2870, in cells and animals, weighing how specific it really is. Blanket antioxidants have repeatedly failed patients, the review notes, because they mop up helpful signals too. Careful validation could make NOX4 a drug target for stroke, heart failure, and scarring diseases.
europmc-pmc3408958:
Mueller and nine colleagues described in 2012 the three crystal-structure beamlines at Berlin's BESSY II synchrotron, run by the Helmholtz-Zentrum Berlin. Researchers need bright, tunable X-ray beams to solve the shapes of proteins and other large molecules. The three stations, numbered BL14.1 through BL14.3, serve that demand across Europe.

The facility paper lays out what each beamline offers experimenters. Methods supported include fast screening of many crystals, deliberate drying of samples, and phasing tricks that use ultraviolet damage or long-wave X-rays. Europe's light sources together supply about a third of the world's deposited structures. The Berlin stations form part of that shared setup, and the paper is the reference for users planning beam time.
europmc-pmc3465558:
Boucrot and colleagues examined how cell membranes split to form small transport bubbles, in a 2012 paper in Cell. Proteins can bend a membrane in two ways: by wedging small parts into it, or by sitting on it as a curved scaffold. The team measured how these two actions work against each other during splitting, called fission.

Using a part of the protein epsin that wedges into membranes, they showed the wedging alone can pinch off bubbles from artificial membranes. Epsin also proved needed for coated vesicle budding in living cells. Curved scaffold proteins, by contrast, held fission back. Boucrot's group found the balance depends on how many wedging parts each scaffold carries. The result offers a fresh frame for how cells cut membranes without motor-like enzymes.

french-constitution-1958:
France adopted the constitution of the Fifth Republic in 1958, presented here in its first, unamended form. The Fourth Republic had collapsed under the strain of the Algerian war, and Charles de Gaulle returned to power on his own terms. Michel Debré drafted the charter under de Gaulle's direction, meaning to cure the ills of shifting parliamentary rule.

The text builds a strong presidency: the president names the prime minister, can dissolve the assembly, and holds wide powers in an emergency. Parliament keeps the laws, but within limits the charter sets. Voters approved the text by a large margin in a referendum. The law that tamed the chaos of the Fourth Republic still rules France today, amended since but unmistakable in its design.
frus-1861-d158:
On 21 October 1861, Secretary of State William H. Seward wrote a second letter to William Dayton. It is document 158 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1861.

The paired form appears in the Paris file as in the London one. Each letter owns its point and its answer. Together they show how a single day's French business could fill two files and still leave the desk clear. Two files, two answers: the habit kept replies swift and the record clean. A clear desk at day's end was Seward's small, daily victory over the war.
frus-1861-d258:
News and judgment from James Shepherd Pike reached Seward's desk in a letter dated 9 October 1861. It was printed as Document 258 in the foreign affairs papers sent to the two houses of Congress. It was written in the autumn of the war's first year, while the North worked to block foreign aid to the South.

Such reports fed the facts and rumors together into one desk in Washington, week by week. Letters of this kind are the raw record from which the story of wartime diplomacy is built. The Foreign Relations series, kept by the State Department's Office of the Historian, preserves the full run.
frus-1861-d58:
On 1 July 1861, William H. Seward wrote to Charles Francis Adams at the London legation. The letter is document 58 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1861.

July opened with Congress called to meet and the armies near Manassas. Seward's first of July letter keeps faith with the plan set in spring. It guided Adams through the weeks just before Bull Run, when a quick Union win still seemed within reach. Congress met on 4 July and voted men and money, which backed Seward's bold tone abroad. Men and money voted at home were the facts that gave his words abroad their weight.
frus-1862-d158:
Document 158, dated 10 October 1862, carries a dispatch from Secretary of State William H. Seward to Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London. It sits in the long Great Britain section of the 1862 Foreign Relations volume.

Three days earlier, William Gladstone had said in a speech at Newcastle that the South had made a nation. Words Union men read as a push toward British backing for the Confederacy. Adams had to answer that mood in London. Seward's steady mail, of which this letter is part, armed him with Washington's position week after week. Seward trusted Adams's calm judgment and rarely overruled the man on the spot.
frus-1862-d258:
William L. Dayton reported to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 18 March 1862, in a letter printed as Document 258 of the 1862 Foreign Relations volume. Dayton represented the United States in Paris as its minister.

Mid-March brought the Union's Peninsula campaign toward Richmond just as France was deciding to go it alone in Mexico after its allies pulled back. Dayton reported on a court balancing two American ventures at once. His letters are a chief source for how Napoleon III's government weighed the Confederate cause against its Mexican design that spring. Edouard Thouvenel ran the French foreign ministry for most of 1862 and set Dayton's agenda there.
frus-1862-d358:
William H. Seward, the Secretary of State, addressed Henri Mercier on 20 February 1862 in a letter printed as Document 358 of the 1862 Foreign Relations volume. It closed a run of three Seward letters to the French minister in two weeks.

Late February 1862 was a bright moment for the Union, with Fort Donelson fallen and Nashville about to follow. Seward negotiated from strength that month, a fact foreign legations registered. His letters to Mercier in this window show a secretary using good news as diplomatic capital while it lasted. Cases in this channel often mixed the war at home with French designs in Mexico.
frus-1862-d458:
On 22 June 1862 John Lothrop Motley sent this report from Vienna to Secretary of State William H. Seward. It stands as Document 458 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, accompanying the President's annual message.

Motley wrote as McClellan stood before Richmond and Europe waited to see if the Confederate capital would fall. Austria, busy with its own Italian and German problems, kept a strict and chilly neutrality. His report told Washington how the war's climax looked from the Danube. Letters like this one, from a minor post in the great question, still mattered. Seward's map of Europe had to be complete. Vienna's silence was itself a fact worth recording.
frus-1862-d558:
On 18 September 1862 Secretary of State William H. Seward wrote to Henry Shelton Sanford in Brussels. The instruction is Document 558 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, printed with the annual message.

Seward wrote the day after Antietam, in the same mid-September round that reached Madrid, Vienna, and The Hague. Sanford's Brussels post gave him a window on French and British thinking through King Leopold's wide family web. Orders to such a post mixed the government's line with requests for what the minister was hearing. The dispatch shows Seward gathering Europe's reaction to the autumn crisis through his most connected small-post minister, even before the battle's result was fully known.
frus-1862-d58:
A dispatch from Secretary of State William H. Seward reached Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London on 5 May 1862. It was printed as Document 58 in Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs for 1862. The date falls in the spring of 1862, a year into the war, when the Union fought to keep foreign powers from backing the South.

Readers see the home office side of the exchange, where policy was set before talks began. Its worth grows in context, as one link in a chain of letters that kept the peace with Europe. The State Department's Office of the Historian keeps the series, called Foreign Relations of the United States.
frus-1862-d658:
William H. Seward addressed this letter to Robert H. Pruyn on 19 December 1861. Pruyn was the incoming American minister to Japan, named to follow Townsend Harris. The letter appears as document 658 in the Foreign Relations volume printed for 1862.

In the last weeks of 1861 Seward sent Pruyn a run of letters, each adding to the charge the new envoy would carry. They dealt with the work of the legation and the stance the United States meant to keep in Japan. This one is a mid-run piece, useful chiefly as part of the full set that sent Pruyn off with his orders in hand.
frus-1863p1-d158:
Charles Francis Adams wrote this dispatch to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 17 April 1863. Three Adams letters in the volume bear the date. Adams was the American minister in London, and this letter is document 158 in part one of the 1863 volume.

A three-letter day late in April shows the ship question still filling the post's plate. Adams gave the yards, the talks, and the press each a sheet. This one opens the set of 17 April. In the volume's long London run, the day is one more crest in a spring of crests. Each charts Britain's slow turn from the South's hopes.
frus-1863p1-d258: On 25 July 1863, a Mr. Hyland wrote to Secretary of State William H. Seward. The letter is document 258 in the 1863 Foreign Relations volume, among the papers on relations with Britain during the Civil War. The record gives no first name or office for the writer, so the letter stands simply as one citizen-era note in the wartime mail.
frus-1863p1-d358:
One entry in the running Washington exchange, this note from Secretary of State William H. Seward to Lord Lyons, Britain's minister in Washington, is dated 10 January 1863. It stands as document 358 of the 1863 diplomatic papers. The document comes from the Foreign Relations of the United States, the government's own published record of Civil War diplomacy.

Washington believed Confederate agents used British ports, ships, and soil too freely. Seward pressed Lyons to have his government tighten its watch. It dates from the month the Emancipation Proclamation took effect, which changed the politics of the war in Britain at once. Alone it settles little; in the run of the volume it helps explain why Britain stayed out of the American war.
frus-1863p1-d458:
Lord Lyons, the British minister in Washington directed a letter to William H. Seward, Secretary of State on 11 April 1863. The letter was later printed in the 1863 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, issued with the President's annual message. Readers meet it in the first part of the 1863 Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, the government's own record of its dealings abroad.

For historians, the value lies in the run of the letters. Together they trace, almost day by day, how the Union kept its most dangerous foreign problem from boiling over. Trade ran through the whole exchange. British mills wanted Southern cotton, while Union officials watched every cargo for war goods bound to the South. Alone it is one note among hundreds. In place, it is part of how a war stayed between the two sides that started it.
frus-1863p1-d558:
In the flow of wartime mail, William H. Seward wrote to Lord Lyons on 8 June 1863. Lyons was Britain's minister in Washington, and Seward was the American Secretary of State. Behind the formal phrases stood a live question: would Britain stay neutral, or step into the American war? It forms part of Foreign Relations of the United States, the official printed record of American diplomacy.

The real subject under all the polite wording was British neutrality. Washington wanted it kept strict, and London wanted no quarrel it could avoid. Single letters rarely settle anything here. Their worth is in the chain they form, which lets a reader watch a dispute rise, cool, and fade in real time. Alone it is one note among hundreds. In place, it is part of how a war stayed between the two sides that started it.
frus-1863p1-d58:
Secretary of State William H. Seward resumed the London file with this letter to Charles Francis Adams on 19 January 1863. Adams was the American minister in London. The letter is document 58 in part one of the Foreign Relations volume for 1863, set after the Confederate papers.

The volume's order puts the foe's captured letters between two runs of the London mail, and this letter picks the thread back up. Seward wrote to keep Adams aimed at the standing aims: no British aid for the South, no warships out of British yards. It is a hinge piece, joining the winter run to what came before.
frus-1863p1-d658:
The 9 November 1863 mail between Washington and London included a letter from William H. Seward to Charles Francis Adams. Adams was the American minister in London, and Seward was Secretary of State in Washington. Behind the formal phrases stood a live question: would Britain stay neutral, or step into the American war? The exchange belongs to the Civil War years, when Washington's first task abroad was keeping Europe out of the fight.

That autumn the sharpest issue was the pair of ironclad rams built for the Confederacy at Birkenhead. Britain held them back, and this mail ran while that fight played out. Students of the war use this mail to see foreign policy as the men on the spot lived it, page by page. The volume's editors printed it without comment; its meaning comes from the company it keeps in the file.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d158: An editorial note dated May 5, 1943 stands as Document 158 of the Cairo and Tehran volume, far from the volume's opening where its twin note sits. Editorial notes in the Foreign Relations series mark seams where the editors joined bodies of papers, and this one opens the Moscow Conference section that follows. Reading it tells the reader whose files the next papers came from and how the editors handled them.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d258:
The Chinese record of a Cairo conversation between President Roosevelt and Generalissimo Chiang Kai-shek is introduced by an editorial note in the Foreign Relations volume. No official American record of the talk was found, and none appears to have been prepared, so the editors print a Chinese summary instead.

The Chinese government held the record in its own files, had it translated from Chinese, and gave leave for its printing in 1957. The note also flags gaps in the Log. The Log lists the Chiangs, Hopkins, and Colonel Elliott Roosevelt as dinner guests. The colonel's own account gives no sign he attended. Topics his book adds, missing from the Chinese summary, include a coalition government for China, British rights in Shanghai and Canton, and the future of Malaya, Burma, and India.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d358:
Charles Bohlen's minutes record the first meeting between President Roosevelt and Marshal Stalin, at Tehran on 28 November 1943 at three in the afternoon. The two leaders had never met, and Roosevelt opens with pleasure: he has tried for a long time to bring this about.

Stalin blames the delay on military business. Then he gives a frank front report. The Soviets have lost Zhitomir and are about to lose Korosten. They hold the initiative elsewhere, but can attack only in the Ukraine. Roosevelt says he wishes he could pull thirty or forty German divisions off the Eastern front, a question he wants Tehran to address. Talk turns to postwar trade and a surplus merchant fleet for Russia. It turns then to China, whose fighting Stalin faults on its leaders. Last comes Lebanon, which Roosevelt blames wholly on de Gaulle's committee.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d458: Number 458 in the Cairo-Tehran volume is an editorial note. Department historians use the note form to speak in their own voice. They add facts, explain references, and point to other documents. The record here covers the Allied conferences of late 1943. Strategy for Europe and Asia dominated those meetings. So did early arguments about the postwar world. The note gives readers footing before the papers resume.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d558:
A second Churchill message to President Roosevelt is dated March 4, 1944, hard on the heels of the first. The pair continues the dense exchange of that week. The message appears in the State Department's Cairo-Tehran conference volume.

Two messages a day, two days running, tells its own story about March 1944: the invasion was three months off, and every theater's claims collided in the leaders' in-trays. Churchill separated his subjects into single papers, and Roosevelt answered in kind. For readers, this message helps reconstruct a week of alliance management at full stretch, preserved because the State Department printed the conference volumes generously.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d58: Churchill wrote to Roosevelt on October 26, 1943, as the Moscow Conference neared its close. His message is Document 58 of the Cairo and Tehran volume. October 26 was a crowded day in the volume, full of letters between capitals and conference rooms. The record for this one gives the date and the names and nothing narrower. It survives in the Foreign Relations series with the rest of that day's traffic.
frus-1944-quebec-d158:
