Admiral Leahy wrote to Hull for the Joint Chiefs on August 29, 1944, giving the military view of French participation in the war against Japan. Indochina, the letter stresses, lies in the China theater and is an area of American strategic responsibility. It quotes the views Chiang Kai-shek expressed at Sextant on how the two theaters should divide Thailand and Indochina.

From a military standpoint, the chiefs concurred with the British proposals. One exception mattered: French participation in planning political warfare should be restricted to the Southeast Asia Command area. The letter also counsels recognizing French desires about Indochina where consistent with American policy, with extent and timing kept under continuing review.
frus-1944-quebec-d258:
Control of the strategic bomber forces in Europe is addressed in C.C.S. 520/4, the United States Chiefs' paper of September 13, 1944. With Allied armies now on the continent, the wartime arrangement under Eisenhower's direction was ending. The Americans agreed in principle with joint control by the RAF's Deputy Chief of the Air Staff and the commander of the United States Strategic Air Forces in Europe.

Those two officers, Bottomley and Spaatz, would act jointly for Portal and Arnold as agents of the Combined Chiefs. The Americans found the British draft directive inadequate in several respects, however, and attached a revised directive of their own. The Combined Chiefs approved it, as amended, the following day.
frus-1944-quebec-d58:
President Roosevelt answered Prime Minister Churchill on September 6, 1944. The reply appears in the State Department's Quebec 1944 volume, among the final pre-conference exchanges.

Roosevelt's answers that week kept the welcome warm and the American positions intact. He faced a guest who would argue hard for Britain's share in the Pacific war and for generous aid terms, and the President's letters prepared his ground. For readers, this message closes the transatlantic preparation: within a week the two men would be talking across a table in Quebec City instead of across an ocean.
frus-1945-50-intel-d158: A memorandum dated 28 June 1946 was prepared for the Secretary of State's Special Assistant for Research and Intelligence (Langer). It is document 158 in the Foreign Relations volume on intelligence for 1945 to 1950. Notes of this kind put a matter before one named man, so work could move at once. His office led the State Department's own research and intelligence work at the time.
frus-1945-50-intel-d258:
A memorandum from Director of Central Intelligence Hillenkoetter reached the Assistant Director for Special Operations (Galloway) on 22 December 1947. It is document 258 in the Foreign Relations of the United States volume on intelligence for 1945 to 1950. The CIA was only weeks old, having replaced the Central Intelligence Group in September 1947 under the National Security Act.

Memos like this one did the quiet work of the system. They carried facts, advice, and requests from one office to the desk that could act on them. Whole policies can be traced through chains of such notes, each one moving the matter a step. Kept with its neighbors in the volume, it shows the new system being built one dated paper at a time.
frus-1945-50-intel-d358:
Dated 1 January 1949, "Report From the Intelligence Survey Group to the National Security Council" comes from the top level of the government. The Office of the Historian kept it as document 358 in the Foreign Relations intelligence volume for 1945 to 1950. An outside survey team led by Allen Dulles was then reviewing the CIA, and its findings would drive a round of reform debate.

Reports were the heavy guns of paper work: slower than a memo, but built to end an argument. The replies it drew, kept near it in the files, show how the findings stood up to attack. The report is the Dulles Report. It holds the survey team's full findings and its fixes for the young CIA, sent to the Council in early 1949.
frus-1945-50-intel-d58:
Brownell, an executive officer for the assistant secretary of war for air, wrote to the Lovett Committee members on 17 December 1945. The committee's work was still live at year's end. It is printed in Foreign Relations of the United States, in the retrospective volume on American intelligence from 1945 to 1950.

Staff officers keep committees alive: they call the meetings, circulate the drafts, and chase the members' views. Brownell's memorandum shows that machinery turning in December, weeks after the Lovett report. Readers might pass over such a paper, but it marks something real, the refusal of a hard question to die. The intelligence design was still being argued in committee rooms while the secretaries settled its outline above.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d158:
Stalin answered Roosevelt on Poland on 29 December 1944, and the answer closed the door. His message, received in Washington in translation, is printed in the Malta and Yalta volume. He had the President's note of the middle of the month in hand.

On the American statement of 18 December, Stalin says he would rather speak in person; in any case, events in Poland have moved well past it. Intercepted radio traffic, he charges, proves that talks with Mikolajczyk screened men who waged criminal terror against Soviet officers and soldiers in Poland. Moscow cannot accept a state of things where émigré agents kill Red Army men. Mikolajczyk's replacement by Arciszewski, he adds, has made matters still worse.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d258:
General Arnold weighed in on the basic paper for planning Russia's entry into the Pacific war. His memorandum of 3 December 1944 is enclosed in a Joint Chiefs paper of 5 December, J. C. S. 1176/1, printed in the Malta and Yalta volume. The covering note comes from the Joint Secretariat in Washington.

The enclosure carries Arnold's approval of J. C. S. 1176, the staff paper on Russian participation in the war against Japan. He approves it with the recognition that it is a basic paper, limited in scope. The secretaries record that the paper has gone to the Joint Staff Planners, working with the Joint Logistics Committee, for necessary action. The distribution list reads like a roll of the American high command, from Admiral Leahy to General Marshall and Admiral King.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d358: Harry Hopkins passed this slip to the President during Stalin's long statement on Poland at the third plenary meeting, February 6, 1945. It reads, in full: why not let this wind up today when Stalin is through, and say we will talk it over again tomorrow. Hopkins added the time: it is 7:15. The note is undated, but the editors place it by its content. It shows the adviser managing the clock and the President's patience in the middle of the conference's hardest debate.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d458:
For the conference's last plenary session, no full minutes exist, and this editorial note explains what survives instead. The Bohlen Collection holds a list of those present and of subjects: the communiqué, reparations, and Japan. Against them stands a blunt notation: no report was written up on this conference.

A later page in the same collection, headed "Report of Last Day's Proceedings," does cover the session's first part. The editors reproduce that paragraph here. Hiss's notes, printed after, supply the detail the official record lacks. The note teaches readers to weigh the famous final day by fragments, not by a full transcript.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d58:
From Moscow on 16 January 1945, Ambassador Averell Harriman reported to President Roosevelt on where the American party would sleep at Yalta. His top secret telegram is printed in the Foreign Relations volume on the Malta and Yalta conferences. It deals with rooms, not strategy.

Harriman says Roosevelt will stay in the Livadia palace, the czar's former summer home. The site has one building of 21 rooms, one of 41, and a third once used by guards. Space for the enlarged military party is still unsure, so he is asking the Soviets for more rooms. The support ship Catoctin, he notes, can only be based at Sevastopol.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d158:
The British Embassy handed the State Department an aide-mémoire on Turkey on June 18, 1945. Only an extract is printed, as document 158 in the Foreign Relations volume on the Potsdam Conference. The full text appears later in the volume, attached to another document.

The surviving passage says that if the Turkish government has no objection, London hopes Washington will agree to a joint Anglo-American approach to the Soviet government. The approach would be in firm language and made soon. It would concern Soviet demands on Turkey. And it should come before the Big Three meeting, where the whole question might have to be discussed anyway. The note shows the West bracing over Soviet pressure on Turkey, a dispute that fed the later quarrels over the Turkish Straits.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d258:
Assistant Secretary Dunn noted British doubts on the Yalta Declaration in an extract dated July 14, 1945. The extract is document 258 in the Foreign Relations volume on the Potsdam Conference, taken from his long talk with Sir Alexander Cadogan at Potsdam.

Cadogan felt the Americans had more faith in the Declaration on Liberated Europe than he did, Dunn reports. Still, the British delegation would come along behind the United States in any effort to secure its carrying out. Cadogan was explaining London's wish for peace treaties with the ex-satellite states. He pointed to a legal snag. Unlike the United States with Italy, Britain cannot resume diplomatic relations with a country it is still at war with. The short passage shows the two Western delegations aligned on Poland and the Balkans, but for different reasons.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d358:
A safeguard on reparations shares is proposed in Pauley's cable from Moscow of June 25, 1945, sent after talks with the British representative, Sir Walter Monckton. It supplements his June 19 wire on the formula for dividing reparations among the Big Three. Pauley now adds a condition to protect the smaller claimants and the three themselves.

The three powers would state publicly that they will give up shares, in proportion, to other nations as justified. But unless all three later agree on the actual amounts for others, and pay them on a 55, 22½, and 22½ percent basis, the whole division among the Big Three would reopen.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d458:
Frontier incidents in northern Greece are enclosed with MacVeagh's despatch No. 1282 from Athens, dated July 4, 1945. Its subject is the north of Greece: frontier incidents, and Anglo-Russian relations. The enclosure is a secret report of July 2. Its author is the embassy's assistant military attaché. He was stationed for a time at Salonika as a special political observer.

His report covers incidents from May 20 to June 20. They occurred along Greece's Yugoslav and Bulgarian borders. Most, it states, were small in themselves. In total, though, they were hard to dismiss, and they weighed on men's minds. The printed list ends with six Greek civilians kidnapped near the Albanian frontier on June 20. They were taken into Albania.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d558:
A top secret briefing paper on Yugoslavia was prepared for Potsdam and dated June 27, 1945. The extract printed here is document 558 in volume one of the Foreign Relations papers. Its focus is Venezia Giulia, the disputed land around Trieste claimed by both Italy and Yugoslavia.

The paper notes that Stalin backs the Yugoslavs and blames Field Marshal Alexander. Yugoslavs read the June 9 Belgrade deal to mean their committee rule stays in place under Allied military government. The writers call that a bid to keep control and to sway the final outcome. They urge that no more ground be given and that the deal be enforced in full. The land's final fate, they say, must wait for a peace treaty with Italy.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d58:
Churchill told President Truman on June 14, 1945, that he would bring Labour leader Clement Attlee to the Berlin conference. The telegram, number 88, is document 58 in the Foreign Relations papers on Potsdam. The conference opening on July 15 would still be running when Britain's election results came out.

Bringing the leader of the opposition, Churchill explains, will assure full continuity of British policy, whoever wins the election. He says he has told Stalin of the plan in the same terms. The note proved wise: Churchill lost the election mid-conference, Attlee took his place at the table, and British policy carried on without a break. He closes by saying he looks forward to meeting Truman.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d658:
Ambassador Winant sought orders on U.S. membership in a restored Tangier regime on June 26, 1945. His secret wire is document 658 in volume one of the Foreign Relations papers on the Potsdam Conference. It reports early, informal talks at the Foreign Office in London.

Winant found U.S. and British views on Tangier much alike. London meant to give the French its draft pact for an interim regime the next day. That would let Paris weigh it before the talks opened on July 2. The British proposed a neat shortcut for U.S. entry. A copy of the pact would be sent to Washington with a request to join the zone's administration under its terms. The U.S. reply could carry any conditions it wished, saving the time of separate notes. Winant also asks how a U.S. money share might be funded.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1058:
British Foreign Secretary Ernest Bevin sent Secretary Byrnes a copy of his letter to Molotov on July 31, 1945. The letter answers Soviet claims that German troops in Norway were not being disarmed. Bevin reports the facts as London's authorities gave them, and calls the Soviet allegations groundless.

In all, 365,000 Germans in Norway were gathered into guarded reservations and disarmed. Only officers and two percent of the men kept pistols or rifles, to keep order inside the camps. That comes to about 7,300 armed men in total. The regions Moscow named hold far fewer troops than claimed: under 50,000 near Mo and Trondheim, not 260,000. Bevin also raises how the Germans will be evacuated home.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1158:
London reported to Washington on 18 July 1945, in this dispatch from Ambassador Winant to the Acting Secretary of State. The summit was in its second day. The embassy sent home its read of British official views and press talk at the start of the talks.

Winant's job was to make sure Washington never misread its closest ally. His post heard what the conference room could not: party talk, press mood, and private doubts. This cable is the London listening post at work early in the summit. It set the baseline against which later London reports would be read.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1258:
Prime Minister Suzuki of Japan spoke at a press conference on 28 July 1945. His words gave the world's first public sign of Tokyo's answer to the Potsdam Declaration, issued two days before. The statement reached Washington fast and was read there as a refusal.

Suzuki used a word, often rendered as killing the terms with silent contempt, that hardened Allied views. Whether he meant flat rejection or a wish to wait for Moscow, the effect was the same. The summit's leaders took Japan's answer as no. This statement is that answer in its public form, a hinge on which the war's last weeks turned.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1358:
George Allen wrote to Assistant Secretary James Dunn for a third time in this run on 25 July 1945. Allen's Near Eastern and African affairs office kept a steady file of papers flowing to Dunn during the conference. Foreign Relations of the United States, the official American diplomatic record, prints it in the second volume on the Potsdam Conference.

Dunn sat close to the center of the American effort at Potsdam, so papers addressed to him reached a man who could act. The Allen notes show a regional bureau working its questions into the summit's crowded agenda. For readers tracing Middle East policy in 1945, the Allen papers are a thread worth following. It runs from start to end of the volume's closing section.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d710a-158:
A rapporteur's report dated August 1, 1945 closed a working group's account as the Potsdam Conference ended. Rapporteurs stated what their groups had settled and what they passed upward. On the final day, such reports fed the last drafting. This one was printed in the second Potsdam volume.

A final report reads like a ledger being shut. Most lines are firm; a few stay open for ministers to judge. Readers learn how much of the settlement was built below the top level. The piece honors the conference's least seen workers: the officers who turned talk into text.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d710a-58:
War booty was discussed at a Potsdam meeting whose minutes have never been found. An editorial note in volume two reports the loss. It is the fifty-eighth unnumbered item following document 710. Unlike its neighbors, this note does name the subject that was discussed.

No minutes of this meeting, at which the question of war booty was discussed, have been found, the editors write. They direct the reader to a later summary of the discussion instead. That summary is printed as document 980, at pages 942 to 943 of the volume. War booty was no side issue at Potsdam. The term decided what the Soviet Union could seize in its zone as trophies of war, apart from reparations. The note thus points past its own gap to the nearest surviving account of a contested topic.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d758:
The United States delegation tabled this proposal on July 25, 1945, as document 758. The date falls in the conference's second week. American texts from this stage were aimed at closing gaps. The proposal was printed in the second Potsdam volume of Foreign Relations of the United States.

A proposal written after eight days of talks is a tuned tool. Its writers had heard every objection. Readers can judge how far the American side had moved from its opening drafts. The document also shows the endgame forming early. By July 25 the final protocol's shape was already being sketched, one text at a time.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d858:
Document 858 gathers the texts the Economic Subcommittee considered on July 19, 1945. Rival drafts on Germany's economic future lay before the experts. The bundle was kept as one record in the second Potsdam volume. It dates from the conference's first week.

A set of rival texts is the negotiation in miniature. Readers can lay the drafts side by side and find the fight. Each side's words about production and payment reveal its fears. The document spares readers the hunt through scattered files. It also shows the subcommittee's real work: not deciding, but making the decision possible for those above.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d958: President Harry Truman wrote to General Eisenhower from Berlin on July 30, 1945, about Marshal Zhukov's report to Stalin. Zhukov had charged American and British forces with removing property from the Soviet occupation zone. Truman encloses an informal translation of the report, passed to him during the conference. He asks Eisenhower to investigate the charges and report back to him. The editors note that no reply from Eisenhower arrived during the conference. Stalin raised the matter at the eleventh plenary meeting the next day.
frus-1961-63v11-d158: A 1961-1963 FRUS summary from the Missile Crisis volume. The thirteen days, summed. This entry preserves that summary. Such papers rarely see the light of day. The file is now open to the public. Its contents inform the historical record.
frus-1964-68v01-d258: A 1964-1968 FRUS editorial note from the Vietnam 1964 volume on a White House meeting. Johnson's war council. This note provides that context. The archive keeps the paper open to all. Its pages add to the record of the past.
gadbury-doctrine-nativities-1658:
John Gadbury teaches birth-chart astrology in Genethlialogia, his Doctrine of Nativities, from 1658. The great English manual tells how to cast a horoscope and read a life in it. Gadbury, rival to the famed Lilly, served the Civil War generation with forecasts drawn from the stars at each client's birth.

Rules for houses, aspects, and judgments fill his orderly, confident pages. Health, wealth, marriage, and death all submit to his method here. Judicial astrology stands at its most systematic in this work. Readers meet the heavens treated as a book of lives, open to any reader who learns the signs aright.
gao-gaoreports-b-295958: Integration Technologies Group doubled its May 2005 protest — two case numbers, one tech fight — and GAO's combined ruling settles both. The firm challenged the awards, and the call weighs each claim. Paired filings get one careful answer. Two dockets, one fair verdict.
gao-gaoreports-b-296158: Zebra Technologies took its June 2005 contract fight to GAO, and this ruling is the verdict on the claims. The firm said the agency's award was unfair, and the call tests the protest. Tech firms get the same full hearing as all.
gao-gaoreports-b-297758: United Paradyne took its March 2006 contract fight to GAO, and this ruling is the verdict on the claims. The firm said the agency's award was unfair, and the call tests the protest. Every challenger gets the full fair-play hearing.
gao-gaoreports-b-299058: OK Produce and Coast Citrus Distributors doubled the February 2007 protest — two case numbers, one produce fight — and GAO's combined ruling settles both. The firms challenged the awards, and the call weighs each claim. Even fruit fights get full hearings. The produce aisle got its day in court.
gao-gaoreports-b-299258: SourceLink Ohio took its March 2007 contract fight to GAO, and this ruling is the verdict on the claims. The firm said the agency's award was unfair, and the call tests the protest in full. Regional names get the same national-standard hearing.
gao-gaoreports-b-299858: Computer Cite took its August 2007 contract beef to GAO, and this ruling settles it. The firm said the agency's award was unfair; the call measures the protest against procurement law. Small tech firms live and die on such calls — each one a public ruling on whether the bid game was clean.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-458: Chemical regulation options got a GAO review in 2005, and the report says approaches existed to improve EPA's health risk assessment. The findings take the measure. The report warns that the toxic substances deserved smart rules. The options had to be understood.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-558: Airline screening fees got a backward look in 2005, and GAO's report reviews the carriers' year 2000 passenger and property costs. The review digs into the old bills. The airports' fee math was studied. The costs were reviewed. The airports' fee math was studied.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-658: Polluters' cleanup obligations needed enforcing in 2005, and GAO's report says EPA should do more to ensure liable parties paid. The findings demand the action. The report warns that the dirty sites deserved real cleanup. The obligations had to be met.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-858: Navy ERP needed best practices in 2005, and GAO's report says adherence to proven methods was critical to avoid past failures. The findings demand the discipline. The report warns that the sailors' software deserved doing right. The practices had to be followed.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-358: Paying small businesses faster needed e-invoicing in 2006, and GAO's report says electronic invoicing could further reduce delays. The findings prescribe the tech. The report warns that the little contractors deserved prompt pay. The invoicing had to go digital. The little contractors deserved prompt pay.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-658: The Pentagon's business systems overhaul was improving in 2006, and GAO's report says the institutional approach was getting better, though further steps were needed. The findings balance credit and prodding. The report warns that the money machine's modernization could not stall. The improvement had to continue.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-958: The VA's health budget needed better math in 2006, and GAO's report says budget formulation and reporting on execution wanted improvement. The findings demand the numbers. The report warns that the veterans' care dollars deserved honest books. The budget had to be sound.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-1058: The Pentagon's research wish lists did not add up in 2007 — GAO's report says its R&D budget asks to Congress were patchy and hard to compare. The findings demand cleaner books on the billions bet on future weapons. Lawmakers, GAO argued, deserved numbers they could actually grade.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-58: NASA's bonus pay needed better aim in 2007, and GAO's report says the use of award fees for program outcomes should be improved. The findings target the incentives. The report warns that the rocket bonuses should reward rockets that worked. The fees had to follow the results.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-658: Homeland Security's buildings were a management muddle in 2007 — GAO's report says the department had improved on real property but still owed more. The findings target the bricks-and-mortar backlog. The report's point: a security giant should know where its own houses are.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-758: Homeland Security's hiring halls were half-empty in 2007 — GAO's report tracks the department's push to recruit, keep, and legally mind its staff gaps. The findings grade the people pipeline of the security giant. The report's warning: a department is only as strong as its bench.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-258: In 2008, the Government Accountability Office published this report on aviation Weather: FAA Is Reevaluating Services at Key Centers; Both FAA and the National Weather Service Need to Better Ensure Product Quality. GAO is Congress's watchdog, and its work lays out what the team found and what should change. Its conclusions can shape how agencies run their programs.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-58: This 2007 GAO report takes a hard look at iran Sanctions: Impact in Furthering US Objectives Is Unclear and Should Be Reviewed. Congress relies on GAO for straight fact-finding on federal programs. Reports like this give Congress the facts behind funding and reform choices.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-958: This 2008 GAO report takes a hard look at transportation Security: TSA Has Developed a Risk-Based Covert Testing Program, but Could Better Mitigate Aviation Security Vulnerabilities Identified Through C. Congress relies on GAO for straight fact-finding on federal programs. Reports like this give Congress the facts behind funding and reform choices.
gesner-historia-animalium-lib4-1558:
Gesner went down into the waters for the fourth volume of his Historiae animalium in 1558. It treats fishes and water creatures of every kind, the largest survey of sea life yet attempted in print. Rivers, lakes, and oceans all contribute their tenants to his catalogue.

Whales, sharks, and common food fish receive the same careful order. Among them stand the sea serpent and other marine monsters that sailors swore were true. Gesner weighs the reports as best his age allowed. The volume keeps one foot in marvel, and is the more fascinating for it. No earlier book had tried to hold the whole watery world at once.
hansard-admission-of-baron-de-rothschild:
The House of Commons record for July 26, 1858 tells of the day Baron Lionel de Rothschild took his seat at last. Hansard, the verbatim record of Parliament, holds the whole scene in its pages. He had been chosen by the City of London for eleven years, yet kept out by the form of the oath.

The law was changed so a Jew could swear on the Old Testament and sit in the House. Lionel, the head of the London house, thus became the first professing Jew to sit in the Commons. The record is the high point of the long fight for Jewish rights in Britain.
harris-treaty-1858:
Townsend Harris, the first American consul in Japan, negotiated the 1858 treaty of amity and commerce with the Tokugawa shogunate. Four years after Perry's visit, the United States wanted real trade, not just ports for supplies. Harris argued that Japan could gain from open commerce, even as British and French power loomed over Asia.

The terms opened more ports to American ships and let Americans live and trade in set districts of Japanese cities. They also fixed low tariff rates and gave foreigners legal protections outside Japanese courts. Many Japanese saw the deal as unequal and humiliating, and anger at such terms helped fuel the movement that later toppled the shogunate.
herodotus-histories-rawlinson-1858:
Herodotus wrote his Histories in Greek in the fifth century BC, and George Rawlinson gave England its standard version in 1858 to 1860. Rawlinson, an Oxford scholar, added maps and learned notes. His brother Henry, famed for cuneiform work, helped with eastern lore.

Herodotus tells how Greece fought Persia and won against huge odds. Along the way he reports Egypt's customs, Scythian rites, and marvels galore. He mixes inquiry, travel tales, and speeches into one wide survey. Later ages named him the father of history, with cause. His notes draw on fresh finds from Egypt and Persia.
heuvelmans-on-track-of-unknown-animals-1:
Bernard Heuvelmans, a Belgian zoologist, gave the hunt for unknown beasts its first full map in 1958. On the Track of Unknown Animals, in Richard Garnett's English rendering, is the founding book of cryptozoology. Seven parts and nineteen chapters sweep the globe for hidden life.

Heuvelmans weighs reports of the orang-pendek, the yeti, sea serpents, and a mammoth said to live in the far north woods. He sorts strong tales from weak ones and asks what beast each could be. His method treats rumor as a clue to be tested, not a joke. The book shaped every beast hunt that came after.
hocus-pocus-junior-1658:
Hocus Pocus Junior calls itself the anatomy of legerdemain, the art of sleight of hand. First printed in 1634, it appears here in its fifth edition of 1658. It is the first English book of conjuring tricks, and it gave the world the phrase hocus pocus, taken from the patter of stage jugglers.

The book explains cups and balls, card tricks, and feats with string and coin. Its aim is exposure as much as teaching: readers learn how the wonders are done. That honesty made it a landmark in the history of stage magic. Generations of conjurers learned their first tricks from its pages. A working manual and a small delight, it still performs its tricks on readers.
holmes-autocrat-1858:
Oliver Wendell Holmes published The Autocrat of the Breakfast-Table in 1858, gathering essays he had run in The Atlantic Monthly. Holmes, a Harvard doctor and professor, imagines himself as the autocrat of a Boston boarding-house table. His monologues, interrupted by fellow lodgers, made him famous on two continents.

The Autocrat discourses on everything: conversation, poetry, trees, theology, and the young fellow who sits across the table. Poems break up the talk, including The Deacon's Masterpiece, about a carriage built so logically it ran a hundred years. Holmes's wit is learned, warm, and quick with metaphor. The book founded the American familiar essay's reigning style and stayed a favorite for generations.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-lowinsohn-jacob:
Jacob Mordecai ben Judah Löb Löwinsohn (1832–1878) was a Russo-Polish scholar and journalist born in Grodno, and a Jewish Encyclopedia entry from 1906 by Herman Rosenthal and Isidor S. Beaumache profiles him. A rabbi’s son trained in Talmud, he quickly mastered Russian, German, Polish, and French. That training launched his career in the press.

Löwinsohn wrote for Russian papers and, from 1862, for the journal “Jutrzenka,” where he defended the interests of his fellow Jews. The article recalls his heated debates with Hirsch Kalischer and with L. J. Shapiro, and notes that he was ordained at Wilna about 1868 yet never took a rabbinate. It also lists his early book of 1855, printed in a small run for friends. Readers get a portrait of a multilingual writer who argued for Jewish rights in several languages at once.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-mandl-moritz-10:
Moritz Mandl, an Austrian dramatist and journalist, receives an entry in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Born in Presburg on May 13, 1840, he went to Vienna for newspaper work. He joined the staff of the Wanderer in 1862. Later he moved to the Neue Freie Presse. Since 1877 he had been assistant editor of the Fremdenblatt.

The article lists his writings beyond the newsroom. A pamphlet, Germany and the Moment, printed at Leipsic in 1861, won some attention. His German epic Kathchen von Heilbronn appeared at Vienna in 1873. He wrote a dramatic prologue for the Vienna Kleist celebration of 1876. Several plays of his are also noted, though not named. The brief entry preserves a journalist whose bylines reached the stage as well as the press.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-masarjawaih-or-:
Masarjawaih, who lived at Bassora about the year 883, is remembered in a Jewish Encyclopedia entry from 1906 by Richard Gottheil and Max Schloessinger. He ranks among the oldest Arabic-writing Jewish physicians and as the oldest translator from the Syriac. Even his name is a puzzle: scholars quoted here debate whether its ending marks it as Persian and what the original name really was.

His main work was translating the medical pandects of the presbyter Aaron from Syriac into Arabic, adding two chapters of his own to Aaron's thirty. He also wrote Arabic treatises on the virtues and dangers of foods and of medicinal plants. None of his three writings survives whole; the entry notes that their contents are known only through quotations and fragments preserved by later authors.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-mendel-hermann-:
Hermann Mendel was a Berlin music publisher and writer. Isidore Singer and Joseph Sohn profile him in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He was born at Halle in 1834. He trained in music there and at Leipzig and Berlin. He worked for the publishers Schlesinger and then Bote and Bock. He kept his own firm from 1862 to 1868. He wrote steadily for the musical press. From its founding in 1870 until his death, he conducted the "Deutsche Musikerzeitung."

His monument is the "Musikalisches Konversations-Lexikon." It is a dictionary of music. He launched it in 1870 with a large and distinguished staff. Mendel died at Berlin on October 26, 1876. By then the work had reached only the letter M. August Reissmann carried it to eleven volumes. They rank among the most comprehensive of their kind. The entry also credits his biographies of Nicolai and Meyerbeer. It credits his edition of some ninety opera libretti too.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-meyer-ludwig-be:
Ludwig Beatus Meyer, born in Gandersheim, Brunswick, on January 3, 1780, was a Danish author best known for a dictionary that still carried his name in 1906. Isidore Singer and Frank Cramer wrote his Jewish Encyclopedia entry. He came to Copenhagen as a young private teacher and tutored in the family of Count Schimmelmann.

Naturalized as a Danish citizen in 1810, Meyer headed the bureau of the national debt before resigning in 1821 with the title of professor. He then wrote full time, starting with a handbook of German poetic literature in 1828. His lasting work was an 1837 glossary of foreign words and phrases in Danish, Meyer's Fremmedordbog, which passed through several editions as a standard authority.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-minnesota-10858:
Minnesota's thirteen thousand Jews are surveyed by Cyrus Adler and S. N. Deinard in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906: six thousand in Minneapolis, five thousand in St. Paul, a thousand in Duluth, and the rest scattered five to twenty families to a town. The first settlers seem to have been three English brothers named Samuels.

The Samuels brothers kept an Indian trading-post at Taylor Falls on the St. Croix as early as 1852, and Morris Samuels became a Union captain in the Civil War. Isaac Marks traded with the Indians from Mankato on the same frontier terms. St. Paul's Jews organized the state's first congregation, Mt. Zion, only in 1871 — Minneapolis then still had hardly any Jews at all.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-moses-ben-abrah:
Moses ben Abraham Provençal was rabbi of Mantua in the middle of the sixteenth century. Joseph Jacobs and Alexander Kisch wrote his Jewish Encyclopedia entry. His fame rests on one decision: he approved the first printed edition of the Zohar. The book appeared at Mantua in 1558, with the Inquisition's approval as well.

Not all agreed with him: Meir Katzenellenbogen of Padua and others had opposed printing the Zohar. Provençal also wrote a treatise on two lines that approach but never meet, printed in Hebrew in 1548 and in Italian in 1550. A responsum of his on a divorce case appeared at Padua in 1566. The entry catches a rabbi at the meeting point of print, Cabala, and censorship.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-moses-ben-todro:
Moses ben Todros was a Spanish rabbi who lived about 1150 and served for many years as nasi of Narbonne. Wilhelm Bacher and J. S. Raisin wrote his Jewish Encyclopedia entry. He was known both as a scholar and for his charity. His modest temper earned him the standing nickname he-anaw, the modest one.

His name appears among the signers of a famous appeal about Torah reading. The appeal asked leave to use an ordinary Torah manuscript in public worship when no regulation scroll could be had. His son Levi is praised by the poet Al-Harizi as a philanthropist. The short entry preserves a communal leader remembered for humility as much as rank.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-nabal-lit-fool-:
Nabal, whose name means fool, was a rich Calebite sheep master in the story of David's wanderings. Emil G. Hirsch and M. Seligsohn tell his tale in the Jewish Encyclopedia, from First Samuel. His flocks fed at Carmel while he lived at Maon. The text calls him churlish and a man of Belial, and his wife was Abigail.

David's men had guarded Nabal's shepherds, and at shearing time David asked for provisions in return. Nabal answered with insults, calling David a runaway slave, and David set out to kill him. Abigail rode out with gifts and talked David down. When she told her drunken husband next morning, he fell into a fit and died ten days later.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-nathan-jedidiah:
Nathan Jedidiah ben Eliezer was an Italian Hebrew poet. His entry was written by the Editorial Board's Executive Committee and M. Seligsohn for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He was born at Orvieto in 1607. At Sienna in 1625 he turned to verse. His models came in part through his own family.

Jedidiah put three confessional prayers into Hebrew verse. He used the Italian three-line form called terza rima. One prayer came from Bahya and one from R. Nissim. A third was by an unknown writer. He followed an Italian verse version by his grandfather Alatrini. He also wrote sonnets in Hebrew and Italian, plus a dirge.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-neuburger-ferdi:
Ferdinand Neuburger was a German dramatist of Frankfort. Isidore Singer and Franklin S. Wilson wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He was born at Düsseldorf on Aug. 28, 1839. He died at Frankfort on Oct. 27, 1895. He began as a tutor at the Philanthropin.

Neuburger soon left teaching to write for the stage alone. His first play, Markgräfin von Pommeraye, succeeded at Stuttgart in 1876. Laroche followed, a heroic drama built on Lassalle's career. Politics forced its withdrawal after one performance in 1882. A youthful piece, Das Gastmahl des Ponteus, also survives in mention. His record is short, but it marks a bold attempt. Lassalle on stage was a daring choice for the time.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-nissim-benvenis: Don Nissim Benveniste was a Spanish scholar of the fifteenth century. Joseph Jacobs and Isaac Broydé wrote his brief entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Little of his life is recorded in these lines. His fame rests on legal consultations with Isaac Aboab. Those exchanges of question and answer were printed long after. Abraham Meldola published them at Leghorn in 1745. They appear in his work called Shib'ah 'Enayim, under one title. The title is simply She'elah u-Teshubah, question and answer.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-odeka-11658:
Odeka is the first word of a verse in Psalm 118. Cyrus Adler and Francis L. Cohen wrote the entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. The psalm forms part of the Hallel, a set of praise psalms. Odeka marks the point where two choirs end their turn and turn singing. From there, the last verses are sung twice.

The way this is done shifts from rite to rite. In the Polish rite each man doubles the verses himself. Parts of one verse may thus be sung four times. The entry gives the tunes used for this verse. One tune comes from the Sephardic rite of Spain. One comes from the Ashkenazic rite of Germany. Both tunes are old and well loved by their groups.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-oren-11758:
Oren is a word used by German Jews for prayer. Cyrus Adler and Francis L. Cohen wrote its entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. It comes from the Latin word ora, which means pray. A German verb end was tacked on to that root. The word was known to all in the Middle Ages.

Oren does not mean just to pray in broad terms. It means to say one's set prayers, line by line. A man may do this with the flock in prayer. He may do it at home, in private, as well. Jews in Slav lands use a word dawenen in its place. In England and America, men say daven for the same act. The piece weighs where that word daven first came from.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-palaggi-falaji-:
Abraham Palaggi was a Turkish author and chief rabbi. Isidore Singer and M. Franco wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He was born at Smyrna in the year 1809. He died there in the year 1899. His father was Hayyim Palaggi, chief rabbi of Smyrna.

When his father died in 1869, Abraham took his post. An imperial decree gave him the chief rabbi's chair. He held that chair for a full thirty years in all. He oft stood up for Jews against a dire charge. That charge was the false claim of rite based murder. He wrote sixteen works in the Hebrew tongue in his life. He wrote one work in the Spanish tongue of Jews. Each Hebrew work held his name, Abraham, in its title.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-pavia-julius-lu:
Julius da Pavia was an Italian Jewish scholar of the eighth century. He is one of the first European Jews known by name. Isidore Singer and Umberto Cassuto wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. The record of him comes from Alcuin.

About 760 Julius held a public debate at Pavia. His opponent was Pietro da Pisa, a famed grammarian. They argued over religion before an audience. Alcuin later told Charlemagne about the dispute in a letter. He said the debate would be written down in a book. In some copies the scholar's name reads Lullus.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-pesaro-aaron-12:
Aaron Pesaro wrote a guide that links Bible verses to rabbinic books. Richard Gottheil and Ismar Elbogen wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. No one knows where or when he lived. He likely worked in Germany after 1400. The book served preachers and students for centuries.

His book is called Toledot Aharon, the Generations of Aaron. Beside each verse it notes where the Talmud explains it. It does the same for verses treated in the Midrash. Froben first printed it at Basel in 1580. Later editions in Venice and elsewhere kept it in use.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-pinczow-eliezer: Eliezer Pinczow was a Polish rabbi of the late 1600s. Herman Rosenthal and A. S. Waldstein wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. His grandfather had been rabbi of Lublin. He served as rabbi at Pinczow and other towns. He also sat as a lay leader at Cracow. Two of his books were printed after his death. One gives notes on the Masoretic text of the Bible. The other expounds the tales of the Talmud.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-polotsk-phineha:
Phinehas ben Judah of Polotsk was a Polish writer of notes on the Bible. The Editorial Board and Schulim Ochser wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He lived at Polotsk in the eighteenth century. His books deal with both wisdom books and song.

Phinehas wrote notes on Proverbs, printed at Wilna in 1803. He wrote on Canticles and Ecclesiastes at Grodno in 1804. His notes on the Book of Job came out in 1808. He also shortened a large work by Kalonymus ben Kalonymus. His Rosh ha-Gibeah treats morals and gives sermons. A further work on the commandments stayed in handwriting.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-priest-12358:
Priest, meaning one set apart for service at the altar, is the subject of an article by the Editorial Board and Moses Buttenwieser. It appeared in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. The writers warn that the word fits late times best. In early Israel no special setting apart was needed. Any man might come to the altar with a gift.

Gideon offered a sacrifice in person, the article notes. He belonged to the tribe of Manasseh, not Levi. Manoah the Danite did the same at an angel's word. Both acts are told as done at God's own command. The article traces how a free act became a priest's sole right. It follows the priesthood from clan days to Temple days.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-queensland-1245:
Queensland is a British colony in Australia, cut off from New South Wales in 1859. Joseph Jacobs and Jonas M. Myers wrote its entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. At the split, a few Jewish families moved from Sydney. They settled for good at Brisbane, the new capital. Their names are given in the entry one by one.

The families formed a congregation in about 1864. They called the Reverend Joseph E. Myers from Sydney to lead them. Coleman and Davis stood among the first names. Jewell, Mendoza, and Goldsmid stood there too. The entry traces the group's growth in Brisbane and beyond. It shows how a handful of homes became a settled body.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-reicherson-mose:
Moses ha-Kohen Reicherson was a Hebrew grammarian born on October 5, 1827. Herman Rosenthal and A. S. Waldstein wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. He was born in Wilna. He died in New York on April 3, 1903.

The article says he studied Talmud, Hebrew, and European languages. He taught Hebrew at Wilna for many years. About 1890 he moved to New York and taught there. His writing centers on Hebrew grammar in detail. Books treat punctuation, verbs, particles, and the noun. He made a grammar catechism for beginners as well. He translated fables by Krylov and by Lessing. Many commentaries stayed in manuscript at his death. The entry shows a teacher devoted to Hebrew's fine points.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-right-and-right:
Right and righteousness translate a family of Hebrew words. Emil G. Hirsch wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. The root is zadak, with forms like zaddik and zedek. English also uses just, justice, and justify for them.

The article admits the root's first sense is in doubt. One guess links it to being hard, even, or straight. A better reading is that a thing is as it should be. Weights and measures called zedek are simply right. Paths called zedek are easy to travel. A king or judge who acts properly is just. Speech that fits the facts is truthful speech. To justify means to show someone is in the right. The entry roots a moral idea in physical fitness.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-rosensohn-moses:
Moses Rosensohn was a Russian Hebraist who lived his whole life at Wilna, in comfort. Herman Rosenthal and Isidor Warsaw wrote his entry for the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia. He was born there early in the nineteenth century and died in 1896.

Rosensohn wrote several Hebrew works on the future of Judaism. One book urged reforms in Jewish religious life. Another praised the broad, universal spirit of the Mosaic religion. A third, in three volumes, defended the Cabala against its critics. His suspected leanings toward Christianity made Orthodox Jews of Russia shun him.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-saalschutz-loui:
Louis Saalschütz was a German mathematician born at Königsberg, Prussia, on December 1, 1835. Isidore Singer wrote his entry for the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia, working alone. He was a son of the rabbi Joseph Lewin Saalschütz.

Saalschütz studied mathematics and physics at Königsberg and took his doctorate in 1861. His dissertation studied heat changes deep in the earth's upper layers. For over twenty years he taught mechanics and engineering at the Royal School of Mechanics. He also lectured at the university, becoming assistant professor in 1875. For years he presided over Königsberg's Jewish orphan asylum.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-samaria-hebrew-:
Samaria was a city of Palestine and capital of the kingdom of Israel. Joseph Jacobs and M. Seligsohn wrote its entry for the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia. King Omri built it on the mountain Shomeron early in his reign.

Omri bought that mountain for two talents of silver from Shemer. He named the city Shomeron after its former owner, the Bible says. The entry doubts the tale, since the mountain already bore the name. It may mean watch mountain instead, a fit name for the site. Set in a fertile basin near Shechem, Samaria long ruled the Ten Tribes.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-samiler-smieler:
A. G. Samiler, born Eliakim Götzel and called Mehlsack, was a Russian Talmudist born at Smiela about 1780. Gotthard Deutsch wrote his entry for the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia, working alone. He belonged to a prominent rabbinical family of the region.

Samiler gave special care to the historical setting of rabbinic literature. He wrote valuable genealogical essays, still held in private hands at Lemberg and Vienna. His only printed work is Sefer Rabiyah, issued at Ofen in 1837. It criticizes Zunz's lectures on Jewish worship and Rapoport's life of Kalir. He died at Brody on July 17, 1854.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-samun-joseph-ha:
Isaac Broydé wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia entry, issued with the Executive Committee of the Editorial Board in 1906. It profiles Joseph Ḥayyim ibn Samun, an Italian Talmudist. He lived at Leghorn across the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries. Leghorn was a busy port with a large Jewish community. Samun wrote on the Talmud and on points of law.

His book 'Edut bi-Yehosef appeared at Leghorn in 1800. It fills two volumes. The first gives new readings on the tractate Baba Meẓi'a. The second gathers his responsa, his formal answers to legal questions. Appended to the work is Leḳaḥ Ṭob. That part holds readings and responsa by his son Shem-Ṭob. Shem-Ṭob served as rabbi of Leghorn.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-scherschewski-b:
Herman Rosenthal and Peter Wiernik wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia entry, published in 1906, on Benjamin Scherschewski. He was a Russian physician. Scherschewski was born at Brest-Litovsk in 1857. He studied medicine at the University of Warsaw. He graduated there in 1883. In 1885 he went to Palestine and settled in Jerusalem.

Two years later Scherschewski left for Vienna. There he took a special course in medicine. After another short stay in Jerusalem, he settled at Odessa. He still practices there in 1905. His book Mishnat 'Olam Ḳaṭon treats two sciences in Hebrew. Its first part covers anatomy, and its second part chemistry. Jehiel Michael Pines corrected and annotated the work. It was printed at Jerusalem in 1886.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-scroll-of-the-l:
Joseph Jacobs, Judah David Eisenstein, and Ludwig Blau wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, issued with the Executive Committee of the Editorial Board in 1906. It treats the Scroll of the Law, the Sefer Torah. That is the Pentateuch written by hand on parchment. The rabbis count writing such a scroll among every Israelite's duties. A king had to keep a second copy by his throne.

One who cannot write must hire a scribe or buy a scroll. An inherited scroll does not free a man from the duty. The scroll may not be sold, even in dire need. Exceptions cover a teacher's fee and marriage costs. The parchment must come from a clean animal's skin. It is dressed with gallnut and lime for strength. Lines are ruled, and only the best black ink is allowed. The scroll runs about six handbreadths wide.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-shammash-lit-se:
Shammash, literally servant, was an officer of the synagogue and the Jewish community. Joseph Jacobs and Peter Wiernik wrote the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia entry on the office. In Talmudic times the same worker was called hazzan. He helped lead parts of the prayer service then.

By the Middle Ages the shammash held real power and duty. He assessed members for taxes by their means. He ran the synagogue and carried out court sentences. In some places he even gave court-ordered lashes. One writer calls him a permanent under-secretary who governed quietly. The entry reveals the hired hand who kept self-governing Jewish towns working.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-shofar-12558:
Shofar is the ancient ritual horn of Israel, still blown in synagogue worship. Cyrus Adler, Francis L. Cohen, Abraham de Harkavy, and Judah David Eisenstein wrote the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia entry on it. Calling it trumpet or cornet misleads, the authors warn. Its name points rather to tuba or clarion.

The Bible mentions the shofar often, from Exodus to Zechariah. Its loud voice from Sinai's cloud made Israel tremble. Other instruments changed with each age's craft and fashion. Silver trumpets served the Temple in fixed form. The shofar alone never changed its simple, crude shape. That stubborn sameness marks it as a prehistoric survival. The entry traces its uses, from war calls and alarms to the solemn blasts of the New Year season.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-silberstein-otv:
Adolf Silberstein, called Ötvös, was a Hungarian art critic born at Budapest in 1845. Isidore Singer and Ludwig Venetianer wrote the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia entry on him. He studied philosophy and medicine at Leipzig University. Berlin added comparative philology, and Heidelberg added history and economics.

He took his doctorate at Leipzig in 1866. Journalism then claimed him across German-language papers. He edited a weekly on drama with two collaborators. Back in Hungary from 1870, he edited the Temesvarer Zeitung. Later he wrote for Budapest's leading German dailies. His Bible of Nature, printed in 1877, caused a sensation. Bradlaugh translated it into English for wider readers. Russia suppressed the book outright, the entry reports. He died at Budapest in 1899.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-solomon-ben-eli:
Solomon ben Elijah Sharbit ha-Zahab was an astronomer, poet, and grammarian. Crawford Howell Toy and Isaac Broydé wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. He lived at Salonica and later at Ephesus. His time was the second half of the fourteenth century. His Hebrew name may match the Greek name Chrysakokka.

He rendered Persian astronomical tables into Hebrew from the Greek. He also translated Ptolemy's treatise on the astrolabe. His own works include a grammatical treatise, Heshek Shelomoh. He wrote a commentary on Ibn Ezra's Sefer ha-Shem as well. Many of his liturgical poems entered prayer books. His Pentateuch commentary attacked Karaite views with great force.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-spielmann-sir-i:
Sir Isidore Spielmann was an English engineer and communal worker born in 1854. Joseph Jacobs wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. He was born in London on July 21 of that year. He trained as an engineer but loved art deeply. In 1887 he proposed the Anglo-Jewish Historical Exhibition in London.

He served as honorary secretary of that exhibition throughout. He later led the Jewish Historical Society of England for years. He directed British sections at Brussels, Paris, Glasgow, and St Louis. For those services he was knighted in 1905 by the king. He edited Darkest Russia to expose abuse of Jews there. He refused a Russian exhibition post on principle as a Jew.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-stokvis-barend-:
Barend Joseph Stokvis was a Dutch physician born at Amsterdam in 1834. Isidore Singer and E. Slijper wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article about him in 1906. He was born on August 16, son of a physician. He studied in Amsterdam, Paris, and Vienna. He died on September 28, 1902.

Stokvis won a Brussels Academy gold medal in 1867. His prize essay studied the causes of albuminuria. In 1874 he became professor at the University of Amsterdam. He taught pathology and the action of drugs. He led congresses of colonial and Dutch doctors. Edinburgh gave him an honorary law degree in 1884. His books cover liver sugar, diabetes, and tropical medicine. The entry profiles a doctor honored across Europe.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-theodora-14358:
Theodora, born Sarah, was a Jewish woman who became queen of Bulgaria. Isidore Singer and M. Franco wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. She was born at Tirnova to a family of Byzantine Jews. She reigned beside Czar Ivan Alexander from 1335 to 1355.

The czar met her when she presented a petition. He married her after she accepted Christianity. They had three children together. A council in 1352 condemned heretics and Jews alike. Her pleas saved three condemned Jews from death. Still, Tirnova's Jewish community was dispersed for good. Theodora also secured the throne for her own son. Bulgarian historians blamed that choice for weakening the kingdom.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-tosefta-lit-ext:
The Tosefta is a collection of early legal sayings fuller than the Mishnah's. Wilhelm Bacher and Jacob Zallel Lauterbach wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. Its name means additions or extensions. Teachers such as Akiba and Judah added notes to old rulings. A saying with its additions was itself called a tosefta.

The Mishnah gives traditional law in condensed form. The Tosefta gives the same sayings more completely. Talmudic literature cites a Tosefta collection often. Most critics identify it with the work still extant. R. Johanan's remarks support that identification, the article argues. The name is properly a plural, Tosefata. Usage settled on the singular form by mistake. Few texts show rabbinic law growing so clearly.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-u-ba-le-ziyyon-:
U-Ba le-Ziyyon is the closing prayer of the daily morning service. Cyrus Adler and Francis L. Cohen wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. Its opening words quote Isaiah: the Redeemer shall come to Zion. Worshipers should not leave synagogue before it, the code says. The prayer gathers a series of sacred texts.

Among them stands the Kedushah with its Aramaic paraphrase. Two brief ancient prayers ask for enlightenment through study. Ashre, Psalm 145, always precedes the prayer closely. Most of it is read in an undertone. The cantor intones only the opening lines aloud. Ashkenazic chant borrows the Sabbath afternoon motive. Sephardic tradition uses a special older melody. Its roots reach back before 1492 in Spain.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-veigelsberg-leo:
Leo Veigelsberg was a Hungarian journalist and editor. He was born on January 18, 1846. Isidore Singer and Ludwig Venetianer wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia entry, published in 1906. He studied at Budapest and Vienna. After brief teaching, he joined a newspaper staff in 1867. Since 1872 he has edited the Pester Lloyd.

His signed lead articles drew wide attention in Hungary. In 1904 the emperor gave him the Order of the Iron Crown. The entry also notes his son Hugo. Hugo became a noted young writer of poems and stories. He wrote under names like Dixi and Ignotus. His books include verse collections and a translated novel.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-wakrulkar-solom:
Solomon Elijah Wakrulkar was a Beni Israel soldier in India. Joseph Jacobs and J. Hyams wrote this short entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He enlisted in the Nineteenth Regiment Native Infantry in 1838. He rose step by step through the native ranks. By 1872 he held the rank of subahdar major.

Wakrulkar fought in three hard campaigns. In Afghanistan he saw Ghazni taken and Kabul held. In the Punjab he fought at Multan and Gujarat. He also marched in the Central India campaign of 1858. In 1877 he won the Order of British India. Its titles were the highest honor for native officers. He retired in 1878.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-yannai-15058:
Yannai was a scholar of Palestine in the third century of this era. Joseph Jacobs and Schulim Ochser wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He was the father-in-law of the scholar Ammi. He says in one place that he had a grandson of his name.

He is known for one debate on the books of King Solomon. That debate asked which book the king wrote last of all. Yannai held that Kohelet was the last book from his pen. The entry is short and rests on two learned books. One is a study of the tales of the Palestine schools. One is a chain book of the past of the rabbis. No works of Yannai are named in the piece at all. The note keeps him in mind for one clear stand he took.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-zamosz-israel-b:
Israel ben Moses ha-Levi Zamosz (born about 1700) was a Polish Talmud man and math mind. Joseph Jacobs and M. Seligsohn wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Born at Buberki, he died at Brody in 1772. He taught at the great school of Zamosz in his prime.

At that school he read the works of the world as well. Math drew his mind more than all else there. He wrote notes on two old books of math and faith. In those years he penned a work on the frame of the sky. That work still lies in draft to this day. In 1742 he left for Berlin for some years. There he taught Moses Mendelssohn in math and in logic. The famed Lessing held his lore in high awe as well.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-zilzer-antal-an:
Antal Zilzer was a Hungarian painter known chiefly for his portraits. Isidore Singer and Newell Dunbar wrote his short entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Zilzer was born at Budapest in 1861. He trained at the national model school of design there, under Rauscher, Gregusz, and Szekely.

He later studied at the Munich Academy under several teachers, then finished his training in Berlin, Paris, and London. In 1887 he received the Munich gold medal. His paintings named here include Alone in the Woods and Ludwig II on His Funeral Bier. Forest Idyls and Sunset on the Lake of Constance are also listed among his works.
king-henry-viii-pg2258: Wolsey falls in this edition: the great Cardinal, stripped of power, finds his conscience at last. "Had I but served my God with half the zeal I served my king." Pageantry and pathos fill Shakespeare's last history.
liddell-scott-abridged-greek-lexicon-185:
Henry Liddell and Robert Scott published their great Greek-English Lexicon in 1843, and the abridged version, nicknamed the Little Liddell, followed for students. The 1858 printing comes from the sixth edition of the parent work. Generations of schoolboys and undergraduates learned Greek with it open.

The abridgment keeps every common word with its main senses, forms, and constructions, in compact type. Students could carry it where the giant lexicon could not go. Liddell, dean of Christ Church, was also the father of Alice, of Wonderland fame. This little book remains a monument of Victorian classical schooling.
linnaeus-systema-naturae-vol1-1758:
Carl Linnaeus's Systema Naturae appears here in Volume 1 of its tenth edition, dated 1758. No public-domain English translation exists, so the text stands in Latin. The tenth edition is the starting point of zoological naming, the baseline every later name is checked against.

Volume 1 covers Animalia, the animal kingdom, arranged in classes from mammals to worms and insects. Linnaeus gave each species a two-part name, genus and species, the binomial system science still uses. He placed humans among the primates, a bold step for his age. The volume founded binomial nomenclature for animals and remains the reference from which zoology counts its naming history.
longfellow-miles-standish-1858:
Henry Wadsworth Longfellow published The Courtship of Miles Standish in 1858, drawing on the history of Plymouth Colony written by his own ancestor. Longfellow claimed descent from John Alden himself. The poem sold tens of thousands of copies within weeks, in America and England alike.

Captain Miles Standish, the colony's blunt little military leader, loves the newcomer Priscilla Mullins but is too awkward to court her. He sends his young friend John Alden to plead his case. Priscilla's answer became famous: why don't you speak for yourself, John? The love triangle plays out against Indian alarms, sickness, and the work of planting a colony. Longfellow's hexameters helped make Plymouth the American origin story.
marguerite-de-valois-memoirs-1658:
Marguerite de Valois, queen of Navarre and wife of Henri IV, wrote her Mémoires around 1594 about the court she grew up in. They were first published in 1628, and the English translation of 1658 carries them here. Marguerite was sister to three French kings and daughter of Catherine de Medici, placed at the heart of power and danger.

Her memoir covers the French wars of religion from inside the palace, with weddings, plots, and the shadow of massacre. She writes with grace and self-defense, eager to set her own story straight. The book became the classic insider memoir of the Valois court. Its voice, a queen's own, still sounds clear across four centuries.
memoirs-of-the-court-of-louis-xiv-and-of:
Book four of the Duchesse d'Orleans's memoirs opens with Victor Amadeus II. The Grand Duchess of Florence and the Duchesse de Lorraine follow in the heads. The Duc du Maine, Louvois, and Louis XV stand there as well.

Victor Amadeus, King of Sicily, is said to quarrel with his mistresses. Madame de Verrue shared some stolen gold medals with the writer. She bought 160 medals, half of those the lady stole, she admits. A counter poison once saved Madame de Verrue at a dinner table. Her brother was sent to fetch her back from Turin by night. A small parrot rode with her on that flight from the King.
michaelis-maieri-cantilenae-intellectual:
Michael Maier's intellectual songs on the resurrection of the phoenix appeared in this Paris edition in 1758. Maier had died more than a century earlier, in 1622. The volume prints his Latin text with a French translation on facing pages. The translator signs himself only M. L. L. M., and the bookseller Debure sold the bound book for three livres.

In alchemy, the phoenix stands for matter destroyed by fire and reborn in finer form. Maier casts that doctrine as songs, mixing poetry with chemical teaching. French readers of 1758 thus met a German physician's Latin verses in their own tongue. The edition shows how alchemical classics kept circulating long after their authors died.
morris-defence-guenevere-1858:
William Morris was twenty-four when The Defence of Guenevere appeared in 1858. It was his first book and the first volume of Pre-Raphaelite poetry published in England. Morris, a wealthy young Oxford graduate, filled it with the medieval world he loved.

In the title poem, Queen Guenevere defends herself before Arthur's court against charges of betrayal, arguing with passion and cunning. Other poems retell Arthurian tales and dark medieval stories of love and violence. The verse is vivid, strange, and deliberately old-fashioned in diction. The book sold poorly at first but now stands as a landmark of Victorian medievalism.
nightingale-subsidiary-notes-nursing-185:
Before her famous nursing work took shape, Florence Nightingale wrote her Subsidiary Notes in 1858. The memorandum, privately printed, treats female nursing in military hospitals in peace and war. She drew on her Crimean War experience with sick and wounded soldiers. The paper laid out how army nursing should be organized and trained.

Her plan covered staffing, discipline, pay, and the standing of nurses in the ranks. It became the policy paper behind the Nightingale Fund. That fund built the training school that reshaped nursing. The Gutenberg text preserves a reform at the planning stage. Readers see her mind working on systems, not slogans. It rewards close study.
olaus-magnus-compendious-history-streate:
Olaus Magnus, a Swedish churchman, published his great history of the northern peoples in Latin in 1555. This English version of 1658 shortens that vast work for London readers. It describes the Goths, Swedes, and Vandals, and the cold lands they came from.

Early modern Scandinavia appears here as a land of marvels. Sea serpents coil in northern waters, and mermen rise from the deep. Snow, ice, and the midnight sun shape every custom he reports. English readers of 1658 met the north mainly through such wonders. The book mixes real report with sailors' tales, and both halves are worth reading.
openalex-w1549441458:
B. Abelev and the ALICE Collaboration reported this measurement. It appeared in Physical Review Letters in September 2013. The team studied D mesons in lead-lead collisions. D mesons are particles that contain a charm quark. Noncentral collisions leave an oval overlap zone, they explain.

The team measured how particle flow favors that oval's plane. This favoring is called elliptic flow by physicists. D meson flow matched light particle flow in size. The signal was clearly positive at lower momenta. The result shows charm quarks move with the hot medium. That medium is the quark-gluon plasma formed in collisions.
openalex-w1896237858:
Yaritza Salas and three co-authors studied tumors in female dogs. Their paper appeared in PLoS ONE in May 2015. Mammary tumors are a growing health problem in dogs, they note. The team reviewed cases diagnosed from 2002 to 2012. Records came from a pathology service in Mexico City.

Nearly two thousand biopsies of intact dogs were reviewed. Benign and malignant tumors each made up near half. Epithelial tumors were the most common type found. Pure breeds formed most submissions to the service. Poodles, Cocker Spaniels, and German Shepherds led the list. Adult dogs aged nine to twelve were most affected.
openalex-w2111179758:
Pedro Alonso, Graham Brown, Myriam Arevalo-Herrera and colleagues set out a research agenda for malaria eradication. Their paper appeared in PLoS Medicine in 2011. Ending malaria transmission worldwide is a huge challenge. Aggressive use of current tools can gain much ground. New tools are still needed to finish the job.

Experts reviewed where research must focus. Vaccines, drugs and mosquito control all feature. Diagnostics need to find silent infections better. Health systems research matters as much as products. The agenda grew from a broad expert consultation. It lists priorities for funders and researchers. Eradication needs long-term, coordinated investment, they argue.
openalex-w2138134458:
Omid Hamid, Henrik Schmidt, Aviram Nissan, and colleagues published this trial in the Journal of Translational Medicine in 2011. They tested ipilimumab, an immune drug for advanced melanoma, and hunted for tumor signs that predict who benefits. The drug frees T cells to attack cancer by blocking a brake protein called CTLA-4.

Eighty-two patients with hard-to-treat melanoma received one of two dose levels. Tumor samples were taken before treatment and soon after the second dose. Response and safety matched earlier trials, and gene variants showed no link to benefit. Tumors starting with high levels of two immune markers responded better. So did tumors where immune cells flowed in more after treatment began.
openalex-w2154761658:
Jozef Vercruysse, Jerzy Behnke, Marco Albonico, and colleagues published this study in PLoS Neglected Tropical Diseases in 2011. They measured how well one dose of albendazole, a standard deworming drug, works in school children. Three gut worms spread through soil are among the world's most common parasites, yet drug monitoring lacked standard procedures.

Seven trials ran in Brazil, Cameroon, Cambodia, Ethiopia, India, Tanzania, and Vietnam. All used one shared protocol with a single standard dose. Success was scored by cure rate and by how far egg counts in stool fell. The trials together set reference values for judging this drug against roundworm, whipworm, and hookworm in future programs.
openalex-w2171372458:
Anna Rosanas-Urgell, Enmoore Lin, Laurens Manning, and colleagues published this study in PLoS Medicine in 2012. They tested whether Southeast Asian ovalocytosis, an inherited red blood cell shape trait, protects children against Plasmodium vivax malaria. The trait was already known to guard against severe falciparum malaria, but its effect on vivax was unclear.

Nearly two thousand children in Papua New Guinea were genotyped across three studies. In an infant cohort, carriers had almost half the rate of clinical vivax episodes. In older children, carriers also showed far fewer blood-stage reinfections, by both gene tests and microscopy. The results extend the trait's protection to the second great malaria parasite.
openalex-w2411750058:
Francesca Sprovieri, Nicola Pirrone, Mariantonia Bencardino, and colleagues published this study in Atmospheric Chemistry and Physics in 2016. Mercury drifts globally through the air and poisons food webs, yet monitoring was patchy where data mattered most. The Global Mercury Observation System built a coordinated worldwide network to fix that, starting in 2010.

More than forty ground stations now span regions that previously had no records at all. This paper presents the network's first five years of concentrations, examining trends, seasons, and comparability between sites. One headline stands out: mercury levels form a clear gradient between the northern and southern hemispheres. The authors trace that divide mostly to local and regional sources, natural and human-made combined.
openalex-w2588228158:
Isabelle Romieu, Laure Dossus, and Simón Barquera wrote this 2017 paper in Cancer Causes & Control for an IARC working group. The International Agency for Research on Cancer convened experts in December 2015 to review evidence on energy balance and obesity. They paid special attention to low and middle income countries. The paper asks what mainly drives the global obesity epidemic.

The group links the epidemic to poor diet quality and unbalanced energy intake. In poorer countries, undernutrition and overnutrition now coexist in the same populations. Mediterranean-style diets and other quality measures can support long-term weight control. Cutting sugar-sweetened drinks plays a particularly important role, they find. Genes alone cannot explain the epidemic's speed. Still, genetics, epigenetics, and gut microbes shape how individuals respond to food and activity.
openalex-w2607179358:
Adeera Levin, Marcello A. Tonelli, and Joseph Vincent Bonventre lead the authors of this 2017 Lancet Commission roadmap on global kidney health. It grew from a 2016 summit in Vancouver held by the International Society of Nephrology. Over eighty-five experts from many fields and countries took part. Their task: plan how to close the world's gaps in kidney care, research, and policy.

The group set priorities for the next five to ten years across ten themes. Early themes demand counting chronic kidney disease properly and cutting its major risk factors. Others target preventing kidney injury episodes and understanding genetic causes of the disease. Better diagnosis of kidney structure and function also ranks high. The plan names partners inside and outside nephrology and sets a performance framework. Clinicians, patients, scientists, industry, and governments are its intended users.
openalex-w2803280558:
Massimo Sartelli, Gian Luca Baiocchi, and Salomone Di Saverio lead the POSAW study of appendicitis care worldwide. It appeared in the World Journal of Emergency Surgery in 2018. Acute appendicitis is the world's most common surgical disease. Removing the appendix cures most cases, but diagnosis and complicated cases still challenge hospitals. This prospective study watched real practice across the globe.

One hundred sixteen surgical departments in forty-four countries enrolled patients over six months in 2016. The study captured 4,282 patients with a median age of twenty-nine. Doctors used CT scans in about a fifth of cases and ultrasound in over two-fifths. Nearly ninety-six percent of patients had surgery, split between open and keyhole approaches. About four percent were managed without an operation. The snapshot exposes how differently the same disease is handled worldwide, and where practice could converge.
openalex-w2804562858:
Axel Hollmann, Melina María Belén Martínez, and Patricia Maturana reviewed antimicrobial peptides in Frontiers in Chemistry in 2018. Antibiotic resistance is eroding treatments for common infections worldwide. Failure would endanger surgery, cancer chemotherapy, and fights against HIV and malaria. These peptides, made by organisms from microbes to humans, offer a fresh strategy.

They form part of the first line of immune defense in many species. They attack bacteria largely by breaking their outer walls. The review studies how they interact with model and real cell membranes. It also covers synergy, where they boost standard antibiotics beyond either alone. Action against drug-resistant bacteria is their most prized feature. Grasping these membrane actions should guide designing peptide drugs that survive clinical use.
openalex-w2886207958:
Bruno Lima Giacobbo, Janine Doorduin, and Hans Christiaan Klein lead this review of BDNF and brain inflammation, published online in 2018 in Molecular Neurobiology. BDNF is a growth factor that keeps neurons alive, adaptable, and communicating. Patients with psychiatric and degenerative brain disorders often show reduced BDNF in blood and brain. The review explores whether chronic brain inflammation explains those low levels.

Activated glial cells release inflammatory molecules and reactive oxygen species. Those signals can disrupt the pathways BDNF depends on, harming neurons. Understanding inflammation's role in disease onset and progression could unlock new treatments, the authors argue. The hypothesis ties two separate literatures together: neurotrophin biology and neuroimmunology. If inflammation suppresses BDNF, calming it might restore the factor's protection. The review maps the evidence for that chain, link by link. It speaks to researchers hunting drug targets in diseases from depression to Alzheimer's.
openalex-w2898783558:
Shan Wu, Kin H. Lau, and Qinghe Cao lead an international team sequencing sweetpotato's wild relatives in Nature Communications in 2018. Cultivated sweetpotato is a hexaploid, with ninety chromosomes, and ranks seventh among world food crops. It feeds subsistence farmers across sub-Saharan Africa with fiber, vitamins, and resilience. Orange-fleshed varieties combat vitamin A deficiency, a breakthrough honored with the World Food Prize.

The cultivated genome's complexity slows breeding, so the team turned to two diploid wild relatives. Their genome sequences are far simpler to assemble and read. Comparing them with the crop reveals targets for genetic improvement. Candidate genes touch traits breeders need, from nutrition to stress tolerance. Wild relatives thus become a parts catalog for upgrading a food security staple. The work shows how sequencing the cousins of a complex crop can shortcut its improvement.
openalex-w2917335258:
Aziz Bousfiha, Leïla Jeddane, Capucine Picard, and colleagues present the 2017 phenotypic classification for primary immunodeficiencies in the Journal of Clinical Immunology.
