These disorders, now called inborn errors of immunity, are genetic defects that weaken the body's defense against infection.

Since the 1990s, an expert committee of the International Union of Immunological Societies has published a full catalog of these disorders about every two years. That catalog serves researchers and specialists worldwide, but it was hard to use at the bedside. Since 2013 the committee has also issued a phenotypic version, grouping disorders by their clinical features so doctors can apply it in practice.
openalex-w2969767558:
Toste Tanhua, Andrea McCurdy, Albert Fischer, and colleagues wrote this 2019 review in Frontiers in Marine Science. It looks back at the Framework for Ocean Observing, a plan that reshaped how the world watches its oceans. The review traces how the Global Ocean Observing System evolved under that framework.

The authors take stock of lessons learned while building a coordinated worldwide ocean watch. Such a system joins data from floats, ships, satellites, and coastal stations into shared products. It serves climate forecasts, weather warnings, and marine management. By reviewing what the framework achieved and where it fell short, the paper guides the next stage of global ocean observation.
openalex-w2990643258:
Mao-Qiang He, Rui-Lin Zhao, Kevin Hyde, and colleagues published this reference work in Fungal Diversity in 2019. It gives a full outline of the Basidiomycota, a major phylum of fungi second only to the Ascomycota in species numbers. Mushrooms, bracket fungi, and many yeasts belong to this group.

The authors list every genus in current use, nearly two thousand names, arranged into families, orders, classes, and subphyla. For each accepted genus they add brief notes on classification, species count, type species, way of life, habitat, range, and DNA sequence data. They also run family-tree analyses to estimate when the main lines split. The result is a single reference for the whole phylum.
openalex-w3043776158:
Arti Naidu, Vincent Bennani, John Aarts, and Paul Brunton wrote this review in the Brazilian Dental Journal in 2020. It weighs the evidence for over-the-counter tooth whitening products. Such products are easy to buy, yet solid data on how well they work had been scarce.

The authors reviewed studies from 2006 to 2018 that compared the main product types against placebo, no treatment, or each other. The leading categories are whitening toothpastes, whitening strips, and paint-on gels. Each claims to lift stains and brighten shade, but stains differ in kind and depth. By sorting the trial evidence in one place, the review helps dentists and buyers judge which claims hold up.
openalex-w3173611258:
Mansour Almazroui, Moetasim Ashfaq, M. Nazrul Islam, and colleagues assess the newest global climate models over South America. Their study appeared in Earth Systems and Environment in 2021. The models come from the CMIP6 project, a worldwide comparison of climate simulations. The team checked them against recent climate records for the continent.

The models captured the main climate patterns well, though skill varied by region, mainly at high altitude and latitude. Looking ahead, rain falls over Amazonia and the southern Andes but rises in the southeast. Warming, by contrast, appears under every scenario, even the mildest. Most rain changes stay within the range of natural variation seen today.
openalex-w4200189258:
Shen Yuan, Bruce Linquist, Lloyd Wilson, and colleagues argue for growing more rice with less harm, in Nature Communications in 2021. Rice feeds nearly half the world's people and uses a large share of farm water, fertiliser, and pesticide. Demand keeps rising, yet yield growth has stalled in some major rice regions. The authors call the needed path sustainable intensification.

A key measure is the yield gap, the distance between what a field could produce and what farmers actually harvest. Regions with wide gaps hold the largest room for gains. Closing gaps toward a realistic share of potential needs better seeds, advice, and market access. The paper maps where research money could raise output while cutting environmental damage.
openalex-w4293207258: Marc Humbert, Gábor Kovács, Marius Hoeper, and colleagues present the 2022 guidelines on pulmonary hypertension from two European medical societies. They appeared in the European Respiratory Journal and cover how the disease is found and treated. In this condition, blood pressure runs high in the arteries of the lungs. The sample holds only the publisher's citation page and author list. It has no readable guideline text, so the guidance cannot be described from it here.
openalex-w7163351058: Certain crystals can turn light directly into electricity, no junction needed. This theoretical paper studies that bulk photovoltaic effect in a single atomic layer of tin sulfide, using quantum models of electron hopping. The authors compare short- and long-range models. Condensed-matter theory chasing better solar materials atom by atom.
openalex-w7203590458: Light can grab and hold objects far smaller than a cell. This Japanese-language review covers nanoscale optical trapping for chemistry: how focused light and plasmon waves manipulate matter, and what the technique enables. The authors survey the physics and the applications. An optics review of tweezers made of light.
openalex-w7208831058:
Adson Antonio Vieira Santos and three colleagues tell of a shop class on farm life goods and rot heaps, held for new farm-craft staff in Brazil. Farm life goods are live or wild-born goods used in fields in place of some man-made feeds and sprays. The class ran in March 2025, after three months of plan work. Some forty folk came.

To run the class, the new staff had to turn tech lore into teach stuff. They fit words to the crowd, set the day's shape, and met doubts on the spot. The crowd joined most in the hands-on parts. The team grants their tools cannot prove gains that last. Still, the class was a true drill ground: the kind of run that shapes a staff hand before the first real class.
openalex-w7213241158:
Igor Barbosa Henrique da Silva leads a team on why small firms in Brazil die young. Such firms fill a huge share of the land's trade, yet crowds of them fold in their first years. The team read books, studies, and trade briefs on the theme. Their ask: what part do cash rule and books play in the fall?

The flaw, they find, is not blank minds. Most heads know the tools by name. What lacks is the day's grind: no cash watch, thin plans for lean weeks, and home cash mixed with firm cash in one pot. Their fix is a shift in the books trade: from tax forms ground out by rote to a guide at the head's side. Watch the cash, watch the health signs, and a firm can see a storm while it can still turn.
openalex-w7213589958:
Aline dos Santos Araujo, as spelled in the sample byline, leads a literature review on social media and dental aesthetics. Their 2026 review gathers studies from 2020 to 2026 in PubMed, SciELO, and Google Scholar, mixing quantitative and qualitative work. Smile content online now shapes beauty ideas widely.

Social media influence how people judge their own appearance, self-esteem, and social acceptance, the review finds. That influence reaches the decision to seek dental aesthetic procedures. Patients arrive with expectations formed by images seen online. The authors set out to measure that impact on aesthetic perception and treatment choice. Their synthesis helps dentists read patient demand against the pressures of a feed-driven beauty culture.
openalex-w7213975858:
Natália Santos Moreira and Daniella Barreto-Santana report active methods in a ninth-grade literature class in Curaçá, Bahia. Their 2026 descriptive, reflective report covers eight pupils in a public school class. The book at the centre is Carolina Maria de Jesus's diary of favela life, Child of the Dark in English editions.

A planned teaching sequence used literary gatherings, guided debates, writing production, and conversation circles. Pupil participation, talk, and written work supplied the evidence, observed by the teacher. Engagement in reading and discussion rose, the authors report, along with reflection on the social questions in the book. Active methods, they conclude, can deepen pupils' critical relationship with literary text.
openalex-w7215724258:
Paulo Roberto Barbosa dos Santos and Tarcykelly de Sena Santos da Silva wrote a 2026 article on inclusive education for autistic students in Brazil, joining teaching methods, human rights, and education policy. Inclusive education, they stress, means real conditions for access, participation, learning, and development, not simply placing a student in the room. Their study joins a literature review and policy documents with watching of specialized support sessions held across late 2025 and 2026.

Visual resources, hands-on materials, art activities, sensory proposals, and teaching games widened taking part when chosen from each student's known needs, barriers, and goals. The sessions also showed how much depends on joining that support, the regular classroom, plans for each student, school heads, and support staff. Inclusion, the authors conclude, rests not on any single method but on teaching planning, teamwork, and respect for rights.
openalex-w7220981258:
Mariana Domingos de Lima, João de Sousa Pinheiro Barbosa, and Elisângela de Andrade Aoyama reviewed recent literature on humane nursing care for older patients in hospital, publishing in 2026. With populations aging and elderly admissions rising, they ask what care looks like when it treats the patient as a whole person rather than a set of physical problems.

Studies from 2021 onward show hospital stays can bring lost autonomy, separation from family, loneliness, anxiety, and confusion for older people. The reviewed work answers with welcome, trust, clear communication, and a say for patients in their own care. The authors present humanization not as kindness added on top, but as a core part of safe, respectful hospital nursing.
openalex-w7220981758:
Bruno Matos de Farias and Kátia Ramos Barroso argue for environmental education as everyday work that forms citizens who protect rivers. Their 2026 article is aligned with the United Nations 2030 Agenda. They describe water resources under threat from cleared riverbanks, irregular building along margins, dumped waste, and silting that worsens floods.

Alongside their discussion of conservation and recovery, the authors present a teaching product built from the research: Guardians of the River — Sustainability Mission, an interactive school resource. Its aim is to make reflection concrete, so pupils adopt real preservation habits. The article treats the school as the natural starting point for a culture that values water.
openalex-w7221096458:
Andressa Mendes Sousa and three co-authors reviewed studies from 2020 to 2025 on patients who keep using opioids long after an orthopedic fracture, publishing in 2026. Continued use can harden into dependence, complicate healing, and slow the return of function, so the team searched for who is at risk and how tapering can work.

Seven studies, drawn from nearly two hundred candidates, named the main risk factors: prior opioid use, chronic pain, psychological disorders, older age, multiple illnesses, and generous post-surgery prescriptions. Dependence brought tolerance, withdrawal, intoxication, and overdose. Multimodal pain relief, patient education, live prescription monitoring, and team follow-up worked best, and the authors call for care protocols built on that evidence.
openalex-w7221197558:
Gabriela Luiza Cima Cardoso and four co-authors report a small veterinary case study on colostrum, the first milk that decides a newborn calf's immunity, published in 2026. Calves are born without antibodies and depend entirely on drinking colostrum quickly. The team worked at a school farm in Cascavel, Paraná, with two Purunã cows and their heifer calves.

Colostrum from one cow tested at high quality before birth and the other at intermediate quality, measured by a Brix refractometer. Both calves were vigorous, suckled strongly, and drank within two hours of birth. Blood tests at forty-eight hours showed total protein levels the authors read as sound passive immunity transfer. Careful colostrum checking, they conclude, pays.
pernety-les-fables-egyptiennes-et-grecqu: Pernety, Les Fables Égyptiennes et Grecques, vol. 2, 1758. The Egyptian fables. It endures in the archive. Its contents inform the historical record. The library keeps the document safe. Writers of history may cite it later. The paper lasts as a quiet witness.
plos-pbio-0020158:
Jun Wu, Thomas J. Klein, and Marek Mlodzik studied signal receptors in the fruit fly for PLOS Biology in 2004. Frizzled receptors pass Wnt signals, which guide growth and body pattern. The authors tracked where in the cell these receptors sit, a trait set by their inner tails.

Where a receptor sits decides which signals it can send. The team's work shows the tail acts like an address label, sending the receptor to the right cell compartment. That placement then tunes the strength and kind of signal that follows. The study adds a layer to how Wnt signaling is controlled, a pathway that is central to development and often goes wrong in cancer.
plos-pbio-0020258:
Jennifer L. Nemhauser, Todd C. Mockler, and Joanne Chory studied plant hormone cross-talk in PLOS Biology in 2004. Plants use hormones called brassinosteroids and auxin to guide growth. Both affect stems, roots, and leaves, so their signals must be coordinated rather than sent in isolation.

Using the model plant Arabidopsis, the team showed the two pathways lean on each other. Many genes respond to both signals, and blocking one changes the effect of the other. That interdependence is a design rule for plant growth control. It matters for farming, since tweaks to one hormone path will ripple into the other. The paper helped move plant science past single-hormone thinking.
plos-pone-0000058:
Yuan-Ping Pang pointed drug designers at a fresh target for stopping malaria mosquitoes in a 2006 paper. Acetylcholinesterase is an enzyme in the insect nervous system, and poisons that block it are a main class of insecticides. Resistance and harm to other species limit the old compounds, which hit a well-known site on the enzyme.

Pang identified a novel target site on acetylcholinesterase, a fresh place where a control agent might bind. A new site raises the hope of insecticides that kill malaria-carrying mosquitoes while sparing humans and helpful insects, and that work even where resistance has beaten the old sprays. For a disease spread only by these mosquitoes, better control tools save lives directly.
plos-pone-0000158:
Paul D. Waters, Gauthier Dobigny, Peter J. Waddell, and colleagues published this evolution paper in PLOS ONE in 2007. LINE-1 is a jumping gene, a stretch of DNA that copies itself into new spots in the genome. It makes up a large share of mammal DNA. The authors trace its history across the major clades of placental mammals.

By comparing LINE-1 across species, the team reconstructs when this element was active and how it spread. The story helps explain why mammal genomes differ so much in size and content. It also gives a backdrop for the many gene changes that jumping elements cause, for better and worse.
plos-pone-0000258:
Michael J. Angilletta, Robbie S. Wilson, Amanda C. Niehaus, and colleagues published this urban ecology paper in PLOS ONE in 2007, under the heading of urban physiology. It reports that city ants possess high heat tolerance, handling temperatures that would trouble their rural kin. Cities run warmer than the countryside, a heat island effect ants must cope with.

Urban animals are evolving under new pressures, and heat is one of the sharpest. The authors compare the heat tolerance of city ants with what the species normally shows. The result is an early data point in the study of how wildlife adapts to city life.
plos-pone-0000358:
Justin D. Blethrow, Chao Tang, Changhui Deng, and colleagues published this proteomics methods paper in PLOS ONE in 2007. It presents a modular mass spectrometric tool for analyzing protein complexes. The tool reads what the complexes are made of, and how their parts are phosphorylated, chemically tagged in ways that switch activity. The tool's modules can be combined as needed.

Protein complexes run the cell, and their tags change with conditions. A modular instrument workflow makes such analysis more routine and flexible. The paper is a methods contribution to proteomics, the large-scale study of proteins, as it moved from listing parts to mapping their states.
plos-pone-0000458:
Jennifer Hartt Meyers and colleagues studied how HIV weakens a specialized immune cell, in a 2007 PLOS ONE paper. Plasmacytoid dendritic cells are the body's champion producers of interferon, an alarm signal against viruses. The team measured the impact of HIV on these cells' survival and on their antiviral activity.

If HIV kills or disables the very cells meant to raise the alarm, the immune system starts the fight already handicapped. Documenting that damage helps explain why HIV infection so often becomes chronic. It also points to protecting or restoring these cells as a possible treatment strategy, alongside drugs that attack the virus directly.
plos-pone-0000558:
Yuri B. Yurov and colleagues examined chromosome errors in the developing human brain, reporting in PLOS ONE in 2007. Aneuploidy means a cell carries the wrong number of chromosomes; confined chromosomal mosaicism means only some cells in the tissue are affected. The team documented both in brain development.

The brain was long assumed to be chromosomally uniform. Finding mosaicism there raises questions about how much variation is normal and whether abnormal patches contribute to disease. Counting chromosomes cell by cell in developing tissue is slow work, but it set reference points for later claims about the mosaic brain.
plos-pone-0000658:
Andrei I. Ivanov, Moshe Bachar, Brian A. Babbin and colleagues singled out one motor protein at the seams between surface cells, in PLOS ONE in 2007. Epithelial sheets form barriers, and their strength depends on the apical junctional complex, built from tight and adherens junctions. Actin filaments beneath the surface regulate that complex. Myosin II, a major actin motor, was already implicated.

The team reports a unique role for one form, nonmuscle myosin heavy chain IIA, in regulating these apical junctions. Unique means the other forms do not simply cover for it. Barrier breakdown drives gut and skin diseases, so knowing which motor holds the seams matters.
plos-pone-0000758:
Christophe Fraser developed simpler ways to estimate how fast a new epidemic is spreading, in PLOS ONE in 2007. Reproduction numbers, the average number of people infected by a typical case, play a central role in tracking outbreaks. His aim was methods simple enough to be applied as an epidemic emerges, when data are thin and decisions cannot wait.

Fraser separates individual and household reproduction numbers. Spread within households behaves differently from spread between them, and mixing the two distorts forecasts. Estimating both gives a clearer picture of whether an outbreak will take off. Methods papers like this become the toolbox reached for in the first weeks of a crisis.
plos-pone-0000858:
Li-Tzu Chen, Tzu-Ping Ko, Yu-Wei Chang and colleagues probed five charged building blocks in an archaeal DNA repair protein, for PLOS ONE in 2007. RecA family proteins run an ATP-dependent DNA strand exchange, in which a single-stranded DNA filament finds and pairs with a matching double-stranded sequence. Despite more than 20 years of effort, the molecular mechanism of homology pairing and strand exchange was still not fully known.

Their RadA protein comes from archaea, microbes with ancient molecular machinery. The five conserved positively charged residues sit in the L1 and N-terminal DNA-binding motifs. Structural and functional analyses of exactly those residues test how the protein grips DNA during the search for a match.
plos-pone-0000958:
Alexander Statnikov, Chun Li and Constantin Aliferis studied how environment, genes and analysis choices can mislead a cancer gene hunt, in PLOS ONE in 2007. New genotyping tools let researchers scan the whole genome for variants tied to disease. Early studies suggested panels of markers could flag esophageal cancer risk.

The authors warn that pitfalls in data analysis, and tangled effects of environment and genetics, can inflate such claims. Their paper is a caution worked through a real case. Gene wide studies are powerful, but only when the statistics respect how messy human data are. The work is aimed at everyone building risk panels.
plos-pone-0001058:
Naohiro Kawamura, Fumitaka Kugimiya, Yasushi Oshima and colleagues studied a signaling protein's role on both sides of bone turnover, in PLOS ONE in 2007. Bone mass is held by balance: osteoblasts build bone, osteoclasts resorb it, under many local and body wide controls. Akt is one of the key serine threonine kinases in that control web.

The team examined Akt1 in both cell types. A single protein acting in builder and demolisher alike could coordinate the two, keeping turnover matched. Bone diseases from osteoporosis to arthritis involve that match failing. Knowing which Akt form sits where helps target treatment without upsetting the other side.
plos-pone-0001158:
The prion protein is famous for its role in transmissible spongiform encephalopathies, diseases such as scrapie and BSE. Yet its normal job in the body is still unclear. Marius Lötscher and colleagues found an unexpected one in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. Using histology, immunochemistry, and PCR-based methods in mice, they linked the protein to immune defense.

The team reports that induced prion protein controls retroviruses that the immune system activates in the mouse spleen. In other words, when the spleen's defenses switch on, prion protein helps keep resident retroviruses in check. That gives the protein a concrete normal function to set beside its disease role.
plos-pone-0001258:
Long QT syndrome is an inherited heart rhythm disorder that can kill without warning. John Bankston and colleagues report the case of a newborn carrying a new mutation, in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. The mutation sits in SCN5A, the gene for the heart's main sodium channel, and caused the variant called LQT-3.

The authors describe the de novo mutation as novel and lethal, with distinct molecular pharmacology and a distinct therapeutic response. De novo means it appeared fresh in the child, not inherited. Working out how this channel variant answers to drugs guided treatment of a very young patient.
plos-pone-0001358:
Arcobacter butzleri is a bacterium found in human clinical cases, a member of the epsilon subdivision of the Proteobacteria. William Miller and colleagues present its complete genome sequence in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. It is a close relative of established pathogens such as Campylobacter jejuni and Helicobacter pylori.

The authors worked out the full genome sequence of the human clinical isolate. A complete sequence shows what the bacterium can do, and which of its genes might help it cause disease. For a little-studied relative of two major pathogens, the genome is the reference everything else builds on.
plos-pone-0001458:
Frank Schweitzer and Robert Mach published a 2008 PLOS ONE paper on the spread of giving. When a cause takes off, gifts can surge like an outbreak. The pair show that a disease spread model fits this surge well. In their frame, word of a cause passes from person to person like a germ.

Herding plays a key role, as donors watch what the crowd does through the media. The model uses a shared field that stands for that media pull over time. A good fit lets groups forecast how a drive will rise and fade. It also hints at when a push will do the most good.
plos-pone-0001558:
Michiel van Boven and co-authors published a 2008 PLOS ONE study on when people will take flu drugs. Drugs that curb viruses hold promise for new ills such as bird flu and SARS. But the drugs are not free of harm, so people weigh gain against risk. The team modeled when self interest and group gain pull in unlike ways.

In their model, what pays for one person can fail the group as a whole. That gap can stall a drug drive that needs wide uptake to work. Plans must thus align the two, with clear rules and fair access. The work frames a social snag that pure drug science cannot solve.
plos-pone-0001658:
Juliette Salvaing, Anja C. Nagel, Emmanuèle Mouchel-Vielh, and their co-authors studied two gene-control proteins in the fruit fly in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. Polycomb group proteins keep genes switched off over the long term, while trithorax group proteins keep them on. Together they hold gene patterns steady through development, above all for Hox genes, which set body layout.

The paper centers on Corto, a protein that works with both camps, and its interaction with Cyclin G. The full text gives the binding tests, the fly genetics, and where the two proteins meet. Their meeting point links the on-off memory system to a protein better known from cell growth. It may explain how Corto fine-tunes gene patterns as the fly develops.
plos-pone-0001758:
Nuo Yang, Jia Huang, Joel Greshock, and their co-authors studied how an ovarian cancer gene is switched on in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. PIK3CA is boosted, amplified, or mutated in ovarian and other cancers, making it a promising drug target. How it gets over-activated in living tumors was unclear.

The team reports that NF-κB, a master inflammation switch, transcriptionally regulates PIK3CA in the ovarian cancer microenvironment, the tissue setting around the tumor. The full text gives the gene activity tests and the binding evidence. If inflammation switches on a growth gene, then anti-inflammatory strategies or NF-κB blockers could complement drugs aimed at PIK3CA itself.
plos-pone-0001858:
Robin M. D. Beck, Henk Godthelp, Vera Weisbecker, and their co-authors described the oldest marsupial fossils of Australia in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. New skull and body fossils come from the early Eocene Tingamarra Local Fauna. The team refers them to Djarthia murgonensis, known before only from broken tooth remains.

The new finds show Djarthia is a member of a distinct marsupial group. Its kinship bears on how marsupials reached Australia and spread across it. The full text gives the fossil accounts and the family analysis. The marsupials of Australia are a textbook case of evolution in isolation, and their oldest fossils anchor the timeline of that story.
plos-pone-0001958:
Myriam Rai and co-authors tested a drug fix for a nerve illness in mice, in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. The illness, Friedreich ataxia, is passed down in families and harms both nerves and the heart. It stems from too little frataxin, a protein that works in the cell's power units, caused by a swollen repeat in the frataxin gene.

The team gave HDAC inhibitors, drugs that loosen the chemical marks that mute genes, to a mouse model of the illness. As the title states, the drugs corrected the frataxin shortage in the mice. If a muted gene can be coaxed back on, a drug path opens for an illness with no cure.
plos-pone-0002058:
Steven Schutzer and co-authors read the genome of a weakened form of a biothreat bacterium, in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. Burkholderia mallei causes glanders, which can be lethal in humans and animals, and it is little studied. Safety rules for listed agents have hampered research with it in many labs.

The team used whole genome sequencing to characterize a clinically attenuated strain, one that no longer causes full disease. If its genome proves it is truly weakened, the strain could be excluded from select agent lists. That would let more labs study glanders safely.
plos-pone-0002158:
Hendrik Harms, Konstantin Prass, Christian Meisel, and co-authors ran a clinical trial on preventing infection after stroke, published in PLOS ONE in 2008. Pneumonia is a leading cause of death after a major stroke. In mice, giving the antibiotic moxifloxacin early had prevented post-stroke infections, lowered deaths, and improved recovery.

The team tested the same idea in people with acute ischemic stroke, where a clot blocks blood flow to the brain. Patients were assigned by chance to preventive antibiotic therapy or standard care. Trials like this one decide whether a result seen in animals can be turned into a routine step that saves lives in the ward.
plos-pone-0002258:
Alison McGuigan, Derek Bruzewicz, Ana Glavan, and co-authors described a way to grow cells in tiny gel blocks, in a 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Cells behave differently on flat plastic than in the three-dimensional world of the body. Flat culture is still the most common method in biology, while 3D culture lacks a standard, easy form.

The team used replica molding to make sub-millimeter gel modules with cells sealed inside. The small blocks can be handled, stacked, and combined like building pieces. A simple standard for 3D culture could bring lab results closer to how cells truly behave inside tissues.
plos-pone-0002358:
Domingo Ojer Tsakiridu and co-authors surveyed factors linked to induced abortion among sex workers in Asturias, Spain, in a 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Their aim was to find what circumstances go together with having had an induced abortion in this group. The health needs of this group are often missed by standard services.

The team ran a cross-sectional study using a self-completion questionnaire answered by 212 women who attended the region's three sexually transmitted infection clinics. Mapping the factors that cluster with abortion helps those clinics target contraception advice, testing, and support to the women at highest risk.
plos-pone-0002458:
A research team led by Perfettini reported its work in PLOS ONE in 2008. The byline credits Jean-Luc Perfettini, Roberta Nardacci, Mehdi Bourouba, and others. Its subject is critical Involvement of the ATM-Dependent DNA Damage Response in the Apoptotic Demise of HIV-1-Elicited Syncytia. DNA damage can activate the oncosuppressor protein ataxia telangiectasia mutated (ATM), which phosphorylates the histone H2AX within characteristic DNA damage foci.

Readers get the background first, then the path the team took and the care they took with it. As a record, it keeps the focus on facts and method, and lets readers judge the claims for themselves.
plos-pone-0002558:
Work from Nishimura and fellow authors appeared in PLOS ONE in 2008. The byline credits Tomoko Nishimura, Tamaki Ishima, Masaomi Iyo, and others. Its subject is potentiation of Nerve Growth Factor-Induced Neurite Outgrowth by Fluvoxamine. The title goes on to note role of Sigma-1 Receptors, IP 3 Receptors and Cellular Signaling Pathways. Selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs) have been widely used and are a major therapeutic advance in psychopharmacology.

However, their pharmacology is quite heterogeneous. Key terms are set out in context, so a reader new to the field can still follow the work. The full text is free to read, so any reader can check the work and follow the links to past work.
plos-pone-0002658:
Pawan Gupta led a team whose work appeared in PLOS ONE in 2008. Their subject was PKCε stimulated arginine methylation of RIP140 for its Nuclear-Cytoplasmic export in adipocyte differentiation. The full author list in the catalog record begins with Pawan Gupta, and the article appeared in the open journal PLOS ONE.

The abstract begins from a clear premise. Receptor interacting protein 140 (RIP140) is a versatile transcriptional co-repressor that plays roles in diverse metabolic processes including fat accumulation in adipocytes. Anyone studying the topic can use the article to see how the authors framed the problem at the time of publication.
plos-pone-0002758:
Céline Lafourcade led a team whose work appeared in PLOS ONE in 2008. Their subject was regulation of the V-ATPase along the endocytic pathway occurs through reversible subunit association and membrane localization. The catalog record names Céline Lafourcade first among the authors, and the source is the open journal PLOS ONE.

The abstract begins from a clear premise. The lumen of endosomal organelles becomes increasingly acidic when going from the cell surface to lysosomes. The summary also notes a further point. Luminal pH thereby regulates important processes such as the release of internalized ligands from their receptor or the activation of lysosomal enzymes. For readers, the value lies in how plainly the abstract sets out the problem and what the authors set out to test or describe.
plos-pone-0002858:
Morten Ruhwald led a team whose work appeared in PLOS ONE in 2008. Their subject was improving T-Cell assays for the diagnosis of latent TB infection: potential of a diagnostic test based on IP-10. Authorship is credited in the record to Morten Ruhwald and co-authors, with PLOS ONE as the journal of publication.

The abstract begins from a clear premise. There is a need for simple tools such as the M.tuberculosis specific IFN-γ release assays (IGRA) to improve diagnosis of M.tuberculosis -infection in children. Its abstract frames the work for later readers, who can judge the full text against the aims stated at the start.
plos-pone-0002958:
Sofia Kring, Claus Holst, Esther Zimmermann and co-authors studied the fatness gene FTO across a wide range of body fat in 2008. A common variant in FTO, labeled rs9939609, is linked to total body fatness. What it does for fat placement and related metabolic traits was less clear.

The team checked the variant against abdominal and peripheral fat and obesity-linked traits in middle-aged men spanning a broad range of fatness. Published in PLOS ONE, the design shows whether the gene's effect grows, fades, or changes form as fatness rises. Such detail refines a headline gene link.
plos-pone-0003058:
José Cuevas, Manuela Torres-Puente, Nuria Jiménez-Hernández and co-authors tracked hepatitis C virus change around therapy in 2008. They analyzed selective forces on two genome regions thought to be involved in response to combined interferon plus ribavirin therapy. One region holds three hypervariable parts of the envelope E2 protein.

Comparing virus before and after combined therapy shows which sites selection pressed hardest. Published in PLOS ONE, such maps help explain treatment failure and resistance. Hepatitis C evolves fast within a patient, so therapy must be judged against a moving target. Readers can follow the full methods and data in the complete text of the article.
plos-pone-0003158:
K. Bretonnel Cohen, Martha Palmer and Lawrence Hunter study verb forms in biomedical writing in this 2008 PLOS ONE paper. They present data from the PennBioIE corpus on how common domain-specific verbs change their argument structure, and how their related noun forms behave. Alternation is the linguistics term for such shifts in the surface form of a verb.

Readers learn how biomedical verbs and their nominalizations vary in real text. That detail sounds narrow, but it matters for computer systems that mine medical papers for facts. Better handling of these forms means fewer errors when machines extract who did what to what.
plos-pone-0003258:
Amelia Cimmino, Rosanna Capasso, Fabbri Muller and colleagues study a repair enzyme in blood vessel cells in this 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Natural proteins undergo deamidation of certain asparagine residues in the body on their own, forming isoaspartyl residues. Deamidated, isomerized molecules are changed in both shape and how they work. The enzyme protein isoaspartate methyltransferase acts on such damage.

The title reports that this enzyme prevents apoptosis induced by oxidative stress in endothelial cells, with a role for Bcl-Xl deamidation and methylation. Readers see protein repair linked to cell survival under stress. Vessel lining protection matters in ageing and blood vessel disease.
plos-pone-0003358:
Jochen Brumm, Elizabeth Conibear, Wyeth W. Wasserman and colleagues present a method to find gene modules in this 2008 PLOS ONE paper. A central problem in systems biology research is identification and extension of biological modules, groups of genes or proteins participating in a common cellular process or physical complex. There is a persistent need for practical, principled methods to infer such modules from data.

Their approach discovers and expands gene modules by seeking isolated groups in a random graph process. Readers get an algorithm that grows modules from seeds while testing against randomness. Module maps help turn gene lists into working biological units.
plos-pone-0003458:
Rita A. Busuttil and co-authors measured mutation buildup without a DNA repair protein in 2008. Ku80 helps join broken DNA ends, a quick repair route called non-homologous end joining. Losing that route has been tied to early aging. The team used mice missing Ku80 for their tests.

They counted mutations at a reporter gene, LacZ, across tissues and cells. Both the rate and the kinds of mutations changed without Ku80. The data show which errors pile up when end joining fails. That helps link broken repair to aging and cancer risk.
plos-pone-0003558:
Elena Lesma and co-authors tested a targeted antibody against tumor cells in this 2008 paper. Tuberous sclerosis complex causes benign tumors called hamartomas across organs. Faults in the TSC1 or TSC2 genes drive the syndrome. The team grew smooth muscle cells lacking TSC2 from a patient's tumor.

An antibody against EGFR, a growth factor receptor, was applied to those cells. It inhibited their proliferation efficiently and specifically. Blocking that receptor may offer a treatment path for this syndrome. A related lung disease, LAM, might benefit from the same approach. Tumors in this syndrome are benign yet can still harm by their size and place.
plos-pone-0003658:
Irini Evnouchidou, Frank Momburg, Athanasios Papakyriakou, and colleagues published this immunology study in PLOS ONE in 2008. The immune system displays protein pieces on cell surfaces so T cells can inspect them. An enzyme called ERAP1 trims those pieces down to the right size first.

The team found that the inner sequence of a piece, not just its ends, decides how ERAP1 trims it. That finding changes how the final displayed set is predicted. Knowing the trimming rules helps explain which pieces reach the surface and thus what the immune system gets to see.
plos-pone-0003758:
Xiaodian Sun, Li Jin, and Momiao Xiong published this modeling paper in PLOS ONE in 2008. The dynamics of a system decide how cells, tissues, and organisms behave. Building math models of biochemical networks means estimating their hidden parameters from data. That estimation is the hard part.

The authors adapt the extended Kalman filter, a classic engineering tool, to nonlinear state-space models of such networks. The filter infers parameter values as measurements come in. It helps turn noisy observations of living chemistry into working models of metabolism and gene regulation.
plos-pone-0003858:
Min Pi, Ling Chen, Min-Zhao Huang, and colleagues published this mouse study in PLOS ONE in 2008. GPRC6A is an orphan receptor found across the body. In lab dishes it senses amino acids, osteocalcin, and calcium-like ions. What it does in a living animal was unknown.

The team created mice lacking GPRC6A and characterized their condition. The null mice showed osteopenia, feminization, and metabolic syndrome together. The triple phenotype reveals one receptor quietly governing bone strength, sex traits, and metabolism at the same time. One missing part thus touched bone, sex traits, and body fuel use.
plos-pone-0003958:
Julia Szendroedi, Elisabeth Zwettler, Albrecht Ingo Schmid, and co-authors measured muscle energy output after acromegaly in 2008. Faulty mitochondria and fat stored in muscle link to poor insulin action. Acromegaly, an excess of growth hormone, also reduces insulin sensitivity. The team asked whether effects linger after the disease is treated.

Their PLOS ONE article studied patients with previous acromegaly. Basal ATP production in their skeletal muscle ran low. That lasting deficit may help explain ongoing metabolic risk. The result argues for long follow-up of metabolism after hormone excess ends. The full report sits in PLOS ONE, free to read with all its data shown.
plos-pone-0004058:
Darren J. Gray, Gail M. Williams, Yuesheng Li, and co-authors modeled a parasitic disease in China in 2008. Schistosoma japonicum infects over one million people in China. Another forty million live where infection risk is present. Unlike its relatives, this species also infects many animals.

Their PLOS ONE article studies transmission in lake and marshland regions. Animal hosts keep the parasite cycling even when people are treated. Models that include animals fit the disease's persistence better. Control programs must target the whole transmission web, not humans alone. Readers can find the full text in PLOS ONE, an open science journal.
plos-pone-0004158:
Jérôme Rollin and colleagues published this cancer study in PLOS ONE in 2009. ID2 is a regulator that helps control the balance between cell growth and cell specialisation. In healthy cells it keeps that balance; recent work has tied it to cancer.

The team examined where ID2 sits inside cells in non-small cell lung cancer, whether in the nucleus or outside it. They report that this intracellular location carries predictive value for the disease. In other words, the same protein sends a different message depending on its address inside the cell. A marker like that could help doctors judge how a patient's cancer is likely to behave.
plos-pone-0004258:
Tara Smith and colleagues published this public health study in PLOS ONE in 2009. MRSA, the drug-resistant form of Staphylococcus aureus, had been found in many pigs and pig farmers in the Netherlands and Canada. No study had checked carriage among swine and swine workers in the United States.

The team swabbed the noses of 299 swine and their handlers in the Midwest. They report that the MRSA strain ST398 is present in both the animals and the workers. The finding raised a new occupational and food-chain question for American public health. Swine workers, in other words, can carry what their pigs carry.
plos-pone-0004358:
Natalia Gottig and colleagues published this plant pathogen study in PLOS ONE in 2009. Xanthomonas axonopodis pv. citri causes citrus canker, a damaging disease of citrus crops. The bacterium has several protein secretion systems. They include at least one type V system of the two-partner secretion pathway, mainly used for moving large proteins out of the cell.

The team studied a filamentous hemagglutinin-like protein handled by that system. They report that it is involved in the bacterium's virulence. A surface protein that helps the pathogen attack citrus is a possible target for protecting groves.
plos-pone-0004458:
A small sea creature that can regrow its whole brain offers a fresh model for nerve repair, present Carl Dahlberg, Helene Auger, Sam Dupont, and co-authors in PLOS ONE in 2009. The creature is the tunicate Ciona intestinalis, a marine animal related, distantly, to backboned animals. Unlike us, it can regenerate nerves and a complete adult central nervous system.

Good new models of regrowth are in short supply, and each must come with tools for lab work. The team refined this model, setting out the resources and methods that make it practical. A creature that rebuilds its brain on cue lets scientists watch repair step by step. What it does naturally may suggest what might be coaxed, one day, in injured human nerves.
plos-pone-0004558:
An antibody test can show a tumor dying in response to chemotherapy, report Fares Al-Ejeh, Jocelyn Darby, Chris Tsopelas, and co-authors in PLOS ONE in 2009. Cancer therapy aims to kill malignant cells. Directly measuring tumor cell death in the body would be a valuable part of monitoring whether a treatment is working.

The team had developed an antibody, called APOMAB, that binds a target named La, exposed on dying cells. Here they show it detects the apoptotic tumor response to life-prolonging, DNA-damaging chemotherapy. In plain terms, a scan could reveal whether a tumor is dying weeks before it shrinks. Knowing early whether a drug works lets doctors switch failing treatments sooner and spare patients useless side effects.
plos-pone-0004658:
The structure and working mechanism of an enzyme that can both cut and build sugar chains are solved by Jie Yin, Lei Li, Neil Shaw, and co-authors in PLOS ONE in 2009. The enzymes are endo-beta-N-acetylglucosaminidases, shortened to ENGases. They are dual specificity enzymes, able to catalyze hydrolysis, breaking down, and transglycosylation, building up, reactions.

Because of that two-way talent, ENGases have become a focus of intense research for the synthesis of glycopeptides, molecules part protein and part sugar. The team determined the structural basis and catalytic mechanism for one member, Endo-A. Knowing exactly how the enzyme grips and cuts its substrate lets chemists retune it. Better glycopeptide synthesis matters for making uniform antibody drugs and vaccines.
plos-pone-0004758:
Angela Lai, Murray Cairns, and Nham Tran built a random small RNA library to find RNAs that shift complex traits in mammal cells. In PLOS ONE in 2009. RNA based silencing has given strong tools to find and test genes. Small RNAs can turn down single genes with high precision in cultured cells and in animals.

The team built a library of random small RNAs that cells can produce. Screening that library can reveal RNAs that change cell behavior in desired ways. Such screens may find new drug leads and gene roles. They work without knowing the target in advance.
plos-pone-0004858:
Sonja Grosskinsky and colleagues found a multifunctional surface protein Borrelia recurrentis uses to escape innate immunity, in PLOS ONE in 2009. Borrelia recurrentis causes louse borne relapsing fever with severe disease and high mortality. It evolved strategies including antigenic variation to evade immune defense. The team identifies for the first time a surface protein combining anti complement, anti opsonic, and invasive functions.

One protein performs three escape jobs at once. Such efficiency suits a genome reduced pathogen. Targeting it could restore immune clearance. Relapsing fever remains neglected globally. The work also raises clear questions that targeted studies can now address. The team also set out clear next steps for work in this field.
plos-pone-0004958:
Merkel cell carcinoma is a rare, aggressive skin cancer. Under the microscope it looks almost identical to small cell lung cancer. A new virus, Merkel cell polyomavirus, had just been found in these tumors. Charlotte Wetzels and co-authors searched for it directly. Their PLOS ONE paper appeared in 2009. They used ultrastructural imaging of tumor cells.

The imaging gave direct proof of polyomavirus in the skin tumor cells. The same search found none in small cell lung carcinoma. That contrast marks the look-alike cancers as different diseases. The distinction matters for diagnosis and for treatment choices.
plos-pone-0005058:
Noroviruses cause epidemic stomach illness worldwide. They latch onto human blood-group sugars to infect us. Ming Tan and colleagues studied those gripping surfaces in PLOS ONE in 2009. They compared carbohydrate-binding interfaces across virus strains. Noroviruses are diverse, with two major genogroups and about thirty genotypes.

Despite that diversity, the sugar-binding interface stayed conserved. Human histo-blood group antigens shaped that conservation. Our blood types steered the virus's evolution. A conserved grip is an attractive vaccine target. It is one of the few stable features on a changing virus. The work shows host biology leaving fingerprints on a pathogen's design.
plos-pone-0005158:
TB ranges from silent infection to severe disease. Doctors need markers that tell which patients are in trouble. Zahra Hasan and colleagues measured immune responses in PLOS ONE in 2009. They used ESAT6, a protein secreted by the TB bacterium. Patient T cells respond to it with interferon-gamma. Another signal, CXCL9, was also measured.

The ESAT6-induced responses differentiated severity of tuberculosis. Interferon-gamma and CXCL9 levels separated severe from milder cases. The immune readouts act as severity gauges. They could guide who needs the most urgent care. Defense against TB depends on proper T cell and macrophage activation. This study turns that activation into a measurable signal. Triage in crowded clinics could benefit.
plos-pone-0005258:
Eating fish is linked to better health, but the steps behind the benefit are not fully known. Lankinen and colleagues used lipidomics, a full profile of blood fats, in PLOS ONE in 2009 to see what fatty fish intake changes.

Fatty fish lowered blood lipids tied to inflammation and to insulin signaling. The profile shift gives a concrete mechanism for part of the fish effect. It also hints at blood fat markers that diet studies can use to check whether advice is working. Blood fat maps of this kind could also test which fish, and how much of it, gives the best gain for the heart and for blood sugar.
plos-pone-0005358:
In multipassage experiments, human tumor cells are grown in one mouse, then moved to the next, again and again. The growth curves from those passages hold patterns about tumor behavior. Gliozzi and colleagues built a computational tool to analyze them in PLOS ONE in 2009.

Their tool treats the curves phenomenologically, modeling their shape without assuming one mechanism. Fitted shapes can reveal growth laws that raw plots hide. Better curve analysis helps researchers compare tumor lines and judge how treatments change growth across passages. Mouse-passage tumors are a long-used way to test how cancer grows when it is moved again. Again, much as a tumor spreads in a body over the course of a long illness.
plos-pone-0005458:
Dik Heg and co-authors studied helper fish in a 2009 PLOS ONE report. In some animal groups, young helpers stay with a breeding pair and help raise young that are not their own. One idea says helpers pay for their place on the home ground by working.

The team watched female cichlid helpers and checked which ones later bred themselves. Helpers that worked more were more likely to breed. That link fits the pay-to-stay idea, though other gains may matter too. The study adds real-world evidence to a long debate about why animals help raise others' young.
plos-pone-0005558:
Thomas Duda and Taehwan Lee studied venom change in a sea snail at Easter Island in a 2009 PLOS ONE report. When a species escapes its old rivals and enemies, it may spread into new roles and change fast. Far less is known about the gene changes behind that release.

The snail Conus miliaris is a hunting cone snail whose venom kills its prey. At Easter Island it faced a new setting with fewer rivals. The team compared its venom genes there with those elsewhere to see how release reshaped its weapons. Venom genes change fast even in normal times, which makes the island shift stand out more clearly.
plos-pone-0005658:
Olive Li and co-authors combined flu polymerase parts from birds and mammals in a 2009 PLOS ONE report. Flu viruses swap gene parts when two strains infect one animal, creating new strains. One part from bird flu had entered both human pandemic strains of the last century.

The team tested all mixes of the three polymerase parts from bird and mammal strains. Some mixes worked far better than others, which helps predict which swaps could yield a pandemic virus. That foresight supports flu surveillance worldwide. Surveillance teams use exactly such rankings when they judge which bird viruses to watch most closely.
plos-pone-0005758:
Ahmed Moustafa and co-authors traced the origin of toxin-making genes in cyanobacteria in 2009. Saxitoxin causes paralytic shellfish poisoning, a sometimes fatal illness from eating tainted shellfish. Marine algae make most of it, but cyanobacteria in fresh water carry the genes too.

Where those genes began, and how they jumped between groups, was little known. The team compared gene sequences across species to read that history. Knowing how toxin genes spread helps predict which blooms may turn toxic. It also feeds the broader story of how bacteria trade useful, or harmful, toolkits.
plos-pone-0005858:
Macy Heung and co-authors compared in 2009 two maternal blood fractions for spotting fetal messages during pregnancy. The placenta sheds its own messenger RNA into the mother's blood, raising hopes for noninvasive prenatal tests. Whole blood had seemed a promising source since placental RNA was found there.

The team found fetal-specific RNA is actually easier to detect in plasma than in whole blood. Cells in whole blood add noise that drowns the faint fetal signal. The practical lesson is simple: plasma is the better starting material. Getting the source right is step one for any blood-based prenatal test.
plos-pone-0005958:
Drug-resistant gut bacteria no longer stay inside hospitals. Jonas Bonnedahl, Mirva Drobni, Michel Gauthier-Clerc and colleagues followed one resistant strain of E. coli in the south of France in 2009. Their PLOS ONE paper tracks bacteria carrying CTX-M enzymes, which break down key antibiotics, in both people and yellow-legged gulls.

Finding the same resistant bacteria in gulls and in humans suggests the germs move between the two. Birds that feed near towns can carry resistance far and wide. The study adds wildlife to the map of how superbugs spread, a point that matters for doctors, vets and anyone who plans how to slow resistance.
plos-pone-0006058:
Gene delivery rides on fat bubbles that carry DNA into cells. Sarah Resina, Paul Prevot and Alain Thierry asked in 2009 what makes those bubbles work. Their PLOS ONE paper studies lipoplexes, mixes of DNA and charged lipids, including a house formula called Neutraplex that can be made with a positive, neutral or negative charge.

The bubbles' physical and chemical traits steer how cells take them in and how well the gene transfer works, the title reports. A recipe's charge and makeup are thus design choices, not details. The work helps gene therapy and lab transfection alike, since the same delivery problem sits at the heart of both.
plos-pone-0006158:
When the liver's main antioxidant system fails for good, the cell must find another guard or die. Elena Suvorova, Olivier Lucas, Carla Weisend and colleagues found the backup in 2009. Their PLOS ONE paper studies hepatocytes chronically lacking Txnrd1, a core part of the thioredoxin system that keeps proteins reduced and feeds other antioxidant enzymes.

The protective Nrf2 pathway switches on in those cells, the title reports, compensating for the chronic loss. A standing backup explains why some knockouts look healthier than expected. The result also cautions drug work aimed at antioxidant enzymes: the cell's second line may blunt a drug meant to starve a tumor of its defenses.
plos-pone-0006258:
Ocean life is shrinking under fishing pressure, and reserves usually ban fishing in chosen spots. Natalie Ban and Amanda Vincent flip that logic in a 2009 PLOS ONE paper. Instead of selecting areas where fishing is prohibited, they explore selecting the areas where fishing is permitted.

The rest of the ocean then becomes protected by default. Starting from permission rather than prohibition can soften impacts on fishers and their communities. It also forces planners to justify exactly where extraction should happen. The paper offers a fresh frame for balancing marine protection with livelihoods.
plos-pone-0006358:
A fixed-dose malaria drug pair, dihydroartemisinin with piperaquine, is a promising drug pair built on artemisinin. Julien Zwang and colleagues pooled individual patient data from seven published studies in a 2009 PLOS ONE analysis. They examined efficacy and tolerability in acute uncomplicated falciparum malaria across multiple centres.

Pooling patient-level data gives a sharper verdict than separate trial summaries. Safety and cure rates can be compared across regions and patient groups. Artemisinin combinations are the backbone of malaria treatment worldwide. Rigorous checks like this guide which combinations health systems should buy. Pooled data of this kind is the best check we have on drugs used by so many.
plos-pone-0006458:
Tarek Boussetta and co-authors tested a plant oil compound against gut inflammation in PLOS ONE in 2009. Neutrophils, a type of white blood cell, drive inflammation by releasing reactive oxygen species. A signal called TNF alpha primes them to release even more. Standard anti-inflammatory drugs do not always control this process well.

The compound, punicic acid, is a fatty acid found in pomegranate seed oil. The title reports that it blocks TNF-driven neutrophil overactivation. It also protects rats from experimental colon inflammation. A food-derived compound with this profile could interest doctors seeking gentler options. More work would be needed before any human use.
plos-pone-0006558:
Charlotte Ling, Leif Groop, Silvia Del Guerra, and colleagues measured a diabetes-linked protein in human pancreatic islets for PLOS ONE in 2009. Calpain-10 was the first gene identified influencing type 2 diabetes risk by positional cloning. Studies in beta-cell lines and rodent islets suggested roles for the protein. The team measured its expression in islets from patients with type 2 diabetes.

Their title reports that calpain-10 expression is elevated in those islets. Higher levels in real patient tissue strengthen the gene's link to disease. It also raises the question whether lowering it would help insulin secretion. The study grounds a famous diabetes gene in human data.
plos-pone-0006658:
Hidekazu Kuwayama and Yuzuru Kubohara studied signal molecules in a slime mold in PLOS ONE in 2009. Early in the life of Dictyostelium discoideum, single cells crawl toward cAMP, a signal that draws them together. That chemotaxis builds a joined structure from lone cells. Two factors called DIF-1 and DIF-2 were known to guide which cell fate each cell takes as the structure forms.

Their title says these factors also act as modulators of chemotaxis in this slime mold. One signal can thus steer both movement and fate in the same cells. Dictyostelium is a classic model for how lone cells join into one organism. Dual-use signals are a neat, spare design worth study.
plos-pone-0006758:
Sang Ok Song and Jeffrey Varner built a mathematical model of pain signaling in sensory neurons in PLOS ONE in 2009. Calcium levels inside a cell help carry pain signals. Outside signals can raise or lower that calcium. ATP, released between cells, acts on P2 receptors to modulate calcium. The authors wanted a mechanistic account of these interactions.

Their model links ATP receptor activity to calcium dynamics step by step. A mechanistic model predicts how changes propagate through the system. It can test drug ideas before any laboratory experiment. It also shows which steps matter most for pain transmission. Such models help pain research move from description toward engineering.
plos-pone-0006858:
Kristiina Kanerva and her team studied a brake protein in mast cells in PLOS ONE in 2009. Mast cells are the cells that drive sneezes and rashes in allergy. When set off, they dump stored chemicals that stir swelling and itch. Small cell bits called polyamines shape much of what cells do. The team found that mast cells carry antizyme inhibitor 2.

They also tested polyamines as fine-tuned dials of one mast cell output: serotonin. A dial that turns one output but not the rest is a rare find. It hints that allergy could be calmed with a light touch. The work ties polyamine control to a cell at the heart of allergy.
plos-pone-0006958:
Britta Björkholm, Chek Mei Bok, Annelie Lundin, and colleagues linked gut microbes to liver function in PLOS ONE in 2009. The liver is the body's central site for breaking down foreign chemicals. Nuclear receptors named CAR and PXR steer much of that drug metabolism. The team asked whether gut bacteria influence this system.

They compared liver gene expression in animals with and without gut microbiota. The microbes changed liver genes and altered chemical metabolism. In other words, gut bacteria help set how the liver handles drugs. That effect may partly explain why drug responses differ between individuals.
plos-pone-0007058:
Paolo Fardin, Marzia Ognibene, Cristina Vanni, and colleagues studied an oncogene in mouse eyes in PLOS ONE in 2009. The Dbl protein family is a large group of growth-related proto-oncogenes. Their many parts let them merge signals in networks run by Rho proteins. The team used transgenic mice carrying the Dbl oncogene.

In the lenses of these mice, two changes appeared. Cells underwent an epithelial to mesenchymal transition, loosening their normal form. New vessel growth, called vasculogenesis, also began. Seeing an oncogene reshape the lens shows its reach. It may reveal early steps that tumors borrow later.
plos-pone-0007158: Heiko Stahl, Tanja Fauti, Nina Ullrich, and others studied a small RNA in PLOS ONE in 2009. Blocking that RNA, called miR-155, made helper T cells easier to control. The control came from regulatory T cells, the brakes of the immune system. The cells made easier to rein in were CD4 Th cells. That link is of note for diseases where immune attacks need calming.
plos-pone-0007258:
Patrice Dubreuil, Sébastien Letard, Marco Ciufolini, and colleagues characterized a targeted cancer drug in a 2009 PLOS ONE paper. The drug is masitinib, also called AB1010. It blocks tyrosine kinases, enzymes that act as growth switches, and it targets the receptor KIT in particular.

KIT is a target in cancer, mastocytosis, and inflammatory diseases. The authors profile masitinib in lab tests and in living animals. They describe it as potent and selective for its targets. Their detailed characterization supported later clinical testing of masitinib in patients with KIT-driven disease worldwide.
plos-pone-0007358:
Mukesh Pasupuleti, Markus Roupe, Victoria Rydengård, and colleagues found an antimicrobial role for the prion protein in 2009. The cellular prion protein sits on cell surfaces throughout the human body. It has many functions, and its exposed front region carries positive charge and binds heparin, features shared by many antimicrobial peptides.

That resemblance prompted the authors to test antimicrobial activity. They report the human prion protein acts against microbes. The activity is mediated by its N-terminal region. Their finding adds a possible defense role to a protein better known for prion diseases.
plos-pone-0007458:
Guillaume Sapriel and colleagues published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009 on diatoms, ocean algae that build glass-like shells from silicon. Diatoms produce much of the ocean's biological silica. Yet dissolved silicon can run short in surface waters and limit their growth. The team read activity across nearly the whole genome of one species, Phaeodactylum tricornutum, to see how it manages silicon.

They found that silicic acid transporters, the proteins that import silicon, are regulated at several levels at once. A network of genes responds as supply changes. That layered control lets the diatom adjust uptake to what the water offers. Because diatoms support a huge share of ocean life, their silicon handling matters globally. The study maps the control system behind it.
plos-pone-0007558:
Anne Spaulding and colleagues published an analysis in PLOS ONE in 2009 on HIV and AIDS among people in United States correctional facilities. Groups at high risk for HIV come together in prisons and jails, so infection rates there ran high early in the epidemic. The team assessed the share of the national epidemic borne by inmates and by people recently released, using 2006 data.

That share was declining, yet it remained disproportionately large. Because so many people pass through the correctional system, it stays a key public health setting. Testing, treatment, and prevention there reach people often missed elsewhere. The authors frame this as a persistent opportunity rather than only a burden. The analysis gives policymakers a measured picture of where the epidemic concentrates.
plos-pone-0007658:
Maud Mavigner and colleagues published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009 on HIV that persists despite good treatment. Combination antiretroviral therapy suppresses the virus, yet low-level production continues in many patients. The significance of that residual viremia was debated. The team characterized patients whose immune systems recovered poorly on therapy. They measured the lingering virus and the state of the patients' T cells together.

Residual viremia correlated with persistent T-cell activation in the poor responders. Restless T cells are a sign the immune system never fully calms. The lingering virus therefore looks like more than harmless background noise. It may help drive the incomplete recovery these patients show. The finding argues for watching low-level virus as a clinical signal. It also keeps the search for the virus's hiding places urgent.
plos-pone-0007758:
Nabarun Dasgupta and co-authors published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009. It asks whether heavy news coverage of opioids tracks with more opioid deaths. Past research has linked media reporting to rises in drug abuse. Publicity has been suspected in usage swings for several drug classes.

The title poses the dilemma plainly: breaking the news, or fueling the epidemic? The authors test whether report volume and deaths rise and fall together in time. The answer matters for journalists and health officials. Coverage can warn the public, but it may also spread the behavior it describes.
plos-pone-0007858:
Marietta Dindo and co-authors published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009. It shows how group loyalty keeps foraging traditions alive in capuchin monkeys. Wild great apes are known for rich cultural repertoires and local traditions. Capuchins, among the brainiest monkeys, show traditions of their own.

The authors report that in-group conformity sustains different foraging traditions between groups. Monkeys copy their own group's way of finding food, even when other ways work. Conformity thus acts like cultural glue. The study extends the story of animal culture beyond the great apes. It also mirrors how human groups hold onto local customs.
plos-pone-0007958:
Jian Li and colleagues charted large DNA gains and losses in two population groups for PLOS ONE in 2009. Beyond single-letter changes, whole chunks of DNA can be copied extra times or lost, a pattern called copy number variation. The team mapped where such chunks fall across the genome.

Patterns differed between the Caucasian and Asian groups they studied. Those gaps add a layer of human diversity that letter-by-letter studies miss. A full chart of chunk changes helps explain trait and disease gaps between groups and improves how future gene hunts are planned.
plos-pone-0008058:
Cheng-Yeu Wu and colleagues gave a plain chemical account of the so-called nanobacteria in PLOS ONE in 2009. Tiny granules found in blood were once hailed as living things of a wholly new kind. The team showed they are clumps of two blood proteins, fetuin-A and albumin, bound with calcium minerals.

The clumps form when the proteins both seed mineral growth and check it, a two-sided process the team rebuilt in the lab. No living thing is needed to explain the granules. Settling the claim frees research funds for real causes of the ills the granules were blamed for.
plos-pone-0008158:
Takeru Yoshimura and colleagues read the full immune signal mix in diseased eyes in PLOS ONE in 2009. The samples were vitreous fluid, the gel inside the eye, drawn from hundreds of patients. Many had diabetic eye disease, including macular swelling and advanced retinal damage.

Dozens of immune messengers were measured in each sample, and each disease carried its own pattern of highs and lows. Patterns that clean may one day let a fluid sample name the disease stage, or point to the messenger a drug should block to save sight.
plos-pone-0008258:
Klaus Kessler and colleagues studied a visual illusion in a PLOS ONE paper from 2010. In the flash-lag effect, a flashed object seems to trail a moving one. The two are aligned in space, yet the flash looks behind. The effect has been replicated many times with simple stimuli. The team used biological motion, such as a moving person, for the first time.

They asked whether motor resonance predicts the pattern of the illusion. Motor resonance is the brain echoing observed movement in its own motor system. Links between resonance and the lag effect would tie perception to action. The study extends a classic illusion to human movement.
plos-pone-0008358:
Simon C. F. Rawlinson and colleagues compared adult rat bones in a PLOS ONE paper from 2009. Limb fractures and bone loss cause growing harm in ageing populations. Weight-bearing limbs lose bone with age, yet the skull vault keeps its mass. Why regions differ was the question behind the study. Bones carry markers of their developmental origin.

Adult rat bones maintained distinct regional expression of those markers. In other words, bones remember where they came from. That memory may explain why skull and limb respond differently to ageing. It could also shape treatments for bone loss.
plos-pone-0008458:
Maria Murholm and co-authors track genes in brown fat cells in a 2009 PLOS ONE paper. Brown fat cells burn energy to make heat. White fat cells store energy instead. The split rests in part on mitochondria, the cell's power units. Brown cells hold a protein that lets them waste energy as heat. The team watch cells as they mature in mice.

They measure genes that copy and read mitochondrial DNA. Those genes shift as brown cells form and are recruited. The pattern shows how the power system is built for heat making. It helps explain how brown fat turns on when needed.
plos-pone-0008558:
Kathleen McClendon and co-authors compare tumor suppressor paths in mouse cells in a 2010 PLOS ONE paper. RB and p53 are tumor suppressors that mediate responses to DNA damage. Loss of both together is common in human cancers. Surprisingly, how they cooperate in damage signaling was still enigmatic. That cooperation bears on tumor formation and on response to therapy. The team use a mouse primary cell model to separate their effects.

Inactivating each path has a differential impact on damage response. It also changes how therapy can transform cells into cancerous ones. Knowing which suppressor is lost may predict treatment effects. The work clarifies a common but poorly understood cancer genotype.
plos-pone-0008658:
Giulia Spigoni and co-authors study antisense regulation in mouse brains in a 2010 PLOS ONE paper. Emx2 encodes a transcription factor expressed in embryonic tissues and the central nervous system. It is implicated in cerebral cortex development, including field specification and precursor proliferation. Antisense transcripts are RNA copies read from the opposite DNA strand. They can regulate the sense gene that shares their locus. The team characterize antisense transcripts at the Emx2 locus in cortico-cerebral precursors.

They find those transcripts regulate Emx2 expression in those precursors. Tuning Emx2 levels shapes how cortex areas are specified. Antisense control adds a fine dial to a master developmental gene. The work may illuminate cortical malformations linked to Emx2.
plos-pone-0008758:
Brian Onken and Monica Driscoll asked whether a diabetes drug can lengthen healthy life in worms. Their study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010. Metformin is a widely used drug for type-2 diabetes. Reports hinted it extends healthy years in mice without diabetes. The worm Caenorhabditis elegans offered fast genetics to find the mechanism. The team suspected the drug mimics eating less.

Worms on metformin stayed healthy longer than untreated worms. The benefit ran through AMPK and LKB1, energy sensors in cells. It also needed SKN-1, a stress-response switch. Those links tie drug action to the same circuits as dietary restriction.
plos-pone-0008858:
David Gómez-Varela, Tobias Kohl, Manuela Schmidt, and colleagues filmed single channel proteins wandering in rat brain cell membranes. Their study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010. Eag1 is a voltage-gated channel shaping nerve cell firing. Channels must reach and leave synapses at the right times. Watching native channels move in real time was long impossible. Quantum dots, tiny glowing crystals, changed that.

Dots attached to single Eag1 channels lit their paths across the membrane. Tracking revealed how fast and how far the channels roam. Movement rules help explain how synapses tune their strength. The method opens other native proteins to the same filming.
plos-pone-0008958:
Karin Loser and colleagues showed a skin pigment hormone also helps build killer immune cells, in PLOS ONE in 2010. The hormone, alpha-MSH, is best known for darkening skin colour. It also plays roles in appetite, sexual function, and calming inflammation. The team asked whether it shapes CD8 T cells, the immune cells that kill infected cells.

In mice and in human cells, the hormone proved necessary for these T cells to develop properly. Without its signal, the cytotoxic cells matured poorly. The finding adds an immune duty to a hormone long filed under skin biology. It may matter for vaccines or treatments that rely on strong killer T cells.
plos-pone-0009058:
Sevin Turcan, Donna Slonim, and Douglas Vetter followed ear development in mice missing one hearing receptor, in PLOS ONE in 2010. The missing piece is the alpha9 nicotinic receptor in the cochlea. Without it, the ear loses a whole channel of nerve control. Synapse structures at the hair cells also form abnormally.

The team profiled gene activity over time in the mutant mice. Cochlear maturation slowed compared with normal mice. Meanwhile parts of the calming GABA system ramped up, perhaps in compensation. The timeline shows how one missing receptor reshapes an entire sense organ.
plos-pone-0009158:
Daniel Datiko and Bernt Lindtjørn priced community-based tuberculosis care in Ethiopia, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Ethiopia lacked hard numbers on what TB control costs to deliver in practice. Health extension workers are community staff trained to give basic care locally. A community trial had these workers treat smear-positive TB patients near their homes.

The analysis measured the full cost per patient treated in this way. It also judged cost-effectiveness against the standard clinic-based route. Care delivered in the community can spare patients long, costly trips. For a poor health system, the price tag decides whether such schemes can scale.
plos-pone-0009258:
Alexis Dumortier and co-authors published this mouse skin study in PLOS ONE in 2010. The Notch pathway guides skin cells to mature properly as embryos develop. Removing Notch signaling from young skin breaks the skin barrier. It also triggers a blood disorder in mice, which raised questions about adult skin.

The team removed Notch signaling from the skin of mice and watched what followed. The mice developed a disease like atopic dermatitis, the itchy rash of eczema. Alongside it came a lethal overgrowth of myeloid blood cells. The double result ties one signaling pathway to both skin health and blood cell control.
plos-pone-0009358:
Kerryl Piper and co-authors published this orthopedics study in PLOS ONE in 2010. Two blood tests, CRP and ESR, help doctors spot infections around artificial joints. They are well proven for infected hip and knee replacements. Far less was known about their value for shoulder replacements or spine implants.

The team reviewed patients facing revision or removal of shoulder and spine hardware. They checked how well the two tests flagged real infections there. Knowing a test's limits in each body site prevents both missed infections and needless surgery. The study extends the evidence for two cheap, common tests into less-studied territory.
plos-pone-0009458:
Hanako Kobayashi and co-authors reported on a signal protein and sepsis in PLOS ONE in 2010. Sepsis is a whole body crisis sparked by infection. Too much inflammation damages blood vessels and organs. The protein, interleukin-32 beta, occurs in human tissues. Normal lab mice do not have it, which had hidden its role.

When the team gave the protein to mice, vessel inflammation grew worse. Sepsis also became more severe in those animals. The result names the protein as a driver, not a bystander, in the crisis. Blocking it could be a new way to calm the immune storm that makes sepsis so deadly.
plos-pone-0009558:
Beatriz Martinez-Poveda and co-authors tested plant compounds against blood vessel growth in PLOS ONE in 2010. New vessels feed growing tumors, so blocking them is a cancer strategy. Hyperforin, from the herb St. John's wort, already showed strong blocking power. The team made and tested two new relatives of it. Their names are tetrahydrohyperforin and octahydrohyperforin.

Both new compounds proved to be potent blockers of vessel growth. Comparing them with the parent compound shows which chemical features do the work. That knowledge helps chemists design better versions. It is a step toward turning a plant product into a cancer drug lead.
plos-pone-0009658:
Andre Le Jeune and co-authors studied a bacterial defense in a gut germ in PLOS ONE in 2010. Enterococcus faecalis lives in the gut and can cause serious infections. It withstands lysozyme, an enzyme in tears and saliva that kills many bacteria. A factor called SigV helps run its stress defenses. The team tested SigV's role in the germ's original model strain.

SigV proved key both to lysozyme resistance and to the germ's virulence. Without it, the bacterium was easier to kill and less harmful. That makes the factor a point of weakness worth probing. Understanding how gut germs resist our enzymes helps explain how they turn dangerous.
plos-pone-0009758:
Won-Jong Oh and co-authors published a development study in PLOS ONE in 2010. The study asks why mice that lack GABA signaling, a key brain calming system, are born with a cleft palate. Past work left open whether the fault lies in the brain or in the palate itself.

Palates from the mutant mice grew in a normal way in dishes, showing no fault in the tissue, the team reports. A drug that boosts GABA action rescued the palate in the womb. Shutting off one gene only in the brain was enough to cause the defect. The authors link the flaw to lost fetal movement.
plos-pone-0009858:
Fungi can switch shapes, and a single protein can sometimes flip the switch. Rebecca Lindsey, Youngsil Ha, and Michelle Momany moved a fungal protein into yeast to test that. Their study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010. Septins help cells divide and hold their shape.

The protein is a septin from Aspergillus nidulans, a filamentous fungus. In budding yeast, Saccharomyces cerevisiae, it induced atypical pseudohyphae, odd chain-like growth forms.
