Pseudohyphae are stretched cells that stay attached after dividing. Cross-species tests like this reveal what shape genes really do. Yeast is a far simpler test bed than the fungus itself.
plos-pone-0009958:
Acid soils poison corn roots with aluminum, cutting harvests across the tropics. Allison Krill and colleagues hunted the genes that let maize tolerate that poison. Their study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010.

Association and linkage analysis are two ways to tie traits to gene regions. Both pointed to aluminum tolerance genes in maize. Aluminum harms roots first, stunting the whole plant. Tolerant varieties can grow where acid soil would otherwise stop them. Breeders can use the gene map to build hardier corn. Acid soils cover wide parts of the tropics and beyond.
plos-pone-0010158:
The authors were Ron Dirks, Remon van Geel, Sanne Hensen, and others. Their 2010 PLOS ONE study tried to weaken a stress pathway in frog tadpoles. Heat shock factor-1, or HSF1, directs the protective heat shock response. Its signaling fades with age, a decline that may relate to diseases where proteins clump in cells.

Working in Xenopus tadpoles, the team tried to block HSF1 to model that decline. Neuronal tissues proved refractory, meaning they resisted the added blocking protein. That resistance complicates disease models, yet it also hints that nerve tissue guards this pathway especially well.
plos-pone-0010458:
Caroline Aspord and colleagues built a cancer vaccine from a special donor cell type in PLOS ONE in 2010. Effective cancer vaccines remain elusive despite decades of effort. Plasmacytoid dendritic cells are rare immune cells with strong anti-tumor potential. Their use in therapy had not been worked out. The team used donor cells matched to a common tissue type marker. Matching lets one donor line serve many patients.

An off-the-shelf vaccine would be far easier than growing each patient's own cells. The matched cells could present tumor pieces to the patient's immune system. This study tested whether that strategy can stir real anti-tumor responses. It points toward standardized cancer vaccines, if the responses prove strong and safe. Rare cells, here, might serve many patients.
plos-pone-0010558:
Joana Duarte and colleagues shifted immune cell balance to prevent autoimmune arthritis in mice in PLOS ONE in 2010. Rheumatoid arthritis is a chronic disease where immunity attacks the joints. Two T cell types pull in opposite directions in this disease: Th17 cells drive attack, regulatory cells calm it. Their balance may decide whether arthritis starts. The team tested a non-depleting treatment that adjusts two key markers, IL-17 and Foxp3.

Adjusting the balance protected mice from developing the arthritis. Rebalancing rather than suppressing immunity wholesale is an attractive strategy. It promises fewer side effects than blanket immune shutdown. Mouse prevention does not equal human treatment, but the principle is clear. This study supports therapies that retune, rather than remove, immune cells.
plos-pone-0010658:
Eduardo Rodriguez-Noriega and colleagues built a scoring system for flu triage in Mexico, in PLOS ONE in 2010. The 2009 H1N1 pandemic flooded hospitals with people who had breathing problems. Clinicians at one Guadalajara hospital needed a fast way to sort mild cases from dangerous ones.

Their score combined patient history, lab results, and chest images. Applied to adults with flu-like illness, it separated those needing admission from those safe to send home. A tested score beats guesswork when wards are full. The Guadalajara experience offers a template other hospitals can adapt in the next pandemic.
plos-pone-0010758:
László Bányai, Peter Sonderegger, and László Patthy found a new binding role for agrin, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Agrin is best known for organizing the junction where nerves meet muscle. Part of the protein had a clear job there. The rest of this large protein had stayed largely unexplained after two decades of study.

The team showed agrin can bind three growth factors from the BMP and TGF-beta families. Binding can store, shield, or present such factors to cells. That gives the unexplained parts of agrin plausible work in growth and repair. A famous specialist turns out to hold a second, more general job.
plos-pone-0010858:
Katherine Elliott, Eleftheria Zeggini, Mark McCarthy and co-authors published this large collaborative analysis in PLOS ONE in 2010. Variants in the HNF1B gene are tied to type 2 diabetes, and oddly, the same variants seemed to lower prostate cancer risk. The team asked whether the effect reaches other cancers or belongs to prostate cancer alone.

Pooling data from nineteen genome-wide studies, they examined two common variants across tens of thousands of cancer cases and controls. The cancers included bowel, breast, lung, and pancreatic tumors, plus melanoma. Results differed sharply between datasets, driven by opposite effects in prostate cancer versus the other cancers. Elliott and colleagues conclude the HNF1B effect is not a general cancer shield. Their work is a caution against treating one gene's role as the same in every tissue.
plos-pone-0010958:
Estefanía Rodríguez and Marymegan Daly published this sea anemone evolution study in PLOS ONE in 2010. Anemones live in every ocean habitat, including deep-sea vents and seeps where chemistry, not sunlight, fuels life. Species from those extreme sites are highly specialized and their classification is confused, so the authors rebuilt their family tree from DNA.

Using five molecular markers across the superfamily that holds most deep-sea, polar, and vent anemones, they tested whether the vent dwellers form one clan. They do not: anemones of chemical environments descend from at least two separate lineages, one mostly deep-sea and one mostly shallow-water in origin. Rodríguez and Daly show that extreme habitats were colonized more than once, reshaping how anemone diversity is organized.
plos-pone-0011058:
Renata Dziedzic, Manjot Kiran, Przemyslaw Plocinski and co-authors published this tuberculosis cell biology study in PLOS ONE in 2010. Bacterial division begins when FtsZ protein assembles into a ring at midcell. How the TB bacterium controls that step was largely unknown. The authors focused on ClpX, part of a protein-degrading machine, whose production rises when the bacterium infects the immune cells called macrophages.

Four independent binding methods confirmed that ClpX physically interacts with FtsZ. Adding ClpX raised the amount FtsZ needs before it can form its ring. That restrains assembly. Cells normally keep the two proteins in a fairly tight ratio. Dziedzic and colleagues identify a brake on the division machinery of a pathogen that divides slowly and unevenly. Interfering with division control is a recognized route to new antibiotics.
plos-pone-0011158:
Pappas, Viswanathan, Chandrasekaran and colleagues revisited a past pandemic in PLOS ONE in 2010. Viruses of the H2N2 flu type caused the 1957 pandemic and later vanished from humans, though they still exist in animals. The team tested how well these viruses bind cells and spread.

Their work gauges whether this old flu type could pose a threat again. Most people alive now lack immunity to it, since it left human circulation long ago. Knowing its binding and spread traits helps planners judge risk. The study supports readiness for a forgotten virus that could return.
plos-pone-0011258:
Drogemuller, Becker, Kessler and colleagues studied greyhounds with nerve disease in PLOS ONE in 2010. Some greyhounds develop polyneuropathy, a weakening of nerves across the body. The team searched their DNA and found a deletion in a gene already linked to a similar human nerve disease.

The shared cause mirrors human Charcot Marie Tooth disease in a dog breed. That parallel helps both veterinary care and human medicine, since each species can teach about the other. Breeders can now test for the deletion to reduce affected puppies. Researchers gain a large animal model whose disease matches the human one closely.
plos-pone-0011358:
Yaye Lawaly and co-authors asked in 2010 whether some people are born more likely to pass malaria to mosquitoes. When a mosquito bites a person carrying malaria parasites, it can pick up the parasite and spread it onward. People differ greatly in how infectious they are, and that human pool of infection keeps the disease alive in a region.

The team tested whether that infectiousness runs in families, which would point to a heritable trait. Their evidence supports a genetic share in how strongly a person can infect mosquitoes. If a small share of people fuels much of the spread, control programs could focus on finding and treating those people. The finding shifts part of malaria control from the mosquito alone toward the human hosts who most feed transmission.
plos-pone-0011458:
Manju Mamtani and co-authors searched in 2010 for gene patterns that predict the course of Kawasaki disease in Japanese children. The disease brings fever and inflamed blood vessels in young children, and in the worst cases it scars the coronary arteries of the heart. Standard treatment with IVIG helps most children, but some respond poorly for unknown reasons.

The team linked variants in two immune receptor genes and the copy number of a related gene to the disease itself, to heart artery damage, and to IVIG response. Those clues could one day help doctors spot, at diagnosis, which children need the most aggressive care. For a disease whose worst harm is preventable with timely treatment, a genetic warning system would be a genuine clinical gain.
plos-pone-0011558:
Hediye Nese Cinar and co-authors showed in 2010 that one cholera toxin does the damage in a tiny worm host. Vibrio cholerae, the cholera germ, makes several candidate weapons, and the roundworm Caenorhabditis elegans offers a simple gut in which to test them. The team fed worms the bacterium with and without its hemolysin, a toxin that punctures cell membranes.

Without hemolysin, the germ lost its power to kill the worms, delay their development, and riddle their intestines with vacuoles, hollow damaged pockets. The toxin is therefore required, not incidental, for this harm. A worm model turns a human pathogen's weapon into a trait that can be screened quickly and cheaply. Compounds or bacterial mutations that disarm hemolysin can now be hunted at a scale human-relevant models cannot match.
plos-pone-0011658:
Peter Kraft and co-authors studied a clotting regulator called TAFI in mice, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Clot formation is a key step in ischaemic stroke, when a clot blocks blood flow in the brain. Thrombin, a central clotting enzyme, also activates TAFI, which slows the breakdown of clots and makes them more stable.

Mice lacking TAFI might therefore have been expected to fare better. Instead, they proved susceptible to clots and ischaemic injury in the brain. The surprise vulnerability reveals a protective side to TAFI in cerebral blood flow that simple clot logic would not predict.
plos-pone-0011758:
Young-Sang Koh and co-authors tested a frontline immune sensor against tick-borne germs, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Ehrlichiae are tiny germs that live inside host cells and cause human monocytotropic ehrlichiosis, a rising and at times fatal tick-borne disease. The part played by fast innate sensing, as opposed to later adaptive defence, needed defining.

Working in mice, the team showed signals through the sensor MyD88 add a great deal to host defence against ehrlichial infection. Without it, control of the germs suffered. Pinning down this sensor's role sharpens the picture of the first line of defence against a little-known infection.
plos-pone-0011858:
Jan Zietsch and co-authors studied in 2010 a stretch of extra DNA found in a rare and deadly nerve tumor. These tumors grow from Schwann cells, which wrap around nerves, and they show up in about one in ten people who have the gene fault called neurofibromatosis type 1. Care is hard and life spans are short, so new drug ideas are badly needed.

The extra DNA sits in one small part of chromosome 4 and holds genes that run too hot in the tumors. One of those genes is a known target of the drug sunitinib, so the team asked what the extra copies mean for that drug. Tying a tumor's DNA faults to a drug now in use is one of the fastest ways to find help for rare cancers.
plos-pone-0011958:
Michael Graf, Alessandro Cellerino, and Christoph Englert kept in 2010 a short-lived African fish with the sexes apart to see what changes. Life history theory treats mating as costly: energy spent on reproduction cannot be spent on growth or survival. The turquoise killifish, Nothobranchius furzeri, lives fast and is a favorite aging model.

Females housed without males grew larger, yet their lifespan did not improve. Growth and longevity thus came apart: removing mating costs bought size, not time. That split is a useful check on simple trade-off stories, and it helps aging researchers choose what to measure in this much-used fish.
plos-pone-0012058:
Kenta Nakamura and co-workers studied in 2010 the small RNAs guiding a famous regeneration trick: the newt regrowing its own lens. After lens removal, pigment cells of the dorsal iris change identity and build a new lens; cells of the ventral iris cannot. MicroRNAs, tiny gene regulators, were candidates for enforcing that difference.

The team found microRNAs specifically controlling cell proliferation during regeneration, plus evidence that these regulators work in networks rather than alone. A network view matters because regeneration is a program, not a single switch. Newts remain the champions of vertebrate regeneration, and their small-RNA score is one of the few readable parts of that program.
plos-pone-0012158:
Yong Woo, Michael Walker, and Gary Churchill studied how genes are arranged along mammalian genomes in PLOS ONE in 2010. Gene order is not random: genes that switch on together often sit near each other in clusters. Why the genome keeps that arrangement, and what mechanisms maintain it, were the open questions behind their analysis.

The authors characterized these shared-expression neighborhoods across mammalian genomes and probed what creates them. Clusters may help the cell coordinate whole programs from a few control points. Understanding this layout adds a layer to genetics beyond single genes, pointing at the genome as an organized city rather than a parts list.
plos-pone-0012258:
Phillip Lord and Robert Stevens argued for grounding biological ontologies in how things really are, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Ontologies, formal dictionaries that let computers reason about biology, now underpin databases across the field. They are used to describe everything from genes to anatomy, and models built on them drive real research decisions.

The risk, the authors argue, is ontologies drifting into tidy logic that misdescribes messy living things. Adding a little reality means checking formal categories against actual biology, including its exceptions and gray zones. For infrastructure this widely used, small distortions multiply through thousands of studies, so the call for realism is practical, not philosophical.
plos-pone-0012358:
Hyo-Jeong Lee, Seung-Ae Kim, Hyo-Jung Lee and co-workers tested a plant-derived compound against tumor blood vessel growth in a 2010 PLOS ONE paper. Paeonol comes from the root bark of a peony used in East Asian medicine, and earlier work showed it can slow new vessel growth. The team made a changed form, paeonol oxime, and asked how strongly it blocks vessels fed by growth signals.

In cell tests, the compound curbed vessel growth driven by the signal bFGF and lowered levels of VEGF, another vessel signal, in fibrosarcoma cells. Tumors need new vessels to grow, so blocking two signals at once is promising. The study adds a candidate to the search for gentler anti-cancer drugs.
plos-pone-0012458:
Hari Raghu, Sajani Lakka, Christopher Gondi and colleagues blocked two proteins to cut vessel growth signals in tumors, in a 2010 PLOS ONE paper. The proteins uPA and uPAR help glioma brain tumors build blood vessels, guided by another factor called angiogenin. Earlier work by the group showed silencing the pair slowed vessel growth in glioma cells.

Here they extended the test to vessel-lining cells and glioblastoma lines, and silencing the pair again blunted angiogenin's push. Tumors starved of new vessels grow more slowly. The combined evidence makes the uPA-uPAR pair a candidate target for anti-vessel therapy in aggressive brain tumors.
plos-pone-0012558:
Pablo Fernandez, Stéphane Petres, Salaheddine Mécheri and colleagues tested an antibody-like blocker of placental malaria, in a 2010 PLOS ONE paper. In pregnancy-associated malaria, infected red cells stick to a placental receptor called CSA, endangering mother and baby. The parasite protein Var2CSA does the sticking, and one of its domains, DBL5 epsilon, is a vaccine candidate.

Immune responses raised against that domain blocked infected cells from sticking to placenta-derived cells under flowing conditions that mimic blood flow. Blocking across parasite strains — strain-transcendent protection — is the hard requirement for any malaria vaccine. Passing the flow test moves this domain closer to real candidacy.
plos-pone-0012658:
Khiabanian, Holmes, Kelly and co-authors mined hospital records for early signs of the 2009 flu pandemic. Health officials declared a flu pandemic in mid 2009, the first one of the new century. By July, New York-Presbyterian Hospital in New York City was seeing its effects firsthand.

Their 2010 study searched the hospital's electronic records for patterns that marked the pandemic's arrival. Patient records, gathered for care, can double as an early warning system for outbreaks. Showing that in a real hospital helps cities plan faster responses to the next pandemic.  Record patterns were checked against the known pandemic timeline.
plos-pone-0012758:
Thaker, Vanak, Owen and co-authors watched how zebra and wildebeest groups shift in wooded savanna. Herd animals in open grasslands have been studied for decades, and grouping there trades food access against safety from predators. Woodland changes that trade, since trees block sight lines and ambush cover is everywhere.

Their 2010 field study measured group sizes and movement as risk and habitat density changed across the woodland. The herds adjusted their grouping in ways grassland studies would not predict. Results like these refine how ecologists model prey behaviour across whole landscapes.
plos-pone-0333158:
Brian Dominguez and five colleagues use songbirds to study how a Parkinson's-linked protein quiets the brain circuits for voice, in this 2026 PLOS ONE study. Male zebra finches sing through a dedicated brain nucleus much like the circuits that fail in human speech. The team delivered extra copies of the human alpha-synuclein gene into that nucleus, then recorded individual neurons while the birds were anaesthetised.

One class of neurons — those with broad electrical spikes — fired far less than normal after the gene treatment, with an odd rebound after each peak. Earlier work showed the same treatment makes songs softer and shorter. Connecting cell-level quieting to voice loss may help explain why Parkinson's so often steals speech early.
plos-pone-0335558:
Du and colleagues built a compact vision system for spotting small objects in tennis matches in a 2026 study. The ball moves fast, players block views, and backgrounds are busy, so standard detectors often miss key items. Their system sharpens edges, weighs image channels more wisely, and punishes errors on hard small targets more strongly.

The team also labeled a new set of more than six thousand match images showing players, rackets, and balls. The system beat its base version on accuracy while staying small and fast enough for live use. Such a tool could support referees, coaches reviewing tactics, and broadcasters adding live graphics.
plos-pone-0336358:
Ao Qiao, Siyu Zeng, and Jianing Wang model what happens when two climate policies run at once, in this 2026 PLOS ONE economics paper. Governments increasingly pair cap-and-trade, which limits total emissions, with subsidies for low-carbon production, yet most research studies each policy alone and ignores factory-floor details such as batch sizes.

The authors set up a game between a manufacturer and a retailer, with the factory's production queue modeled to capture real emissions, and test different policy mixes. Comparing the outcomes shows how the two policies can reinforce or undercut each other, and what contract terms keep the supply chain cooperating. The results are meant for policy makers designing combined carbon rules.
plos-pone-0336758:
Shizuka Hashimoto and co-authors tested how bait choice shapes fish surveys that read DNA from river water. In species-rich tropical rivers, the short DNA tags used to trigger copying can miss whole groups. Their 2026 study worked in Brazil's Teles Pires basin, comparing standard and modified tag pairs against global and local reference libraries.

One modified tag pair detected the most species under every library setup. Combining libraries widened detection further, and a locally built library, drawn from fish actually caught nearby, added species that global lists missed. Hashimoto and colleagues conclude that tag choice and reference quality together decide what an environmental DNA survey can honestly claim to find.
plos-pone-0340658:
Karthik Kailasam and colleagues reviewed cardiac arrests inside one medical intensive care unit. Patients there are already critically ill, and many arrest under full monitoring. Survival still stays poor. The team asked which traits of the patient and the rescue effort predicted death. They adjusted for age, illness severity, and the first heart rhythm recorded.

One finding dominates the results. Every extra minute of CPR raised the odds of death. That held for death during the attempt and for death before leaving the unit. Survivors had also arrived less sick than those who died. Minutes are the currency of these events. Long rescues in failing bodies rarely end in recovery, and this study puts a number on that bedside truth.
plos-pone-0343158:
Shiming Wang and colleagues propose a data-driven system for keeping the cost of building commercial complexes, malls and mixed-use giants, under control. Such projects sprawl across functions and trades, and overruns hide until late. Their framework applies value engineering, a discipline that prices every function a building must perform, and ranks those functions with a fuzzy version of a standard priority method that tolerates expert disagreement.

Cost and value coefficients for each function are then watched in real time, flagging construction choices whose price outruns their worth while change is still cheap. The authors validated the approach by re-running an existing complex through it and comparing the outcome with what actually happened. For developers, the appeal is a control room for cost that argues in functions, not just invoices.
plos-pone-0343858:
Xuejing Fu, Zhen Chen, and Wentao Lu built a test for AI systems on drug regulation, published in PLOS ONE in 2026. Rules for medicines differ sharply between China and the United States, and AI assistants giving regulatory advice must handle both. Their benchmark, Sino-US-DrugQA, evaluates large language models on cross-border pharmaceutical regulation questions.

Fu's test reveals which AI systems navigate the regulatory maze and which stumble. Companies use language models for drafting and compliance help, where a confident wrong answer can be costly. A public benchmark lets buyers compare systems on the same hard questions. It also pushes model builders to improve on legal and regulatory knowledge, a weak spot for general-purpose AI.
plos-pone-0346758:
Maureen O'Callaghan and colleagues interviewed five frail older adults living with urinary incontinence. Five family caregivers joined them. The topic was treatments for a condition that is common, burdensome, and quietly endured. Their 2026 study explored how participants view conservative, drug, and surgical options. This perspective is rarely gathered from this group.

Five themes emerged. People managed alone with pads and routines until those failed. Many believed leakage is simply what ageing is, a fatalism that blocked help-seeking. New treatments raised fears of adding to caregivers' loads. Invasive options drew reluctance. Yet both patients and caregivers were cautiously willing to try gentle conservative approaches. The authors say acceptance hinges on dignity, burden, and shaking the myth that leakage is fate.
plos-pone-0347758:
He-Ping Liu and colleagues tested an extract from Syzygium brachythyrsum, a plant long used by the Dai people of Yunnan, China, against artery clogging in mice. The extract is rich in polyphenols, plant chemicals with antioxidant effects. Mice bred to develop atherosclerosis ate a high-fat diet for twelve weeks, with some receiving the extract and others a standard cholesterol drug.

Treated mice developed smaller fatty plaques in the aorta and stored less fat in the liver, with calmer inflammation and less oxidative damage. Cell experiments traced the benefit to a protective antioxidant pathway, and blocking that pathway erased the effect. The authors suggest the extract merits study as a companion therapy for heart disease.
plos-pone-0347858:
Mohammad Kazemi, Reza Naderi Samani, and Narges Kariminejad build a flood-risk map for Khuzestan Province in Iran in this 2026 PLOS ONE paper. Flood mapping depends heavily on which landscape factors the model uses and how it is tuned, so the team combined satellite data from Google Earth Engine with a careful selection process.

Nineteen candidate factors were scored by nine different selection methods, and the most consistently chosen fed a deep learning network whose settings were tuned by an optimization algorithm. One thousand sampled points, half flooded and half not, trained the model before it was applied across the province. Planners could use such maps to steer building and defenses away from the likeliest flood paths.
plos-pone-0347958:
Laila Farouk and colleagues chart drug resistance in urinary infections in Tétouan, Morocco. Their study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2026. Urinary infections rank among the most common bacterial illnesses. Gut-related bacteria cause most of them. Three labs in the city gathered isolates from outpatients in 2022 and 2023. The set held more than four hundred isolates.

Each isolate was named by machine and tested against key drugs. Extra checks hunted for enzymes that defeat whole drug families. Doctors treat these infections before test results come back. So a local map of what still works guides first choices. Outdated guesses breed resistance instead. The study gives Moroccan clinics that map.
plos-pone-0348058:
Shruti Khanduri and co-workers lay out a trial plan testing Trikatu, a classic Ayurvedic spice blend, as an add-on for people with unhealthy blood fats. Many patients in poorer countries stop cholesterol drugs early, so a culturally familiar helper could matter. Their 2026 protocol describes a blinded trial at a major Indian hospital with one hundred seventy adults at raised heart risk.

Half will take Trikatu twice a day for twelve weeks alongside their usual statin, and half a matching dummy pill. Blood fats form the main measure, with sugar, swelling markers, blood pressure, and gut microbes also tracked. As a protocol, the paper reports no results yet; it tests whether tradition and modern care can be judged fairly together.
plos-pone-0348158:
Mark Cortnage, Joseph Lillis, and Justin Roberts sat twenty-four men down in focus groups to talk frankly about dieting, a world most weight loss programs design for women. Their 2026 qualitative study, involving men mostly in their forties with overweight or obesity, sorted the conversation into themes about perceptions, barriers, turning points, and what makes change stick.

The men described dieting as cyclical and faintly embarrassing, driven by misinformation and low expectations, with appearance, more than health, supplying the spark to start. Three supports stood out: a buddy, a mentor, and above all a partner at home. The authors argue programs recruiting men should build that buddy, mentor, and spousal scaffolding in from the start rather than handing over a diet sheet.
plos-pone-0348358:
Hessam Noori-Dokht and colleagues examine a hidden source of noise in cartilage injury experiments, in this 2026 PLOS ONE biomechanics paper. Labs study joint injury by striking a rabbit's knee cartilage with a controlled impact, but the joint is pinned by a metal wire whose exact placement varies from specimen to specimen.

Measuring impacts on cadaver knees, the team found that where the wire sat front-to-back strongly predicted peak stress, loading speed, impact duration, and total work, while its up-down position mattered little. Bone failure measures shifted with placement too. Standardizing wire position, they argue, would make injury models more repeatable, so treatments tested in animals rest on cleaner comparisons.
plos-pone-0348758:
Enjing Xiao and co-workers improve a camera-based defect spotter for the banded edges of wooden furniture panels. Edge banding flaws are small and easy to miss, which costs makers rework and returns. Their 2026 study upgrades a compact detection model with feature blending across scales, a sharper pooling block with attention, and a loss rule that settles faster on the flaw's true box.

On a purpose-built photo set of panel edges, the improved model scored higher on the standard detection measure than the base model it grew from. The authors describe fewer misses and fewer false alarms as the practical payoff. Automated edge checks could steady quality on furniture lines where tired eyes now do the watching.
plos-pone-0348858:
Russell Tronstad and Ibrahima Sall valued education programs for people with limited resources, in a PLOS ONE paper from 2026. Extension programs teach farming and life skills, but they must prove their worth to funders and to the audiences themselves. The authors used a willingness-to-accept experiment, asking what payment people would accept in place of the teaching.

Tronstad and Sall's valuations put hard numbers on what participants judge the education to be worth. Program planners can compare those values with costs when deciding what to offer. The method respects the audience's own judgment instead of assuming benefit. For services aimed at low-income communities, that respect, backed by numbers, strengthens the case for funding what truly helps.
plos-pone-0349558:
Jinmeng Bi, Ye Li, and Yuhang Pan mapped earthquake patterns across North China using records from 1970 to 2025 in work published in 2026. The region is one of continental China's most active, and two pattern measures may reveal stress building before big shocks.

After removing aftershock clusters statistically, the team measured how spread out quakes are in space and the balance of small to large events. Removing clusters raised the spread measure. High spread sat in fractured zones, low in the stable Ordos block. Spread fell before main shocks and recovered after, a rhythm that could one day aid watchfulness, though not prediction.
plos-pone-0349758:
Blanca Lumbreras and colleagues surveyed Spanish doctors about prostate cancer screening with the PSA blood test. Newer European guidance favors risk-based screening and shared decisions with patients, rather than testing everyone. General practitioners and urologists both order these tests, so the study compared the two groups' knowledge, attitudes, and habits across nearly five hundred respondents.

The questionnaire was built through an expert consensus process and covered opinions, daily practice, and guideline knowledge. Differences between the specialties matter because a man's path to diagnosis usually starts with whichever doctor he sees first. Where the two groups disagree on testing or on involving patients in the choice, screening practice will vary for reasons that have nothing to do with the patient.
plos-pone-0349858:
Fiaz Majeed and seven colleagues wrote this 2026 PLOS One study comparing machine learning models that predict the Air Quality Index for Karachi and Peshawar, two major Pakistani cities. Dirty air drives breathing illness, and forecasting its quality helps officials warn the public in time. The authors trained four regression models on recent local pollution data covering gases and fine particles.

All four models predicted the index effectively when judged by standard error measures. Careful scaling of the data before training proved important for getting the best results, and performance differed somewhat between the two cities. The authors argue that such models, fed with current local data, can give city agencies a cheap and timely forecasting tool for smog-prone regions.
plos-pone-0350658:
Yiwen Wei, Lingxiao Guo, and Qunshan Tao studied how China's carbon cutting and public health services develop together across provinces from 2012 to 2023, in work published in 2026. National goals push both agendas at once, and whether they advance in step was unknown.

The team scored carbon governance and health service efficiency for thirty-one provinces, then measured how tightly the two were coupled and where gaps concentrate. National coupling wobbled early, then rose steadily. Regional inequality and clustering patterns were mapped, and factors behind them tested. The results help provinces see whether green and health progress reinforce or crowd each other.
plos-pone-0350858:
Kazuya Hosokawa and colleagues set out a study plan, with no results yet, for spotting a treatable cause of high pressure in the lungs. Blocked lung arteries after clots can raise that pressure, yet diagnosis often comes late and the best scan is scarce outside large centres. A moving chest X ray method can map blood flow in the lungs quickly.

Readers will judge real cases in random order, some with standard tests alone and some with the moving X ray added. Final diagnoses follow Japanese and European rules. The team will compare accuracy, hits, and misses, and check how well the new method matches the scarce scan. If it works, more hospitals could screen without delay.
plos-pone-0351058:
Ziqiao Ding and colleagues argue that supply chains need embodied intelligence, where sensing, thinking, and physical action join in one loop. Most research tunes algorithms on data alone, leaving a gap between digital plans and real warehouses and trucks. Their framework stacks four layers: sensing the world, reasoning in context, acting physically, and feeding results back for learning.

Fragmented sensing and slow feedback are named as core faults in current chains. By naming those faults and mapping how each layer should inform the next, the paper sets an agenda for theory, tools, and practice. Chains that learn from physical outcomes, the authors claim, will adapt faster than chains that only replan on screens.
plos-pone-0351158:
Online shops increasingly let buyers try products virtually, draping clothes or placing furniture through augmented reality. Xiaodong Zhang and colleagues surveyed about four hundred eighty shoppers to learn how such features shape the wish to buy, in this 2026 PLOS One study.

Four features were tested: virtual try-on, hands-on product displays, blending virtual goods into real rooms, and personal suggestions. Each raised buying intention indirectly, by lifting how valuable the shopping felt and how warmly people viewed the brand. None acted straight through. The authors advise sellers to design reality tools around felt value and brand feeling, not novelty alone.
plos-pone-0351658:
Bethany Ridley and colleagues validated new body size scales for young adults. The scales are photo-realistic figures built from three-dimensional scans of real eighteen-year-olds. Clinics and researchers need pictures that people can point to when judging body size. Older sets are often cartoon-like or built from older bodies. A hundred ten volunteers aged eighteen to twenty-five judged the figures. They estimated sizes and ranked the figures twice, three days apart.

The volunteers ranked the figures in step with the true body mass steps built into them. Their size estimates were accurate too. Scores held steady across the two sessions, with reliability from good to excellent. Young adults face high weight-related risk yet are often skipped in program design. A checked visual ruler for this age band fills a real gap.
plos-pone-0351758:
Aishwa Roy and Protima Sarker tested bone meal powder, ground animal bone, as a homegrown phosphorus fertilizer for Malabar spinach. Chemical phosphorus fertilizer is pricey and polluting, and mined phosphate is finite, so alternatives matter. They ran the powder in two soils, one salty and one not, tracking soil chemistry, then grew spinach in pots to watch germination and early growth.

The bone meal raised soil pH and clearly lifted the phosphorus plants could reach in both soils. The plant side was mixed: germination and some early growth measures suffered in the non-salty soil even as shoots lengthened, while roots and fresh weight changed little. The authors call it promising but unfinished business, asking for field trials before farmers swap their fertilizer bags for bone meal.
plos-pone-0351858:
Yitian Ou and colleagues traced how immune cells inside prostate tumors coach the cancer to spread. The cells are macrophages in their wound-healing mode. They release a growth signal called M-CSF. The team's earlier work had already flagged that signal. This study hunted the protein inside the cancer cell that answers it. They scanned the full protein output of treated prostate cancer cells.

One protein stood out: PCLAF. Checks in patient data backed its importance. Tumor tissue from seventy-nine men pointed the same way. Turning PCLAF up or down in lab tests moved invasion and migration with it. The chain now runs from an immune signal to one named effector. That gives drug hunters a narrower target in advanced disease.
plos-pone-0351958:
Savina Chham and colleagues asked whether Cambodia's community health workers could take on a bigger role against diabetes and high blood pressure, two diseases climbing fast while clinics run short of staff. They surveyed a hundred fifty-three active workers on knowledge, attitudes, and current practice, and interviewed officials about the barriers to widening the workers' role.

The workers scored well on general questions about these diseases, risk factors, and prevention, with about nine in ten answering correctly. Gaps showed on specifics: only a fifth to two fifths knew that family history and tobacco count as risk factors. Most already did some related tasks and felt positive about the work. Money and supplies, not willingness, are the choke points, so any expanded role needs funding and kit behind it.
plos-pone-0352158:
Lamia Jouini and six colleagues evaluate anti-stigma training for medical students in Tunisia. Their 2026 study tests a programme called READ. It teaches future doctors to respond to discrimination experienced or expected by people with mental illness. Knowledge, attitudes, and practical skills were measured before and after training. A control group allowed fair comparison, and a mock clinical exam tested real behaviour with patients.

Attitudes improved clearly in the trained group. Their stigma scores fell well beyond the control group's movement. Skills improved too. Trained students were over four times more likely to pass the practical exam. That exam grades how a student actually handles a patient describing discrimination. Knowledge and warmth on paper are not enough in a clinic room. The results encourage wider use of the training, and further research into which parts of it drive the change.
plos-pone-0352258:
Yanni Huang, Fuhua Yang, and Keli Yin surveyed eleven hundred four university students in Yunnan, China, about the good parts of their childhoods and their present happiness. Warm, safe, supportive early experiences are thought to echo into adult life. Scales measured those early experiences, the students' resilience, and their sense of well-being.

Students who recalled more positive childhood experiences reported stronger well-being as young adults. Resilience explained part of the link: good early experiences seemed to build the ability to bounce back, which in turn supported happiness. The tie was partial, so childhood warmth also matters in other ways. The authors urge colleges to train resilience while noting the sample came from one province, so the pattern needs testing in other places and cultures.
plos-pone-0352358:
Weiping Ma proposes a new way to outline organs in three-dimensional medical scans in this 2026 paper. Drawing those outlines by hand is slow expert work. Semi-supervised learning cuts the burden by learning from a few labelled scans plus many unlabelled ones. Ma's framework sets two networks to teach each other. A cross-attention module lets them exchange detailed features as they learn.

The two branches follow a teacher-student design built on a VNet backbone. Extra losses keep their feature distributions aligned and their classes cleanly separated. Knowledge flows in both directions, so each network corrects the other. Tests used left atrium scans and pancreatic scans, two hard segmentation targets. The method outperformed existing approaches on both. Hospitals could gain accurate scan outlines while labelling only a fraction of their image archives.
plos-pone-0352658:
Bony Lestari and seven colleagues count what tuberculosis care costs patients before treatment even starts. Their 2026 study is set in Bandung, Indonesia. It focuses on drug-resistant tuberculosis, which is harder and slower to diagnose. Patients often visit several providers before anyone confirms the disease. Every visit adds fees, tests, travel, and food costs.

Interviews with two hundred fifty-eight patients reconstructed those early expenses. The typical patient had spent roughly forty-five US dollars before treatment began. Costs spread across administration, chest X-rays, laboratory tests, medicines, travel, and food. Most patients first sought help at community health centres, and many lived in rural areas. Knowing where the money leaks out helps programmes shorten the path to diagnosis and protect poor families from early financial harm.
plos-pone-0352758:
Patricia Jurado-Gonzalez and five colleagues developed this 2026 PLOS One questionnaire for measuring how confident Spanish university students feel about cooking. Students often eat poorly after leaving home, and confidence in the kitchen is tied to better diets, yet Spain had no validated tool for this group. The team built items from existing questionnaires, had food experts review them, and piloted the draft at four Catalan universities.

After revisions, the final tool holds twenty-five items in two subscales. Student answers hung together consistently, and scores stayed stable when the questionnaire was repeated two weeks later. The authors offer it as a ready instrument for researchers and campus health programs that want to track, and eventually raise, students' cooking confidence.
plos-pone-0352858:
Karahan and Kasnakoglu designed flight control for a swarm of small drones facing several troubles at once in a 2026 study. Wind, noisy sensors, and delayed messages each unsettle a flying formation, yet past work often handled them one at a time. Their framework plans paths and dodges obstacles while treating all three troubles together.

Math analysis set bounds on how far the swarm could drift from its path under limited disturbance. Computer flights in two formation shapes reached targets, kept formation, and passed fixed obstacles without crashes. Brief shape bending appeared under stress, then the swarm recovered. The unified approach suits rescue and inspection work where conditions rarely stay clean.
plos-pone-0353058:
Abd El-Baky and colleagues, in a 2026 study, try to make an old drug, metronidazole, work better against a germ that infects the urinary tract. The germ, Proteus mirabilis, often strikes people with catheters and can help form stones. It also resists many drugs. The team's idea is to tuck the drug inside ring-shaped sugar carriers called cyclodextrins.

Three kinds of carrier were mixed with the drug by simple blending or kneading. Lab tests checked how the pairs formed and how fast the drug was released. Two carriers improved release, and one pairing needed a much lower dose to slow the germ. At doses too low to kill, the paired drug still cut the germ's swimming, its stone-linked enzyme action, and its ability to build biofilms, the slimy layers that shield germs. The authors say animal studies must come next before any clinical use.
plos-pone-0353158:
Maite Alanya-Pineda and six colleagues report this 2026 PLOS One study linking depressive symptoms to balance problems in older adults living in twelve high Andean communities in Peru. Mountain life brings low oxygen and scarce health services, which may raise rates of both conditions. The team reanalyzed survey data collected between 2013 and 2020 from more than four hundred residents, using a short depression questionnaire and a reach test for balance.

About half the residents showed depressive symptoms, and about half had balance disorders. After adjustment, those with depressive symptoms were about two-thirds more likely to have balance trouble than those without. The authors call for larger studies and for screening programs that catch both problems early, since together they raise the risk of falls and lost independence.
plos-pone-0353258:
Niilo Liuhto and seven colleagues report this 2026 PLOS One study testing whether fragments of DNA floating in blood predict bad outcomes in advanced kidney disease. Such cell-free DNA is a newer inflammation marker never checked in patients whose kidneys are failing but who have not yet started dialysis. The team measured it in nearly one hundred forty patients and followed them for several years.

The marker predicted nothing: not deaths, heart events, emergency visits, hospital stays, or new cancers. Levels did rise later in patients who moved on to transplants or dialysis, suggesting the treatment stage itself shifts the marker. The authors present the negative result as useful guidance, sparing future studies from chasing a marker that does not deliver in this group.
plos-pone-0353358:
Rodrigo Torres-Avilés and three colleagues show that a classic database question can be answered without unpacking the data, in this 2026 PLOS ONE computer science paper. A skyline query finds records that no other record beats on every measure at once — the hotels, say, that are each cheapest or best-rated in some unbeatable combination. The team implemented two flavours of the query inside a compact tree structure that stores data in compressed form.

Working directly on the compressed structure saved memory compared with ordinary approaches in their experiments, while still returning exact answers. They back the method with full proofs and benchmarks. Compact querying matters wherever data outgrow the machine that must answer questions about them.
plos-pone-0353558:
Jiuwei Chi and seven colleagues reconstruct the carbon footprint of farming in Inner Mongolia from 2006 to 2023, in this 2026 PLOS ONE study. The region grows grain in dry country, leaning hard on irrigation, fertiliser, diesel, and plastic mulch. Counting the emissions embedded in those six inputs year by year, the team traced how the footprint evolved as China's farming modernised.

Input use surged early, then steadied or fell back after the mid-2010s for fertiliser, pesticide, and diesel — while plastic film kept climbing and irrigated area jumped late in the period. The pattern shows a system halfway through its low-carbon turn, with film and water now the stubborn fronts for policy.
plos-pone-0353958:
Lu and colleagues, in a 2026 forensic study, ask whether chemistry in the liver and kidneys can tell how a body died in seawater and how long it has been dead. Telling real drowning from a body placed in water after death is a classic hard problem. Sixty rats were assigned to seawater drowning or to being placed in seawater after death, and tissues were sampled across three days.

Thousands of small molecules in each tissue were measured, and machine learning models were trained on the patterns. Time since death dominated the chemistry, yet the models still separated the two causes of death with very high accuracy in both organs. Separate models guessed time since death within a few hours when tested on known time points, and less well on unseen ones. The authors present the approach as a promising forensic aid under controlled conditions, not yet a courtroom tool.
plos-pone-0354158:
Matthew Davitt and co-authors map in 2026 research that uses muscle electrical recording to judge the physical strain on surgeons doing keyhole and robot assisted belly surgery. Their scoping review followed standard guidance and searched many databases for studies in real or simulated surgical settings. Close to a hundred studies spanning nearly three decades qualified.

Most work covered plain keyhole surgery, with far fewer robot studies. Shoulder, neck, and forearm muscles were measured most, often alongside motion tracking or questionnaires. In the small set comparing both approaches, robot assistance consistently showed lower muscle activity, especially in the upper body, though the authors urge caution given the thin base.
plos-pone-0354258:
Nazlı Yanar Tunçel and Züleyha Avşar gave seventh-grade students virtual reality games for eight weeks of physical education and tested their balance and coordination. Schools are weighing headsets as teaching tools, but physical effects need evidence. Their 2026 experiment compared twenty headset students with nineteen controls on standard movement batteries.

The headset group improved more on backward balancing, side-to-side jumping, and platform transport tasks. Total coordination scores and balance reach in both directions also favoured the players. One test, single-leg hopping, showed no group difference. Yanar Tunçel and Avşar conclude that well-chosen virtual games can train real body skills, while noting that not every skill responds equally.
plos-pone-0354358:
Henkin and colleagues, in a 2026 interview study, look inside British teams that build artificial intelligence for health care. Such projects force data scientists, doctors, patients, and managers to work as one, and the social side is inseparable from the technical. Thirteen people in young research consortia described how knowledge actually moves between these camps.

People said they constantly reshaped both their tools and their message for the audience in front of them, especially clinicians and patients. Working in AI research was new to most, which itself created friction. Clinician and patient voices were wanted, but fitting them into technical workflows took effort, and AI knowledge traveled unevenly across the team. The authors take one participant's shrug as the study's spirit: much is improvised, and teams admit they are finding out as they go. Their point is that funding good teamwork is part of building good medical AI.
plos-pone-0354458:
Guanlin Dai, Da Gao, and Chao Zheng improve how AI finds a requested moment inside a video, a task called moment retrieval. Standard transformer models hunt the whole video at once because their search prompts carry no built-in sense of time span, and they falter on events of varied length. The team replaces those loose prompts with bell-shaped time priors that have a learnable center and width, seeded from local video features at several scales.

On a standard public benchmark, the design clearly helped one weak spot: finding long events, where scores rose by about two points over a leading rival with statistical support. Overall recall differences stayed inconclusive. Dai and colleagues present the prior as a cheap, focused part for studying scale-aware search in video models.
plos-pone-0354958: Sakthivel and seven co-authors published a 2026 PLOS ONE study on a material for storing electric charge. The material is BaMoO4, a metal oxide used in supercapacitors, devices that charge and discharge quickly. The team varied how long the material cooked in hot water and tracked changes in shape and performance. Their tests used an asymmetric supercapacitor setup. Small shape changes can shift how much energy such devices hold.
plos-pone-0355158:
Nigatu Madebo, Feleke Yareshe, and Lebsework Lemma propose in 2026 a new controller to guide unmanned aircraft along a set path more closely. They first recorded how a fuzzy logic controller behaved, then trained a combined neural and fuzzy system on those records. The trained system can adjust its own settings during flight, unlike the fixed original.

Simulations covered normal flight, flight with outside pushes, and flight when aircraft traits changed. The new controller cut a standard tracking error score sharply in the harder cases and by a smaller margin in normal flight. The authors present the method for jobs needing precise, steady flight.
plos-pone-0355558:
Christian Jäger and three colleagues describe how a German university medical center moved its lab record-keeping from paper to a digital notebook system, reporting in 2026. The open-source platform they adopted promises better data quality and easier sharing, but such switches often stall on user habits. Their study combines the rollout story with a survey of researchers about how they actually document their work.

Most survey respondents were experienced researchers, yet many complained that documenting took too long, was badly organized, and made old information hard to find. Nearly everyone named ease of use as the top requirement, with training and ongoing support close behind. Over the rollout period the platform grew to hundreds of users across dozens of teams. The authors share checklists and helper apps so other institutions can copy the approach.
plos-pone-0355858:
Proshenjit Sarker and S M Shamsul Alam built a three-stage vision cascade that reads Bangladeshi vehicle license plates. Plate recognition feeds traffic enforcement, but Bangla plates vary widely and older character-reading tools cover too few symbol classes. Their 2026 system chains three detection models, each solving one step.

The first model finds vehicles, the second locates the plate, and the third reads characters directly, with no separate text-recognition engine. Its character set spans one hundred four classes, covering city codes, vehicle types, and digits. Training used more than nine thousand images, with a held-out set for external checking. Sarker and Alam aim for a recogniser shaped to local plates rather than adapted from foreign ones.
plos-pone-0355958:
Maarten Mosch and colleagues reviewed a rare knee-area fracture seen in teenagers at a Dutch trauma centre. The tibial tubercle, where the thigh tendon anchors below the knee, can crack during sport while bones are still growing. Their 2026 series covered forty young patients treated over fifteen years.

Nearly all patients were boys, injured mostly during sports, at an average age of about fourteen. Most fractures needed surgery, usually screw fixation; the rest healed without an operation. Complications were uncommon, at about one in ten fractures, and no compartment syndrome occurred. Mosch and colleagues offer the series as practical guidance for a rare injury that youth sports are making more familiar.
plos-pone-0356058:
Liang He and co-authors tested whether plant and plastic fibres can protect swelling soil in regions with hard winter freezing. Expansive soil swells and shrinks with moisture, and freeze-thaw cycles damage it further. Their 2026 study mixed polypropylene and lignin fibres into such soil and ran swelling, strength, and freezing tests.

Lignin fibre alone performed best overall, cutting swelling most and raising shear strength most. Adding polypropylene fibre on top improved strength further. After repeated freeze-thaw cycles, the mixed-fibre soil lost far less strength than untreated soil. Microscope images showed fibres bridging and overlapping inside the soil, which explains the gains. The authors present fibre mixing as a practical fix for building on difficult ground.
plos-pone-0356258:
Yuling Cui and co-authors developed a freeze-dried DNA profiling kit. It removes forensic testing's dependence on freezers. Their 2026 paper describes a six-color fluorescent reagent. It covers twenty-nine identity markers plus a sex marker. The mix is engineered with a hardy enzyme and protective additives. So the dried reagent survives at room temperature. It wakes instantly when water is added.

In validation, the kit detected full profiles from tiny DNA amounts. It stayed stable for two months on the shelf. It also tolerated common contaminants. Head-to-head against liquid reagents, it matched identification rates exactly. It handled trace samples better. A pocketable, ready-to-use kit could bring reliable DNA identification to crime scenes, disaster zones, and small rural laboratories.
plos-pone-0356358:
Guoqin Wang and colleagues sifted blood gene data from heart attack patients for genes where two destructive processes meet: macrophage-driven inflammation and ferroptosis, an iron-dependent form of cell death. Their 2026 bioinformatics study merged two public datasets, corrected the batch differences between them with unusual care, and published this as a revised analysis with tightened false-positive controls.

Seven candidate genes survived the intersection, and five were confirmed raised in follow-up laboratory tests. Whole-genome pattern checks pointed at inflammatory and oxidative stress programs, and immune signatures shifted most clearly for neutrophils. Because the candidate network proved too sparse for hub claims, the authors present the seven as prioritized leads for heart attack biology rather than established drivers.
plos-pone-0356758:
Zhengyao Che and colleagues surveyed 305 women undergoing IVF treatment at a hospital in Yunnan, China, about their sexual function, a side of fertility care clinics seldom ask about. Their 2026 study scored function with a standard index, measured psychological distress, and used latent profile analysis to let natural patient groupings emerge rather than imposing cutoffs.

Three groups appeared: about a fifth with low function, two fifths in the middle, and the rest doing well. Younger, better-educated, and more distressed women clustered in the middle group, city residents in the good group, and longer infertility with more past pregnancies predicted the low group. The profiles give clinics a screening shortcut for an intimate problem that quietly strains couples already under treatment stress.
plos-pone-0357158:
Wenjie Sun and co-authors build a repeatable traffic monitoring workflow for highways that lack road sensors, testing it on a Sarawak stretch of the Pan Borneo Highway, in Malaysian Borneo. Probe data from navigation platforms can fill the gap if handled carefully. Their pipeline collects platform car data on a schedule, cleans it by fixed rules, stores it, computes pressure indicators, and cross-checks one platform against another over an overlapping month.

One platform's panel stayed available nearly all the time and caught a repeated evening pressure build-up at the same hour. The two platforms told similar stories at matched times and places. Sun and colleagues caution that probe data is not ground truth, but argue it can keep sparse corridors under steady watch.
plos-pone-0357258: Xu, writing alone, published a 2026 PLOS ONE study on keeping coal mine roadways dry and safe. The work searches for the best settings for roadway supports that block water. The search used an algorithm the author calls FFA. Getting support design right guards miners from flooding and roof falls. The study speaks to engineers who plan supports in wet ground conditions.
plos-pone-0357458:
Jianqi Guo and Yingmei Qu compare two kinds of academic English writing in a 2026 language study. One set comes from Chinese students training as translators, and the other from native English academic writers. Using two collections the authors built themselves, they measured sentence build with a standard software tool that tracks clause and phrase patterns.

Trainee writing leaned on longer clauses, joined phrases, and heavy noun groups, while native writing used more layered clauses packed into each unit. The groups differed clearly on most of the measures tested. Guo and Qu link the gap to second-language growth, pressure from the source text, and translation habits, and they point teachers toward training that builds clause-level skill.
plos-pone-0357658:
Masanori Nakajo and colleagues test whether an advanced CT measure can grade worn spinal disks without relying only on standard scans. Disk wear is the most common source of low back pain, and MRI grading is the usual reference. In about one hundred patients who had both scan types, the team measured several signals in the disk's tough rim and soft center across several hundred lumbar disks.

Plain CT values and the new density measure moved in opposite directions in rim and center as MRI wear grades rose. The gap in density between front rim and center tracked wear grade most strongly of all. Nakajo and colleagues say spectral CT density could help grade disk wear when MRI is unavailable or unclear, adding a quantitative option to routine spine imaging.
plos-pone-0357758:
Nazia Fairooz Alam led a team of eight authors designing a vaccine candidate on the computer, published in PLOS ONE in 2026. Human metapneumovirus is a lung virus with no vaccine yet. The team used reverse vaccinology and pan-genomic methods to predict a candidate built from multiple epitopes, the parts of the virus the immune system recognizes.

Alam's in silico design gives vaccine developers a concrete head start instead of a blank page. Computer prediction cannot prove a vaccine works; it narrows the search to designs worth making and testing. Pan-genomic input helps the candidate cover many virus strains at once. For a virus that burdens children and older adults each winter, a faster start matters.
plos-pone-0357958:
Guangjun Liu led a team of five authors designing a lean part for vision models, published in PLOS ONE in 2026. Attention modules help a model focus on the right parts of an image, but they usually add parameters that cost memory and speed. Their module, PSAFM, fuses features across space with attention, yet adds no parameters at all.

Liu's parameter-free design boosts accuracy without the usual bloat, making it cheap to drop into existing networks. Small models for phones and cameras benefit most, since every parameter counts there. A part that improves many models, rather than one bespoke system, spreads its value widely. The study is a reminder that clever structure can beat brute size in machine learning design.
plos-pone-0358258:
Micah Vinet and seven colleagues wrote this 2026 PLOS ONE research article on eye diagnosis. It presents software that automatically measures the thickness of the cornea's central surface layer, the epithelium. The purpose is diagnosing limbal stem cell deficiency, a failure of the cells that renew the cornea's surface.

When limbal stem cells fail, the cornea clouds and vision suffers, yet the condition is hard to measure by eye alone. Automated thickness readings could make diagnosis more objective and repeatable between clinics. Corneal specialists evaluating surface disease are the readers who would use such measurements in practice.
plos-pone-0358558:
Jing Yang, Zhenqing Li, and Yoshinori Yamaguchi studied in 2026 whether teaching by outcomes makes engineering students more skilled. The approach is called outcome based education. It plans a course backward, from the skills students should be able to show at the end, rather than forward from a list of topics. Their test bed was a course on intelligent control, a hard subject about smart control systems.

The team used mixed methods, joining test scores and skill checks with what students and teachers said about the course. Book learning alone does not prove skill in such a subject, so the checks asked students to do real tasks. If planning by outcomes builds real skill here, the case grows for using it across engineering degrees.
plos-pone-0358858: Tufael and seven co-authors published a 2026 PLOS ONE study on how insulin resistance may help liver cancer grow. Part of the work is computer-based, modeling how a protein called IRS-1 meets the core protein of hepatitis C virus, genotype 3. The virus and insulin resistance often occur together. If the link holds, it could explain part of the cancer risk carried by infected patients.
plos-pone-0358958: Bíl and four co-authors published a 2026 PLOS ONE study on road deaths in Czechia across more than five decades. Autopsy records from 1969 to 2024 covered people killed while walking, cycling, or otherwise unprotected. The title reports that these deaths come with greater trauma than other road deaths. Long records like these show whether safety laws and car design have truly protected the most exposed road users.
plos-pone-0359158:
Madeline Fernandez-Pineda and five colleagues study what miscarriage care felt like during the COVID-19 pandemic, in a 2026 PLOS ONE article. Pandemic rules kept support people out of clinics and disrupted appointments, adding strain to an already painful loss. The authors combined surveys and interviews to capture both the numbers and the women's own accounts of that period.

Seventy-one women in North Carolina who miscarried during stay at home mandates took part, and eighteen gave long interviews. About half rated their care experience as poor. Pandemic hardships such as missing support persons were similar across groups, but women with poor experiences reported clearly higher stress, anxiety, and depression. Among those treated with medicine or surgery, a good care experience went together with lower distress.
plos-pone-0359858:
Álvaro Huerta Ojeda and eight colleagues wrote this 2026 PLOS ONE research article on aging and function. It studies community-dwelling older adults, people living in their own homes rather than care facilities. The authors examine the association between the muscle quality index and the time needed to rise from lying face down to standing.

Rising from the floor is a real-world test of strength that matters after a fall. A muscle quality index condenses how much force muscle produces for its size. If the index tracks floor-rise time, clinicians gain a simple screen for older adults losing independence, and exercise programs gain a target.
plos-pone-0360158:
Johannes Aengenheyster, Olav Velthuis, and Alex van Venrooij examined in 2026 what the private museums of wealthy economic elites contribute to the arts. Rich collectors increasingly open museums of their own rather than only donating to public ones. The authors ask whether these institutions are mere bandwagons, fashionable copies of one another, or genuine breeding grounds for artistic innovation.

Their study weighs what private museums add: new exhibition space, support for living artists, and public access to collections that would otherwise stay hidden. It also weighs the concerns, including private taste shaping public culture. The question matters for cultural policy, since cities court such museums while public institutions compete with them for art and attention.
plos-pone-0360658:
Wei Li, Ming Ma, and Jinyue Lu studied in 2026 how the Chinese public judged a cultural heritage scandal across different online platforms. The controversy concerned artifacts donated to the Nanjing Museum and how they were handled. The authors used topic modeling, a computational method that finds themes in large volumes of text, to map what people actually talked about on each platform.

Public judgment in a heritage crisis shapes whether a museum keeps the trust that brings donors and visitors. Comparing platforms shows how the same facts become different stories in different online rooms. Their study offers museums and cultural agencies a method for listening during a crisis, and a record of how this one unfolded.
pmc-13241458:
Kim at Bonn tackles the counting rules behind Whittaker functionals for the general linear group. These functionals anchor the wave analysis of principal series representations. Kim supplies a plain formula for a two-way map on each Schubert cell. Matrix splittings grow markedly simpler under the new map.

Using it yields a fresh proof that Whittaker functionals exist for principal series of real groups. Step-by-step integrating does the heavy lifting. This first part proves the map's counting traits and helper lemmas. The groundwork is laid plainly for the sequel's group-theory arguments.
pmc-13241958:
Vargas-Fernández and Hernández-Vásquez in Lima give Peru its first national portrait of teenage vaping. The 2024 national school survey covered over forty-five thousand urban secondary students. Ever use, recent use, current use, and dual use with cigarettes were weighted. Access routes and motivations for use were tallied too.

Sixteen percent had tried e-cigarettes; about seven percent currently used them. Girls started earlier than boys and reported higher ever use. Corner stores sold to nearly a third of users despite regulations. Flavor led the stated motivations, ahead of curiosity and stress relief.
pmc-13242358:
Cronin's team across four lands built a reflection framework for nurses crossing menopause. It collides with care loads, shifting family roles, and workplace demands. Many women describe feeling alone and threats to who they are. The team blended known thoughtful practice models with studies of the change.

Their MIRROR Cycle packages diaries, reflective guidance, Schwartz rounds, structured debriefs, and calm focus. Stigma, silence, split services, and workplace ageism compound distress in the change. Placing this practice in schools, clinics, and policy may help nurses cope and stay. The goal is workplaces that understand the change, not private silent struggle.
pmc-13243758:
Ruonan Li and colleagues asked whether body weight predicts the headache that can follow a lumbar puncture. Their cross-sectional study appeared in the Journal of International Medical Research in 2026. They reviewed 499 Chinese adults who had the procedure in a neurology department between 2022 and 2024. Sixty-five patients, about one in eight, developed the characteristic headache, and nearly two-thirds of them were women.

Those with headaches were younger and, on average, leaner than those without. They also ran lower blood pressure and lower spinal fluid protein, and had more fluid withdrawn. Statistical models confirmed that lower body mass index raised the odds of headache on its own. The link held steady across sex, age, and fluid subgroups. The authors advise weighing body mass in risk checks before the procedure and in care afterward. A cross-sectional snapshot cannot prove cause, they note.
pmc-13245058:
Felix Jimenez-Rondan, Courtney Ruggiero, Robert Cousins, and co-authors trace how losing a zinc transporter floods the mouse gut with mucus and a mucus-eating microbe. Their study appeared in Gut Microbes in 2026. Zip14 normally rises during inflammation and pulls zinc into gut lining cells. Mice lacking it entirely accumulated excess intestinal mucus and excreted strikingly more Akkermansia muciniphila, a bacterium that feeds on mucus.

Gene and chromatin studies explained why. Two mucus-building genes, including the main mucin Muc2, were switched up because their DNA sat in an open, readable state tied to the inflammatory factor NF-κB. The whole picture proved reversible. Either pasteurized Akkermansia or a single zinc feeding calmed the microbe surge, the inflammation, and the mucus genes. The authors conclude that zinc delivery through Zip14 keeps mucus production in check. The work ties a metal transporter to the gut's microbial balance.
pmc-13248058:
Lin, Song, and Li updated the evidence on high-flow nasal oxygen after surgery in this 2026 systematic review and meta-analysis. Patients recovering from anesthesia often run low on oxygen, and high-flow nasal cannula, warm, fast oxygen through nasal prongs, is widely used, but earlier reviews disagreed on whether it prevents reintubation. The team pooled twenty-five randomized trials with over four thousand patients comparing it against conventional oxygen therapy.

Reintubation rates did not differ significantly overall. The high-flow approach did cut lung collapse and low-oxygen episodes clearly. Certainty of the evidence was graded low to moderate. The authors' practical warning stands out: high-flow oxygen is a comfort and oxygenation tool, not a rescue, and its use must never delay stepping up to stronger ventilation support.
pmc-13249058:
Coskun and colleagues asked whether blood transfusions dull immunotherapy in melanoma, in a 2026 Turkish study. Fifty-seven patients with metastatic skin melanoma received nivolumab as second-line treatment between 2018 and 2023. Transfusions can calm the immune system, which might undercut a drug whose job is to unleash it, so the team compared survival by transfusion history.

Patients who received red cell transfusions during their metastatic phase lived shorter and progressed sooner than those who did not. Transfusion joined brain spread and shorter drug exposure among the markers of poorer outcome. The authors suggest viewing transfusion as a factor doctors can sometimes limit, while noting their small, backward-looking design.
pmc-13249758:
Karangeli and a Greek team mapped how the neck's great arteries sit beside the voice box cartilage, in a 2026 anatomy study. Surgeons use the thyroid cartilage as a landmark, and its upper horn lies close to the carotid arteries, sometimes uncomfortably so. The team measured two hundred fourteen CT angiograms, recording where the carotid fork falls relative to that horn and the gaps between vessel and cartilage.

The fork sat above the horn's level in nearly nine of ten sides. The common carotid artery hugged the cartilage closest, a few millimeters away on average, with the two branches progressively farther. Eleven relationship patterns were cataloged, led by one dominant layout. The authors propose the classification for clearer scan reporting and safer surgical planning.
pmc-13249858: Wang and colleagues issued this correction in Scientific Reports in 2026 for their randomized trial of pulsed radiofrequency treatment on the dorsal root ganglion for battered sensory nerve syndrome. A single word was misspelled throughout the original article: the syndrome's name appeared as battered sensory never syndrome, in the title, abstract, and text. The correction restores nerve in every place, and the journal has updated the article. No methods, results, or conclusions are affected.
pmc-13249958:
Hamed and an Egyptian team profiled the chemistry of three sage species, in a 2026 Scientific Reports study. Salvia plants are rich in compounds that fight inflammation, a process tied to most cancers. Using high-resolution mass spectrometry and molecular networking, the team cataloged the metabolite mix of each species, then docked two hundred eighteen compounds against two cancer-relevant protein targets in the computer.

Network analysis tied the chemistry to hub genes in inflammation and antioxidant pathways. One species, Salvia multicaulis, carried most of the promising compounds, and its extract switched on a protective enzyme in a liver cell cancer-prevention model while suppressing inflammatory nitric oxide in immune cells. The authors nominate it for drug development work.
pmc-13250258:
Rohman and colleagues fine-tune a method for pulling healthy plant compounds from green mango peel. Their 2026 Food Science and Nutrition study treats the peel, a common processing waste, as a source of phenolic compounds with antioxidant power. Ultrasound-assisted extraction was adjusted for time, temperature, and alcohol strength using a structured experimental design.

Seventeen test runs fed statistical models that predicted phenolic yield, free-radical scavenging, and reducing power with strong accuracy. All three settings mattered, and the best balance landed near thirty-six degrees, twelve minutes, and a little over half alcohol in the mix. Lab checks at those settings matched the predictions closely. The authors present the method as a green way to turn fruit waste into useful ingredients.
pmc-13250458:
Farhangiyan and co-authors compare pancreas attacks triggered by very high blood fats with attacks from other causes. Their 2026 Health Science Reports study reviews three hundred patients admitted to one Iranian hospital between 2020 and 2025. Half had pancreatitis driven by high triglycerides, and half formed the comparison group.

The fat-driven group was younger and heavier, scored worse on every severity scale used, and stayed in hospital nearly twice as long. Complications such as lung failure, sepsis, kidney failure, and dead pancreatic tissue all came more often in that group. No patient in either group died during the hospital stay. The authors urge early recognition of this subtype, while noting that their single-center design limits certainty.
pmc-13251158:
Lee and co-authors show that diabetes rewires the brain and blood long before injury, then sabotages repair. Their 2026 Molecular Brain study injures a deep brain region in diabetic mice and compares healing with healthy controls using high-field MRI scans. Diabetes is a known risk factor for poor recovery after brain injury.

Diabetic mice developed larger initial lesions and recovered more slowly, even when starting lesion size was matched. Gene readings from uninjured diabetic brains already showed weakened synapse and skeleton pathways. After injury, their blood immune cells and brain-infiltrating cells carried altered programs, and support-cell activation faltered. The authors argue this pre-set reprogramming explains much of the extra harm diabetes causes after injury.
pmc-13251758:
Feng, Luan, and Zhu measure a sugar-binding protein, galectin-1, in mothers whose babies grew too slowly in the womb. Their 2026 International Journal of Women's Health study compares thirty early-onset and thirty late-onset growth restriction cases with thirty normal deliveries at one Chinese hospital. Blood, placenta, and membrane samples were all tested.

Blood levels of galectin-1 ran higher in both growth restriction groups than in controls, highest in early-onset cases. Inside the placenta the pattern flipped: gene activity for the protein fell, while stained protein deposits rose. Routine traits like age and body mass did not differ between the groups. The authors propose galectin-1 as a candidate marker for this condition, especially its early form.
pmc-13251858:
