Chrysovalantou Xirouchaki and a large team link a muscle enzyme to ageing in this 2026 study. Exercise switches on a protective stress-response system in muscle, steered by a master protein, and that protection fades with age.

The enzyme NOX4, which makes small amounts of reactive oxygen in working muscle, turned out to feed that protective switch. Its levels fell in aged mice and humans. Mice lacking it in muscle aged badly, with wasting, frailty, weight gain, and liver disease. Restoring the enzyme, or switching the downstream system on with a broccoli-derived compound, brought the exercise-like protection back. The findings frame one way exercise keeps ageing at bay.
pmc-13252758:
Jonathan Santana and a large team excavate an island fish-processing site in this 2026 archaeology paper. Playa Chica, on Gran Canaria in the Canary Islands, holds five layers of Indigenous occupation from the 6th to the 13th centuries, left by communities of North African origin.

Focusing on the last phase, the team combined shell, bone, seed, and charcoal evidence. Shellfish and sea urchins dominated, with fish remains, crustaceans, and crowds of fish scales pointing to heavy on-site processing. Goat horn tools and pig-tooth hooks, smoke-friendly fuels, and 29 hearths suggest drying or smoking fish for storage. The site likely fed exchange networks between coast and inland.
pmc-13253658:
Led by Alessandra Giuliani, a 2026 study tests how well trauma memories can be read in young people. The team pooled data from 407 trauma-exposed youth aged 6 to 17 in South Africa and the United Kingdom. One month after the event, each youth told their story and rated their own memory and stress signs.

Self-ratings of memory quality linked clearly to post-traumatic stress signs in both countries. By contrast, scores drawn from the told stories, such as how ordered or sense-rich they were, did not match self-ratings. Those story scores also failed to predict stress signs, so the authors favor self-report for care.
pmc-13253758:
Supaporn Suwanchote and Phatcharawat Chirasuthat report a 2026 case of skin infection after cosmetic filler shots. A 27-year-old woman with no prior illness had firm red lumps along her jawline for 11 months. The lumps began one month after hyaluronic acid filler, a gel used to shape the face, plus other shots in the same session.

Common antibiotics and an enzyme shot did not help her. Tests pointed to Nocardia nova, a soil bacterium, which the authors call the first known case of this skin disease after filler. The paper also reviews other cosmetic cases to warn clinics about slow, odd infections.
pmc-13254758:
Sarah Bennett and a large team ask teens about a sleep app in a 2026 interview study. Sleep Solved was co-created with adolescents from underserved groups in the United Kingdom to improve sleep. Sixty-three participants aged 16 to 18 tried the app and then gave interviews.

Teens saw the app as useful, with clear advice on changeable habits. They praised its reward system, easy-read sleep hacks, and calm level of science, and rated it more trustworthy than social media advice. Many reported better routines, longer sleep, and improved mood and energy, though sleep was not measured by devices.
pmc-13258758:
Keita Murakawa and colleagues explore why people with asthma move so little. Not all activity is equal, so they split daily movement by intensity in this 2026 study. Twenty-nine asthma patients and fourteen healthy volunteers wore through lung tests, walk tests, and activity tracking.

Patients moved less than volunteers at every intensity level. Age and other illnesses best explained shortfalls in moderate-to-vigorous effort. Asthma severity and airway problems, by contrast, limited lighter daily movement. A ratio drawn from the six-minute walk, mixing distance with oxygen dips, flagged real-life inactivity well. The authors suggest different levers for different activity levels.
pmc-13260158:
Alessandro Vanoli leads a 2026 multicenter case series and literature review of neuroendocrine tumors of the gallbladder and cystic duct. Neuroendocrine tumors arise from hormone-producing cells and are rarely found in the gallbladder. Registry data had suggested these tumors behave very aggressively. The team analyzed twenty-six cases in detail, including tumor size, grade, shape under the microscope, and hormone staining, and reviewed seventy-nine published cases.

Their cases were typically small incidental tumors, with a median size of 0.8 centimetres, and eighty-one percent were grade 1, the slowest type. None had spread, and all twelve patients with follow-up were alive without disease after a median of thirty months. Cholesterol polyps and cholesterol deposits were commonly associated. In the wider literature, tumors over two centimetres and grade 3 tumors were enriched among cases that had spread.
pmc-13260258: Martin Schlager and colleagues published a 2026 correction notice for their paper on the western corn rootworm, a beetle pest, and its attraction to floral scent compounds from oil pumpkin. The correction lists changes the published paper needs. They include capitalizing the title in a new form. They change the first sentences of the abstract and introduction to lower-case wording for the species name. They also fix a methods sentence about comparing mass spectra and retention data with published sources.
pmc-13260458:
Muhammad Umar and co-authors present a 2026 review of new treatment plans for osteoarthritis, a wear-and-tear joint disease affecting over five hundred million people. Osteoarthritis is now seen as a whole-joint disorder, with changes across cartilage, bone, ligaments, and joint lining. Standard drugs such as anti-inflammatory medicines and steroid injections often fail to stop its advance or restore function. The review integrates clinical and pre-clinical evidence on therapies aimed at the disease process itself.

Covered approaches include repair therapies, targeted anti-inflammatory agents, and senolytic or senomorphic drugs, which remove or calm aged, harmful cells. The authors map unresolved gaps in causes and in how patient subgroups differ. They outline a path toward precision medicine, matching treatments to patient types, meaning observable disease patterns. Such disease-modifying therapy, they argue, remains the field's central unmet goal.
pmc-13260858:
Elizabeth Crull leads a 2026 methods study on using electronic health records to build a research cohort of pregnant people in the United States Gulf South. Pregnancy spells are hard to pull cleanly from health record data. The team built a rule-based tool using standard clinical coding systems, applied to records set in a common data model between July 2016 and June 2023. They then summed up the resulting cohort and ran simple maternal health measures as a proof of concept.

The method found 74,480 pregnant people linked to 95,503 pregnancies. Median maternal age was twenty-nine, and 80.1 percent of episodes ended in live birth. Preterm birth was 12.8 percent, gestational diabetes 9.1 percent, and high blood pressure disorders 24.2 percent of episodes. Severe maternal illness occurred at 179 per ten thousand deliveries, with 51.1 percent of those births involving non-Hispanic Black patients, which underlines regional gaps the dataset can help study.
pmc-13262958:
Khashayar Farzam reviews how to tailor injectable testosterone treatment in primary care in a 2026 journal article. The treatment serves men with confirmed low testosterone, a condition called hypogonadism. Short-acting forms can make blood levels surge soon after an injection and sag before the next, causing symptoms to cycle. The review argues the injection interval deserves as much thought as the dose.

Diagnosis must rest on symptoms plus repeated morning blood tests, Farzam stresses, not on fatigue alone. Every-two-week dosing is handy but should not be automatic; weekly dosing often steadies levels. Splitting the same weekly dose into smaller, more frequent shots can help men whose symptoms still swing. If weekly dosing is stable, extra injections add burden without clear gain.
pmc-13263358:
Christian Wolfram and co-authors report a 2026 journal article on sealing stubborn lymph leaks in the groin after lymph node surgery. A fistula here is an abnormal channel draining lymph fluid for weeks. The treatment injects Lipiodol, an oily X-ray dye, into a lymph vessel in the foot so it reaches and plugs the leak.

Of 184 patients imaged between 2003 and 2023, thirty-five met the study criteria. The leak sealed without complications in twenty-two of them, about sixty-three percent, taking about seven days on average. Thirteen patients needed further procedures. Success did not depend on how much dye was injected or how much fluid drained beforehand.
pmc-13263758:
Sean Li and colleagues re-analyze a back pain trial to ask whether how treatment was delivered, not just whether, predicted success. The RESET trial's sixty-day nerve stimulation beat usual care for chronic low back pain. Their 2026 post-hoc study isolates patients who received the full intended protocol.

Proper delivery meant stimulating both sides of the spine, covering most of the painful region, for six to twelve hours daily. Patients treated that way had roughly triple the odds of halving their pain at three months. Ordinary clinical traits like age and pain duration predicted nothing. Switzerland's path into the World Court's elections was set by the Security Council on 28 September 1948. Switzerland had joined the Statute of the International Court of Justice under conditions the General Assembly laid down in December 1946. It had even accepted the Court's compulsory jurisdiction. With judge elections due, the Council had to recommend terms for states in Switzerland's position.

The Council recommended that a state party to the Statute but not a United Nations member stand equal with members in nominating candidates. Such a state would vote in the General Assembly for judges in the same manner as members. One bar applied: a state behind on its payments to the Court's expenses, by two full years or more, could not vote. The Assembly could excuse arrears caused by events beyond the state's control. The formula let Switzerland and later others join the Court's system without membership.

Keep a fresh list of ban-breakers and their backers. Send the sanctions group a mid-term and a last word. All states were told the ban still bound them in full. The team was urged to hone its list with care, for steps the Council might take later.

Senegal's path to this text ran through a failed federation. It had shared the short-lived Mali Federation with its neighbor. That union broke apart in August 1960. Senegal then applied for its own UN seat. Resolution 158 was adopted unanimously on 28 September 1960 at the 907th meeting.

The Council recommended that the General Assembly admit the Republic of Senegal. Admission came the same day in the Assembly, a rare same-day double. Senegal joined during the celebrated Year of Africa. Its first president, Léopold Senghor, became a leading voice of the new African bloc. The one-sentence resolution marks Senegal's formal entry onto the world stage.

Haiti had just held the first round of its elections on 7 February 2006, and on 14 February its stabilization mission, MINUSTAH, is extended until 15 August 2006. Haitians are congratulated on the successful vote. Municipal and local elections were still to come in April.

All Haitians are urged to keep taking part in the political process and accept its results peacefully. The mission's central role in supporting the remaining elections and Haiti's longer recovery is restated. The Secretary-General is asked to report soon on the situation, including how the mission should be shaped for the period after the new elected president took office.

A stalled settlement process shadows Resolution 1758 on Cyprus, adopted on 15 June 2007. The island stayed generally calm, though buffer-zone violations had risen. The 8 July 2006 Agreement, aiming at a bicommunal, bizonal federation with political equality, still had not been put into effect. Demining in the buffer zone had stalled, and housing for many UNFICYP troops was poor.

The Council extends the UN Peacekeeping Force in Cyprus, UNFICYP, until 15 December 2007. It says the status quo is unacceptable and time is not on the side of a settlement. It calls on both sides to engage at once, show measurable progress, and stop trading blame so full negotiations can begin. It asks the Turkish Cypriot side and Turkish forces to restore the earlier military position at Strovilia. Talks on the buffer zone, including the Ledra Street crossing, are urged. A report is due by 1 December 2007.

Burundi's integrated office, BINUB, is extended until 31 December 2009 on 22 December 2008. Heads of state of the Great Lakes region had met in Bujumbura on 4 December and agreed steps with the Palipehutu-FNL, the last rebel movement. Carrying out the 2006 ceasefire with that group was the main unfinished piece of Burundi's peace.

The government and the FNL are urged to carry out their December agreements before the end of 2008 and to settle the rest by dialogue, without any return to fighting. The FNL is called on to release child soldiers and join the disarmament process. BINUB would keep supporting peace consolidation, justice, and security reform while the final phase of the peace process closed.

Resolution 1958, passed on 15 December 2010, shuts down the last gears of Iraq's oil-for-food scheme. The scheme, born in 1995, was a stopgap under the bans on Iraq. It let Iraq sell oil to buy food and drugs for its people. It shut in form in 2003. Yet stray tasks dragged on for years: old credit notes with claims still live, as a UN note of that December set out in depth.

The Council told the UN chief to take all steps to end the scheme's last tasks for good. It noted that the stray credit notes had lapsed by their own terms. Two twin Iraq texts passed the same day. With them, the books closed on a huge relief plan, one later stained by fraud probes.

The situation in the Middle East kept getting worse after the 1967 war, and the Council spoke on 18 September 1968. Resolution 258 insisted that the cease-fire the Council had ordered must be strictly respected. It reaffirmed Resolution 242 of 1967, the landmark text on settling the conflict. That text called for Israeli withdrawal from occupied territories and for all states in the area to live in peace. All parties were urged to cooperate fully with the Secretary-General's special envoy, who was working to carry out that plan.

Cyprus was being torn apart in the summer of 1974. After a coup backed by Greece, Turkey had invaded, and fighting continued despite repeated Council demands to stop. Resolution 358, adopted unanimously on 15 August 1974, came one day after an earlier ceasefire order had been ignored, a failure the text openly deplores.

The members recalled their chain of Cyprus resolutions from July and August 1974 and insisted that all parties carry them out in full. Above all, they demanded immediate and strict respect for the ceasefire. The resolution is short, but its tone shows a Council losing patience with orders that were not being obeyed.

Cyprus's peacekeeping force was renewed once more on 14 December 1979, by Resolution 458. A report from the Secretary-General, dated 1 December, recommended six more months. The parties concerned agreed with the recommendation. Cyprus accepted that the force should stay beyond 15 December.

The Council extended the force's stationing to 15 June 1980. It voiced support for a ten-point agreement meant to restart the talks between the two communities. That agreement had been worked out at a high-level meeting in Nicosia in May 1979. The parties were urged to resume the talks without delay. The talks had to be steady and focused on results. The Secretary-General was to continue his mission of good offices and report by 31 May 1980.

Resolution 58, adopted on 28 September 1948, sorts out how Switzerland can help choose World Court judges without joining the UN. Switzerland had met the Assembly's conditions and become a party to the court's statute, even accepting the court's compulsory jurisdiction. Elections for the court were coming at the next Assembly session, and the statute required the Council to recommend the terms for such states.

The Council recommended that a state in Switzerland's position stand on an equal footing with UN members in nominating candidates. It would vote in the Assembly on the same terms as members. One limit applied: a state behind on its payments toward the court's expenses could not take part in electing judges.
